DOROTHY. A little rogue, and mOther's pet, She cannot say her letters yet; And, full of fun, she seldom tries, With mischief dancing in her eyes! • Bat still our darling can behave As good as gold, and look as grave As if the business and the care ~Of all the State were laid on her. And she believes her friends are true, And good, and she will lave them too; And may she wear these graces long, • The faith anklove that thinks no wrong! •O happy child, what books can teach, Or lips of wisdom:strive to preach, That we may learn, from hearts like thine, To make these graces burn and shine! B.Etutwood,in" Little Folks" Magazine for February.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HPRTIi!„ CULTURE, &c.

The Plymouth Society of Cowkeepers' annual report has just been published. It shows that their members possess 177 cows, and that the last year's receipts were nearly .£lOO against an expenditure of £94, the losses of members during the year having been four animals only. The amount paid by each member averaged about ten shillings a cow, and even then a respectable balance was left to carry on to the next year. No one will deny that a man who can insure upon this mutual principle an animal which is to him of far greater value than to the large dairy is extremely foolish if he refrains from doing so. There should be such societies everywhere, more especially where small owners are ex- tremely numerous. A Ducar, LAND MONOPOL‘ST.—At Chilworth, in Surrey, the Duke of Northumberland holds two estates, the Albury and the Chilworth property. At Chilworth some industrial progress has been made until the village is too small for its inhabitants. Overcrowding is the danger to be feared. Application i made to the Duke, and supported by his agent, for the building of a dozen cottigesto meet the needs of a growing population. Will it be credited that so intel- ligent a landlord puts down his foot, forbids the growth of his own property, and lays down the hard and fast rule that, wholly irrespective of circumstances, no more houses are to be erected on his Chilworth estate. The region is on the very borders of his property ; bat he restrains its develop- ment ; and there are actually couples wishing to marry and seeking a house who are denied dwelling-places because of the mere whim of a ducal landlord. He has laid field to field, and gives no room to the people. Of course the natural consequences ensue. The public-spirited men in the neighbourhood are beginning to speak about the nationalisation of the land, and to send subscriptions to the Nationalisation League. And presently fhe Duke will wake up to find that the way in which he has used his property has made enemies to all forms of landed property.— Western Morning News. THE YIIILD OF CROPS IN 1383.—The collection of a number of returns from different of England enables the Mark Lane Express to give the following averages : Yield. Average per Acres. bushels. acre, bushels. Wheat Barley Oats Beans Peas

It is somewhat surprising to find the average yield in the case of every crop but beans above the corresponding ave- rage in the estimates published on August 20 and 27 last, when the estimates worked out as follows : Wheat. Barley. Oats Beans. Peas. 26 4 35.4 43 6 32 4 291 Most of the complaints have been about the wheat crop. and a number of very poor crops of that cereal are recorded in the returns. The mean average, however, has been greatly helped in an upward direction by the satisfactory returns from Essex and Suffolk especially, and by some ex- ceptionally high returns from parts of Kent, Hampshire, and other counties. One farmer in Essex obtained 2,760 bushels of wheat from 60 acres, or 46 bushels per acre all round. The same farmer's average for barley was 52 bushels per acre' and for oats 92 bushels. These are high averages for good land in a favourable season. From Hampshire one correspondent returns 42 bushels of wheat per acre, from Kent there is a return of 40 bushels, while from Suffolk there is a return of 56 bushels of Rivetts wheat per acre. Such figures as these go a long way towards making up for such low returns as 16 and 18 bushels per acre. LORD CARRINGTON AND ms TENANTS.—A Blackburn correspondent, a former tenant of Lord Carrington, kindly sends us an interesting cutting from a Buckinghamshire newspaper. It is a report of an annual dinner attended chiefly by tenant farmers. From the speeches made we get a glimpse of Lord Carrington discoursing pleasantly and profitably on farming at home and abroad, and honoured as a liberal and honourable landlord. He exhibited an ear of seven bearded wheat, which he had brought from America, Of which in some portions of the States a crop of 100 ibushels an acre was grown. The straw grew to the extra- ordinary height of Oft. 4in. In going through these great wheat fields one's first idea was "flow can we compete with such a wheat-raising country ?" Now he thought that in bad seasons they were apt to look too much to the black side of things. Wheat was certainly low, but he got £ll a load for his—(a voice: "You're a favourite, my lord)—well,,the purchaser told him he would buy a lot more at the price: If they could get •£ll a load for wheat, and could grow enongh of it, they must not be down-hearted because they had seven or eight bad seasons. If they only had a few good seasons and luck with their stocks, and could keep out the dreadful foot and mouth disease, he did not see why they should lose heart or resort to any of the desperate remedies sometimes ,advocated. In agriculture there was a, division of profits— there was the rent the landlord lived on and the profit the farmer lived on. If the profits witless rents must go down. There was a margin for the landlord tp live as well as the tenant, and he was sure there was sufficient good feeling among the farmers of England to make them wish not to drive hard bargains with the landlords. Their great wish was that expressed in the motto, "Live and let live." His lordship then described a settler's farm in Dakota. WESTMORLAND SHEEP.—The sheep on the mountain runs , of Weatmorland, Cumberland, and Northern Lancashire are known as Herdwicks. There does not appear ;to be any reliable testimony as to their introduction. One version is that a sheep-laden vessel was wrecked on the Cumberland coast; that the sheep swam ashore, took to the mountains, and' thus established a hardy breed of sheep, for certainly neither the horned Scotch nor the Cheviots could live where do the Herdwicks. In colour they are black and mottled grey; the fleece is coarse, but fairly long, and sells at the present rates of wool at from sd. to 6d. per lb. The valley farms have, as a rule, an unlimited right of pasturage on the nearest mountain, and the flocks range from 100 up to 1,000. Some years ago a very useful book was published with illustrations, showing the ear marks of each farm. As the sheep range the mountains:without enclosure, a know- ledge of the various ear marks enables each farmer not only to select his own sheep, but to recognise stray sheep from other flocks. The rams and the wethers are horned, but the ewes are not. Those for the butcher are drawn at from three to four years old, and they average 81bs. up to 15lbs. per quarter, when in what we may call a state of nature; but from prize flocks we have known them make 251b5. per quarter. Rams from prize flocks make from £5 to £lO each. During recent years a good deal of crossing has been done with Leicester and long-woolled rams, but the produce cannot exist on the mountain tops; they are kept on the lower slopes. The Herdvricks are locally spoken of as Fell sheep, and it is a common saying that a leg of Fell mutton is a joint at for a king, so sweet is the mountain-fed mut- ton. When sold to the butcher they average about £1 each, of recent years a shilling or two more. At clipping time they are brought down from the mountains- and it is at these times that the value of the shepherd's dog is shown, for the men could never oollect the sheep. The sagacity of the dogs in knowing their own sheep is something wonder- ful, and 80 is the knowledge of the shepherds themselves. COMPETITION FOR DAIRY FARM RECORDS.—We have received from the British Dairy Farmers' Association the following conditions of entry for the £5O Challenge Cup offered by Mr. Thomas Higgins, of Liverpool, for the best dairy farm record. The cup to be awarded for the best kept and most practically useful record, which shall show :- 1. The yield of milk for an entire herd of dairy cows not to number lees than ten, of any breed, for 12 consecutive months, from let Feb , 1884, to 31st Jan.. 1885. 2. The breed, age, date of last calving, and number of calves. 3. The value of the cows on the Ist Feb., 18S4, and 31st Jan., 1885. 4. The system of feeding, showing the kinds of food and vari- ations according to season, &a. 5. The gross quantity and cost of food and approximate cost per head. 6. The quantity of milk by weight on one entire day in each week, and the percentage of cream after 24 hours' setting in the' cream tube. 7. The quality of the milk to be ascertained ones a month, by analysis or other means. 8. How the milk is disposed of, whether sold by wholesale or etatl, or made into butter, cheese. &O. legehotnodfiteioacuhtocobewenattirtehlye 9, The amount of returns therefrom. beginning lO ( . iad a nwdh eenndporfalcateict: lactation, optional. , tbhuet twhel 11. A balance-sheet for the period. 12. The records to be the property of the Association, who shall accordingly have the power to publish the whole or any part thereof. The record and valuation of the cows must be approved and signed by the nearest available dairy farmer, or neighbour, who is conversant with the systems pursued by the competi- tor. Competitors are at liberty to adopt any form of record which they think proper, provided that they give the in- formation asked for, and they may give any further information which they think useful to explain their sys- tem of dairy farming. The system of recording the results will be examined by an officer of the Association at (limb dairy farm and reported thereon. In pairing the awards the judges will be instructed to select those returns which are not burdened with elaborate detalla and which are best adapted for the keeping of accounts. The entry fee for mem- bers of the Association is Li lie. 6d., and for non-members £2 25., which sum will include the expenses of inspection. Records must be sent to the Secretary, Mr. Fred Morrison, 191, Fleet-street, E.O , as soon as possible after the let February, 1885, attested in the following form :—"I hereby enter my Dairy Farm Record in competition, subject to the conditions made by the Council of the British Dairy Farmers' Association, and I declare that the particulars con- tained therein are correct." ALLOTMENTS FOR FARM Laßouuvas.—The question of allotments for farm labourers is dealt with in a very inter- esting manner by the Rev. C. W. Stubbs, in the "Land and the Labourers," a book just published by Messrs. W. Swan Sonnenschein and Co., of Paternoster Square. It is, as its sub-title states, a record of facts and experiments in cottage farming and co-operative agriculture." The prejudice still existing among too many landowners and farmers against allowing farm labourers to have a bit of land to cultivate is much to bi regretted. If there is any person to whom you feel a dislike, that is the person of whom yeti ought never to speak. Somebody advertises in one of the Westfield papers for a servant girl" who would not be above placing herself on an equality with the rest of the family." Nothing is more expressive than penuriousness ; nothing more anxious than carelessness ; and every duty which is bidden to wait returns with seven fresh duties at its back.— .Kingsleu. A man should hear a little music, read a little poetry, and see a fine picture every day of his life, in order that the worldly cares of life may not blot out the sense of the beau- tiful implanted by God in the 5001.—Goethe. "Waiter, take away this soup; it's as cold as ice."—" Oh, you must be mistaken, sir! I Voted it as I was bringing it, and it's nice and hot, sir."—" Tasted it !"—" Oh, no, sir ! Beg pardon, sir, I wouldn't think of doing such a thing, sir! I only just put my finger into it !" A French lady, on her arrival in this country, was careful to ..at only such:idishes as she W,14 acquainted with, and, being on one occasion pressed to pa, take of a dish new to her, she politely replied, thinking she was expressing herself In admirable English, "No, I thank you ; I eat only my acquaintances." WHAT LOLLIPOPS ARE MADE OF.—I EMI here repeat the teem,' of a discovery. One day I was passing a sugar house In the docks and saw a dozen casks filled with the nasty ffcrapings of the floor, which was greasy with escaped mo- lassss. "What are these for ?" I asked. "0, they goes to make lollipops, air," was the reply.—Good Words. JA/Cr.T Hastwron.—Janet Hamilton is, indeed, one of the most striking instances of self-culture on record. Never at school, taught to read by her mother at home, but not able to write until she was fifty years of age, when she formed a peculiatcaligraphy of her own, she yet shows a power of expression, a mastery of verse and of EnAish prose, which might well be the envy of writers with the best opportuni- ties of what is commonly called education. —Good Words,

AteciUT Tvaa.—Tyre, the Amsterdam, the London, the brew York of the ancient world, in other words the central city ofa universal commerce both by sea and land, consisted of two cities built, one on an island, half a mile from the coast, and the other on the mainland. The former was bounded by he rock on which it stood, and could never exceed two miles in circumference. The latter spread in every direc- tion, containing temples, fortresses, and aqueducts of great extent and splendour. Many centuries after its demolition by NebuclAdnezzar, the scattered ruins measured nineteen miles round, as we learn from Strabo and Pliny. Alexander the Great made use of these materials to build an enormous causeway, or isthmus, to the insular city when he was pre- paring to besiege it ; and yet the heaps were not sensibly diminished.—From "The Quiver" for February. THE Ontaisr OF THE ROYAL ACADzwg.—That Tenterden Steeplc was the cause of the Goodwin Sands does not seem at all mare strange than that the Foundling Hospital should have been in some sense the parent of the Royal Academy of Arts. Yet such was the case. Not long after the incor- poration of the society the present building was erected, as we have mentioned; but as its funds were not available for its decoration, many of the chief artists of the day generously gave pictures from their own easels for ihe decoration of its several apartments. In course of time these came to be shown to the public on application, and a small sum being charged for admission, they took their place among the sights of the metropolie. Ultimately they proved so attra- tive that their success suggested a combined exhibition of the works of artiste. This, as we have stated, first took shape in the rooms of the Society of Arts in the Adelphi, from which again the Royal Acaderay took its idea. Thus, within the walls of the Foundling the curious visitor may see the state of British art in the era immediately preceding the extension of the patronage of George 111. to Benjamin West.—Cassell's "Old and Nem London." WHAT Is Iscomn.—lt is not the capital, but the income, that we must put on the debit side; but what income? The gross receipts from any source is not the income, for it is only when we deduct from the total receipts of any given source the total cost of producing them that we arrive at the real income. The word "income" is often misleading. The same amounts of income, from lands, houses, consols, terminable annuities, commerce, manufacture, labour, or industry are, and mean, in reality, quite a different thing. Here are five persons nominally receiving £l,OOO each per annum. A has property £33,333 in consols, income £1,000; B has property £6,500 in long annuities, income4£l,ooo; C has property k 15,000 in houses, income £1,000; D has pro- perty £30,000 in land in England, income £1,000; E has property £lO,OOO in life annuities, income £l,OOO. The annual income is alike, but the capital how different, and why? The reason is that the proportion of expenses to be deducted from each description of income differs con- siderably, the number of years the income will last in each case is very different; and whilst in the case of consols the capital is never touched, in the case of terminable annuities the annual income includes part payment of capital. Hence the wake of all these varied incomes is very different at the money markets.—Leisure Hour. TEE ORIGIN OF PARAFFIN CANDLES.—I cannot help in- terpolating an anecdote as to how paraffin candles were thought of. This solid wax from tar has been discovered by Iteichenbach, but was so rare when I first became pro- fessor of chemistry that I was proud of having a quarter of an ounce in a bottle to show my students. One cold day Mr. Young called upon me with some Derbyshire petroleum, and asked me what I thought the solid crystals floating in it could be. I answered that they must be paraffin, and , naked whether he could not prepare sufficient for me to I make two candles. With these I lighted the desk on the lecture table of the Royal Institution, and pointed out that though the cost of these candles was more than 20s. each, yet bsfore long they would become the common candle of the country. This safe prophecy has long since been realised, for paraffin is now manufactured in thousands of tons annually.--Sir Lyon Playfair in "Good Words." THE WITHDRAWAL OF :THE SEA INTO THE EARTH'S Ismaroa.—There is good reason for believing, with Sae- mann, be Meunier, Frankland, and Sterry Hunt, that in the remote future of the earth the waters of the sea will be with. drawn into her interior. The process of withdrawal is in reality taking place even now. Enter any cavern, such as Kent's Hole in Devonshire, on the driest and hottest day, or even after weeks of dry weather, and you shall find the roof wet with the waters which have been slowly making their way from the surface, where they fell in the form of rain months before. \ "Throughout the,whole crust of the earth, except in a few Yspote where rain never falls, the same pro• one is going on all the time. Only a portion of the water, which thus falls on the earth, ever returns to the surface in the form of springs. Artesian wells show how slowly some of the strata of the earth permit water which has thus reached them to pass through; but: they show also how large a portion of the earth's waters are already beneath the surface. . . . It may well be that the amount ac- tually withdrawn from the sea surface in this way, and not . restored, does not produce a change of level of more than a foot in a thousand years. Still even that would involve a very important alteration in the aspect of the:earth in such periods of time as belong to a planet's history. A million years would reduce the sea•level by a thousand feet, and in a period of time, which cannot be reckoned long when com- pared with the vast periods of which the heavens and the earth speak to us, every trace of water would have disap- peared from the surface of the earth.—R. A. Proctor. in Good Words. THE SNARES AT THE Zoo.—Of the serpents at the Zoo it may be said that they "do nothing in particular and do it very well." They give little trouble. They are fed once a week (after the Gardens are closed), and even then some of them decline to eat. When, in the summer of 1883, they were taken out of their dingy old quarters, the re- moval, contrary to what might have been expected, was effected with considerable ease. One of the pythons dis- appeared for a night, but his keeper soon discovered the truant. Some years ago, when the Boas in the Jardine des Plantes, in Paris, were removed to a new dwelling, they were allowed to overfeed themselves. In their gorged con- dition they were as easy to handle as so many cables. The serpents at the Zoo are decent, dull, well-behaved animals, seldom offering any affront to the keepers, who, however, prudently do not give the venomous ones opportunity of sno wing their "spite." The lodgings in the reptile-house have all a shingle floor, partly to facilitate the movements of their occapants, but mainly to spread the heat more evenly. A slate door, for example, might become too hot. The snakes may generally be seen lying in a heap for warmth's sake, or stretched at length along the gravel, or coiled round a tree trunk or branch, or plunged up to their heads in water. Mot of them are very partial to water, anti on the! occasion of my visit the anaconda was lying in its tank shedding its skin. As a rule, the snakes in the Zoo have fl either been presented to the society or purchased. In 1877, however, a boa was born in the Gardens, and is now very tame. "A child might handle it," says the keeper. Con. finement does not seem to shorten their days, and one of the pythons has figured in the Regent's Park menagerie for fully twenty years. He is now a big lazy fellow. In October, 1883; a litter of poisonous snakes was born—an event of rare occurrence. The non-poisonous snakes, it may be added, are usually hatched from the egg.—" Little Folks"

I have a great many of my own, and I have tried the experiment with some really good labourers of giving them two acres each to:caltivate, The great difficulty in giv- ing labourers a quantity of land is that men cannot live really well upon two or three acres unless they earn wages besides. Bat certain men do it, and I have tried it on my own property' with great success. I have tried it with farm labourers; one works for me, and has never ceased to work for me all the time, and I do not find his labour less than before he had the two acres of land. The other three work for tenants, and I don't see any fault with them. I say this because I think those labourers who have a large quantity of land ought to be picked men, for it is not every labourer that is able to do his work and cultivate so much land." A plot of two acres is not enough for a man and his family to live on, independently of working for hire, and it is enough to spoil him for service uniler a large farmer. If a man is to have more than an acre, he should have enough to enable him to get a living; but from half an acre to an acre, ac- cording to the amount of help which his family can render, may be managed by an industrious man, especially if he can get it ploughed for him. Lord Henniker says it is hard to be compelled to take charity land away from a good tenant to let it to labourers. No doubt it is hard for the tenant; but there are plenty of large farms to be had, and there are not plenty of plots for labourers. The commons have been filched from the poor, and the Allotments Extension Act IS only a tardy and insufficient instalment of compensation for the monstrous abuses of the enclosure of common lands. Yet so persistent is the obstruction of local trustees, and even of the Charity Commissioners, to the operation of the Act, that Mr. Jesse Collings has felt compelled to organise an Allotments Extension Association to see that the provi- sions of the measure are enforced. TIIE " ROYAL'S" SECRETARY'S VISITS TO SILOS—The tour of inspection of upwards of a dozen silos, situated within a convenient circle in Yorkshire and Durham, orga- nised by Mr. H. M. Jenkins, the secretary of the Royal Agricultural Society, commenced on Monday week, and has been participated in by about fifty agriculturists on some days. The gentlemen comprising the party were most courteously received by the proprietors of the various silos, and all the information sought for on matters of detail was readily forthcoming. The Pepper-Arden Silo, belonging to Mr. W. Stobart, J.P., was visited on Monday. Although Mr. Stobart believes that ordinary buildings may be utilised as silos, his first two pits do not partake of this character. They are approached on one side several feet above the top, and upon the opposite side there is a level sufficiently low to effectually drain the pit floor. There is also a doorway from which the ensilage can be taken out as required. In these two silos the material deposited weighed 120 tons; The ensilage in one of the pits is cut down in sections; and on the upper surface lay the weights beneath which were thin scantling boards. Along the edges of the latter, strips of sheet zinc protected the aperture and excluded the at- mosphere, while about an inch of bran had been placed on the top of the weighted fodder. The ensilage consisted of chopped grass, long clover, unchopped, prickly comfrey, tares, oats, Ac. On Tuesday morning a similar party an- sembled at the farm of Captain C. G. Johnson, Oaklands' Croft, Darlington. This gentleman's silos are buildings upon, instead of beneath the ground level, one of them be- ing an old shed. The pressure per square foot is reckoned at about 2001bs. PraCtical experiments are now being con- ducted with the view of testing the relative merits for feed- ing purposes of ensilage and ordinary food. Capt. Johnson ' believes that his ensilage costs less than hay. The sewage farm belonging to the Corporation of Darlington was next visited. The silo is in a portion of an old barn. Thirty- one tons of grass, from land which had never been sewaged, having been deposited in this silo, the whole Was pressed with about nineteen tons of weights, equalling about 147 pounds per square foot. At Bodnant, in Wales, Mr. H. D. Pochin, feeling convinced that the storage of green food will prove an important feature in British farming, has constructed two silos. Each silo measures 24 feet long, 9 feet wide, and 12 feet deep; the walls are 2 feet thick, and built strongly of stone and mortar, and lined with cement. A doorway 4 feet wide leads into each silo, and before being filled with grass both doorways were made up with railway sleepers and the joints filled up with clay and MOSEL A wall 2 feet separates the two silos. From August 110 to 20 both silos were filled with newly-cat grass, well trodden by heavy cart horses. A thin layer of straw was placed on the grass, and then old railway sleepers, laid cross- ways and closely packed together, were weighted with stones to the extent of 2001 b. per square foot. The usual amount of sinking and heating took place. The highest tempera- ture registered was 120 deg. The...pits have been opened, and the results were most satisfactory. The silos will be capable of holding about 70 tons of valuable fodder. The ensilage weighs 5211 b. per cubic foot —On Tuesday, Dr. Fowlis, Cairnes Lodge, Caper, displayed his silo and ensil- age. The silo is simply dug out in a bank close by the steading. One end is flush with the ground, and the other end made up to the level, the soil excavated being used for that purpose, and the made-up portions being lined with a few battens. A drain 18 inches deep was laid below the floor, and 3 feet deep on each side to catch surface water. The silo is 14 feet long, 9 feet wide, and 7 feet deep. Clover aftermath was the substance used, and the silo contains 23 heaped cartloads, estimated to weigh a ton each. The dairy cows have used it since, and are very fond of it. The yield of milk has increased about 15 per cent., and the cows are in nice blpem. The quality of the butter is most excel- lent, equalling, if not surpassing, the very beat summer make, being rich in colour, soft in texture, and very pleasant , tasted. mere

The latest Yankee "notion" is zinc tombstones, which are now sold in New York at from five to twenty-five dollars each. These articles do not rust, are more durable than marble, will not chip easily, and will stand any climate. In a tramcar a man sitting by the side of a woman is struck with apoplexy. The car is stopped. They try to help him. He is dead. "When a man is subject to such acci- dents," said the woman, who was in a great hurry, "he should not get into the ears !"

Teacher John, what are your boots made of ?" "Of leather, sir." Teacher : "Where does the leather come from ?" Boy: "From the hide of the mt." 'reacher: "What animal, therefore, supplies you with boots and shoes, and gives you meat to eat ?" Boy: "My father." A gentleman in New Hampshire, U.S., keeps a brood of chickens in a part of his back yard. They are fed on moist- ened meal, in saucers, and when the dough gets a little soar it attracts a large number of flies. An observant toad noticed this, and every day towards evening he hops to a saucer, rolls over and over in the meal till he is all covered with it; then when the flies come swarming about he thrusts out his tongue and makes away with the unsuspi- cious insects.

Whymper in "Good Words." VOX POPOLI, VOX Dim—A story is going the rounds about the Democratic statesmen from Philadelphia, repre- sentatives Crawford and Mackie. Sponaler, the Constitu- tional orator of the House, was making a speech on the Revenue Commission Bill to regulate the assessment of mercantile taxes, and closed with the quotation:—" Vox vox del." Crawfard and Mackin had both been lis- tening with great admiration to Sponsler's rounded delivery, and Mackin, turning aside, cried to Crawford, "Al, wasn't that a fine climax ?" "Oh, it was grand!" replied the Eleventh Ward member. Mackin eyed Crawford sus- piciously for a moment, and then offered to bet ten dollars that he did not know what he said. "Pll take that," said Crawford; "of course I know what he said. It was ' War popu/i, war del," and it means 'My God, my God, why bast thou forsaken me ?" Mackin plunged his hand into his pocket, and meekly said, "There's the tanner, Al; didn't 'know you were such a good Latin scholar." COTTAGE GARDENING.

FRUIT TREES.—MR. GLADSTONE AND HIS CRITICS.— In consequence of the advanced state of apples and pears, it may be wise to take off some grafts and lay them in the ground in a shady place, so that the rays of the sun will not strike them. Others may be taken off about the end of the month and treated in a similar way. When gardeners speak of laying-in, what they mean is that the plants, or cuttings, are only temporarily placed in the soil, and they are usually placed obliquely. As the grafts are cut, they should be tied together, each sort separately, and 3in. or 4in. of the bottom placed in the ground mode- rately firm, till they are required in April for grafting. They are treated in this way with the view of retarding them, so that the stock may be in advance of them. Were it otherwise, the sap would not be sufficiently active to meet the excitable condition of the scion, and it would perish. The ,most successful instances of grafting large trees we have seen recently was at G. Dewhurst's, Esq., Clayton ' Green. Mr. Carne, the gardener, has operated oa several apple trees which he has proved worthless. We were so struck with their appearance during the autumn that we requested Mr. Carrie either to count or weigh the produce of one of those grafted three years last April. The variety was .Rylance Surprise, and this is the result-353 apples, weighing albs. The tree occupied about two square yards, and any one with a knowledge of tree growth will conclude that the branches cannot yet be very numerous with only two years' growth. Mr. Gladstone has been much ridiculed for advocating extended fruit culture in this country at the Hawarden rent audit. We heard one scornfully remarking, during the past week, "Let Mr. Gladstone come to Lanca- shire to grow fruit, and he would find out his mistake." Now, if we value the produce of the tree we have alluded to at 95.. or 3s. per score, an acre would realise over £9O. This is making two blades of grass grow instead of one. The apple is not a fruit tree one would select as the best for Lancashire, but we have seen samples during the season that were not far behind some from the reputed fruit-grow- ling counties. Mr. Rylance, of Ormskirk, had a collection at the Liverpool show which contained individual speci- mens as attractive as those from the best fruit-growing dis- tricts. Where can such gooseberries be grown as in Lan- cashire, and how seldom does the crop fail ? Currants, again, come fine and clean, and equally, if not more, certain than the gooseberries. The raspberry is always at home in a cool, moderately moist climate. We should like to know how often it fails. The strawberry is nearly always a cer- tain cropper, and only gives us anxiety at the time of gathering, if the season is wet. No, no, Mr. Scorner ; it is the landlords who prevent fruit being more extensively cultivated in Lancashire and elsewhere, and not the climate. THE FRONT Gaanex.—Weedy grass plots should now be seen to. Most weeds are destroyed by the use of a knife; if thrust in slantingly, the hearts may be severed and drawn away, and if any holes are made they should be filled, and the whole surface have a good beating with the back of the spade. During the past summer a correspondent inquired in The Guardian as to the best method of destroying weeds on a large lawn, and we gave the most suitable reply for the time of the year. Weeding, unless industriously pur- sued, is a delusion. For instance, if an odd daisy is left to flower it soon matures its seed, which, in the following year, will produce hundreds of plants. Watson's lawn sand will kill the plants for the time, but it is alleged that the weeds come up, if anything, stronger the following year. It is a mistake to think that they are parts of the one de: stroyed ; they are the produce of seeds, and as there is more space, on account of there being so many less weeds or other vegetation that may have been destroyed, the seedlings thrive all the aetter. If these remedial measures besome ultimately alders and abettors of the mischief, it is Cole we should seek more radical ones. We therefore propose to strike at the root of the matter, alias noxious weeds, in the following manner :—The turf should be skimmed evenly about 2in. thick, and in pieces a foot square, or in yard lengths and a foot wide, which can be rolled and unrolled at pleasure. Whichever dimension is selected, each piece as it is cut should be placed with the grassy side downwards, and we feel sure the weeds and their seeds will be innocuous. As there is more time for such extra work at this season of the year, we have thought fit to draw attention to itt, though it cannot be really completed before the first or second week in April, when it will be necessary to Bow the inverted turf over with proper lawn mixtures. TEE Wrienow.—The Fachsias, with all the retarding measures we have adopted, are determined to grow, and there is nothing for it but to bring them to the front win- dow, or where they will receive the full benefit of the light. The growth of the past season should be reduced to three or four buds from that of the previous year, and lees than that when the plants are old. Nothing more will be required by them for a few weeks beyond watering when they become so dry that the soil on the surface will not adhere when the particles are pressed between the thumb and finger. Water, as a rule, is applied for the benefit of the green leaves and shoots, which the Fuchsia does not yet possess.

answer, "Preserving their game." That is just what the great majority of them are doing at the present hour. Con- sider the advantages these men possess. Ample wealth, complete leisure, the highest education, full publicity if they have anything worth saying, influence out of all pro- portion to their intrinsic merits. The nation has heaped , upon them all possible advantages. What are the services they render in return? Who are those who have distin- guished themselves in statesmanship or in literature? You can count them on your fingers. As for those who have made a name as philanthropists you may count them on your thumbs. Thus much for living lords; let us go back a little, and take the Settlement of the House of Hanover as a starting point. Who among our statesmen of the first rank was a member of the House of Lords, or could hope to reach there by right of primogeniture? Not Walpole, nor either of the Pitts, nor Fox, nor Burke, nor Canning, nor Palmerston, nor Russell, nor Gladstone. Among living peers, born to a peerage, only Earl Granville, the Duke of Argyll, the Earl of Carnarvon, the Earl of Derby, and the , Marquis of Salisbury, rise above the level of respectable , mediocrity, and the last was born a younger son. Consider- ing the splendid traditions of many of the noble houses, we might have expected greater things. With their large acres, their vast wealth, their exalted position, how much might the peers of the United Kingdom achieve! how small are their actual performances! With but very few exceptions, their translation of the phrase "Noblesse oblige" seems to be, "Nobility obliges us to do nothing."

At the meeting, Sir Gilbert Greene!!, Bart., presided, and I supporting him on the platform were the Rev. S Wilkin- son, Rev W B Pratt, Rev E St A Duke, Rev J C Pigott, Rev F Slater, Rey J Ward, Mr T Jolley, Mr Thos Morris, Mr T Sutton, Mr D W Finney, Mr Ashnrst, and Mr Yeo- mans.

The CHAIRMAN said it was a grand thing to see men who were engaged in a good work associated together and work- ing harmoniously. Previously their tea party had been confined to St. Paul's but now, he was glad to find, St. Barnabas was included. One of the objects of that meeting was to raise funds on behalf of the church expenses. Churches ought not to be in debt. He had never been in debt—(laughter)—and he defied any man to come forward and say that Gilbert Greenall ever left a bill unpaid at Christmas. Mr. Wilkinson ought not to be in debt in con- nection with his parish at Christmas. He was told that if Mr. Wilkinson had £5O he would have no debt left. If it ifere shown to him that after the close of that evening's gathering £5O would entirely clear off the debt he would gladly give that amount. (Applause) The Rev. S. WitatiNsox said it was a pleasure to have their dear friend Sir Gilbert Gresnall amongst them once more. He had given them more than kind words; he had made them a generous offer, which he was sure would fled its way to the heart ot everyone in that room. Sir Gilbert had acted like his noble self, and they as a parish thanked him most heartily for his generosity. (Applause.) He dare- say they knew that in connection with St. Paul's they had a Mutual Improvement Society. At the meeting of this society papers were read upon various subjects, and he hoped a profit and advantage were derived. He thought their life at St. Paul's had been without any very great adventures, but they had been working steadily and quietly all the year, and they had a good number of parochial organisations in excellent working order. They had their "mothers meetings," and if they could see how happy the mothers and the ladies were together they would say that et was a good work. Then they had a Girls' Friendly Society, and at the present moment they occupied the grand poeition of having the largest branch in the diocese of Liverpool. ; Their temperance societies ware going on apace. They had 500 children in connection with the Band of Hope. Their , mission room in Catherine-street had succeeded. They had L every Sunday a special service in the school for children, i conducted by gentlemen of the parish. Looking to the ; future, they must show more zeal, more enthusiasm. He 5 was thankful to be able to say that in their day and Sunday L schools there was a good work going on that would in the , f uture influence not only their parish, but Warrington, in an important manner. (Applause.) ' The Rev. J. ti. Pigott, a former curate of St. Paul's, addressed the meeting, as also did the Rev. W. B. Pratt, : Rev. E. St. A. Duke and Mr. T. sutton. ; A hearty vote of ;hanks was accorded the chairman, on ; the motion of Mr. T. JOLLEY, and the proceedings were • brought to a close. The enjoyment of the proceedings was nauch enhanced by songs, duets, choruses, dm., given by Mr. and Mrs. Law- less, MrJohnson, Mr. Black, Mr. Reddish, Private Daley, : Miss Williams, the choir, and St. Paul's handbell ringers. : Mr. T. M. Pattison officiated as accompanist.

Tag PHCENIX PARK MEIRDERS : PERSECUTION OF A WITNESS.—The man Meagle, who was an important witness in the Phcenix Park murder trials, and is employed at the Inchicore Railway Works, near Dublin, states that lain life , is made miserable by persecution from sympathisers with the assassins of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke. He has been seriously assaulted and stoned several times, and pre-arraimed attacks have been made upon him. MR. MICHAEL DAYITT AND ROME RULE—Mr. Michael Davitt, addressing a large meeting of Irishmen in Glasgow, on Monday night, said he would go a step further than Home Rule for Ireland. He would have self-goverment, similar to that in Canada, so that they could have the pri- velege of making laws in Ireland to defend the interests of the people and lift them lID socially, to guarantee their rights, and to attend to all their wants and requirements. THE " INVINCIBLES."—Twenty prisoners under sentence of penal servitude were removed from Mountjoy Prison, Dublin, on Wednesday, for transfer to England They in- cluded ten of the Dublin" Invincibles," the other ten con- sisting of men convicted of conspiracy to murder in dif- ferent districts in Ireland. The gunheat Amelia came up alongside the North Wall at five o'clock in the morning, took the convicts on' board, and conveYed them to the Valorous, at Kingstown, which sailed immediately for Portsmouth. AN IRISH LIBEL CASE—The Queen's Bench Division, Dublin, on Tuesday. granted a motion on behalf of the plaintiff in the case of Mr. French, chief of the detective department of the Royal Irish constabulary, against Mr. O'Brien, M.P., editor of United Ireland, for libel. The alleged lib,l attributed very shocking offences against Mr. French, and the present application was to procure further particulars as to the acts alluded to by the defendant. Mr. M'Dermott, Q C., opposed the motion on the ground that to reveal the names of witnesses would be to subject them to odium and possible interference. AGRARIAN OUTRAGES.—A Tullamore telegram states that two men named Keenham and Reynolds have been arrested for causing the death of Patrick Egan, farmer, of Clon- shanny, King's county, whom they attacked and fatally injured near his residence. The outrage is attributed to an agrarian dispute.—A farmer named Ronan was arrested on Monday, near Castlegar, county Galway, and remanded, charged with a desperate assault on a farmer named Hig- gins. The injured man is in a dangerous state.7A mur- derous assault was committed on Monday evening on a farmer named Goulding, residing at flarristo7n, county Kilkenny. The affair originated in an agrarian dispute. The man lies in a very precarious state, his assailants bay- ing left him for dead on the road. PARTY RIOTS AT BOYLE : THREE NATIONALISTS WOUNDED. —A Nationalist demonstration was held at Ballymote, county Sligo, on Sunday, at which a party of Orangemen attended. A disturbance ensued, and three Nationalists were wounded by shots. Their names are M'Loughlin, Hynes, and Brennan. The mob then attacked the Orangemen, and two of these were also wounded, one of them, Saltry, receiving a pistol shot in the cheek, and the other, Murray, sustaining wounds on the head. A num- ber of police surrounded the residences of the Orangemen to prevent them being wrecked. The two Orangemen, and another, also named Murray, were arrested. Four Orange- men who ascended the belfry of the Protestant church were discovered, and had great difficulty in escaping. A meet- ing was held subsequently, at which strong speeches were delivered by four priests and two ex-suspects.—A meeting was held at Ballymote, county Sligo, on Sunday, to pretest against a circular issued by the local Orange lodge, calling on the landlords to let farms to Protestant young men from Belfast. Before the meeting was held three young Orange- men were attacked, and in return fired upon their assail- ants, wounding one of them dangerously.

A FACTORY BURNED DOWN.—A destructive fire broke out at the factory of Messrs. Samuel Fielding and Co. earthenware manufacturers, Stoke-on-Trent, early on Wed! nesdav morning, and although four fire-engines were promptly on the scene of the conflagration, it was not got under till a large range of workshops, the showroom, *re- house, and engine-house were completely gutted. A !age quantity of machinery and valuable manufactured ware were also destroyed. The damage is covered by insurance. KAY'S COMPOUND, a demulcent anodyne expectorant, for Coughs and Colds. Sold by all °hamlets, so., h. 1;c1 ,2e. 9cl —Advt.

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY."
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY."
[Published by Mr. E. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavistock-strest, London, W.C., and reprinted by perniission]. THE POWER OF THE LANDED.

My work having extended to double the length which I had at •first projected, I consider that I may now bring the inquiry to a close. It would not be difficult to continue it for another year, but having sketched the agrarian history of most of our leading families, including every English ducal house, I think I have travelled over sufficient ground for all practicil purpoi.S. Before finally closini, this series of articles, however, I deem it useful to sum up the results of this inquiry, and to supplement it by a few general observations which could hardly find a place when dealing with particular families. I am not conscious of having done any man an injustice. That the corrections I have had to make have been so few and so trivial is to me ample proof that there is hardly anything for which need offer an apology. I have a strong conviction that, if the whole truth could only be ascertained, the only thing that [should have to apologise for would be that my record of the mis- deeds of our great houses has been so incomplete. I have had to use such materials as lay ready to hand, chiefly peer- ages of ancient date and county histories, the compilers of which found a market for their wares among the great houses or those connected with them. Such writers almost invariably represent everything in the most favourable light, and it is only by carefully observing their unguarded admis- sions that it is possible to get at the truth. From historians like Macaulay, Froude, Burton, Green, Massey, and even Lord Stanhope, I have derived much valuable information, and that able, but now almost forgotten, writer, Mr. William Carpenter, has been often useful in putting me on the right track.

We must never forget that, while in France and other Continental countries an aristocratic title involves nothing more than the right of its owner to use a certain style in denominating himself, in England it means that the owner thereof shall have the right of sitting in the Upper House, and of helping to mar or put an actual veto upon the legis- lative work of the representatives of the people. Since 1832 these powers have rarely been exercised in a direct manner. Indirectly, however, they are of great impottance. The fact that such powers exist continually has a strong influence in shaping legislation. At the same time, I cannot but admit that so long as a landed aristocracy exists it does less mischief sitting apart, for• it cannot hope successfully to contend against the clearly-expressed whl of the House of Commons. _ _

Even as it is, the landed interest dominates to such an extent in that House, that only in a qualified sense can we call it the House of the People. No less than 176 of its members are connected with the Peerage by birth or mar- riage, and beside these there is a very large number wko represent the landowners who are commoners. The state of our county representation is truly lamentable, not .so zmuch on account of the party politics of the great maprity. of county members, but because of the legislative qualifications of a large proportion of them. It would puzzle the most ardent Conservative to discover the senatorial merits of Lords Burghley, Bective, Emlyn, Dalkeith, Holmesdale, Percy, Newport, March, Stafford, Yarmouth, the Hon. W. Egerton, and the Marquis of Hamilton. They sit for counties as representatives of land—not of men. If they were not their fathers' sons no one would have thought of nominating them. There are sons of peers like Lord Har- tington, Lord E. Fitzinaurice, Lord George Hamilton, and Lord Sandou, who stand in quite another category, but these are brilliant exceptions. As a rule, the aristocratic county members represent pot even the Conservatism of the bucolic mind, but simply themselves and their fathers. Could any- thing be more humiliating than the present position of South Warwickshire ? The farmers very properly insist upon a direct representative; one of the two sitting mem- bers is obliged to retire; but the man who is forced to retire is the best of the two. There can be no comparison between Sir J. Eardley Wilmot and Lord Yarmouth in point of ability or usefulness; yet the former has to withdraw, and the latter, with no qualification save that he is the son of the Marquis of Hertford, remains. Rural superstitions are proverbially tenacious of life, and the electoral superstitions are perhaps the most tenacious of all. Until adversity forced men to think, agricultural tenants, as a rule, seemed to regard it to be as much their duty to vote in accordance with their landlords' wishes as to pay their rents and rates. If the landlords or their fathers before them had created the land, they could not have been more docile. It probably never occurred to them to consider how the land had been acquired. As these articles of mine have been extensively quoted in provincial papers, they probably have set not a few thinking upon the subject; and if the result has been that some agricultural tenants have been led to take a more accurate view of their position, I shall not have written in vain. Alike to the urban population, to the tenant-farmers, and to the agricultural labourers, there is nothing more per- nicious, from a political point of view, than the agrarian electoral superstition. Intrinsically there is little to fear from the Conservative instincts of Englishmen; it is only as those instincts are made subservient to landlordism that they become a grave national peril. Lord Beaconsfield has told us in one of his novels that "we owe the English Peerage to three sources : the spolia- tion of the Church, the open and flagrant sale of its honours by the elder Stuarts, and the bcrroughmongering of our own times. These are the three main sources of the existing Peerage of England, and, in my opinion, disgraceful ones." For once I agree with his Lordship, both in his statements and in his inferences. Of course there are exceptions, though not of great importance. That which strikes me most forcibly is that almost all of these great houses, whether ancient or modern, seem to have run to seed. 'With such a vantage-ground for nobleness," how few dis- tinguish themselves. Even the Dukes, the duces, are no longer leaders of the people. " What are they doing ?' I asked Carlyle a generation ago; and he gave the scornful

- On Saturday morning eleve 'n of the Tipperary fox-i bounds were found dead in a .kennel fiom the effects of poison.

Four young men, who had persoi4. Ated women and, robbed men in the streets in Liverpool, we, -e each sentenced on Monday by the Recorder to five years' p, enal servitude. The second mate and a seaman of the a teamer Crystal, of Sunderland, from Cardiff to Bombay, sts ere drowned on Saturday morning through an accident in weighing anchor.
At Leeds Assizes, on Saturday, James Marsl4. 11l was or- dered by Mr. Justice Day to receive 50 fasbb's and 15 months' imprisonment for robbing a drunken ma..l, with violence.

THE DYNAMITE SCARE AT OBAN.—An Oben corren.Non- dent telegraphs that the six young men arrested in Mall .9tl suspicion of conspiracy to commit dynamite outrages have been discharged. MILLS FLOODED NEAR LEEDS.—The extensive mills of Sir Titus Salt and Co., Saltaire, near Leeds, have been thrown idle by the floods carrying away the reservoir con- nected with the mills.

THE HANGMAN'S ASSISTANT FINED.—OR Monday after- noon, at Dewsbury, Sydney Swift, a money-lender, of Hud- dersfield and Dewsbury, and also the hangman's assistant, was fined £5 for assaulting a policeman. . ANOTHER CRASH—The suspension is announced of the firm of Henry Monteith and Co., of Glasgow, Turkey red and fancy yarn dyers. The liabilities are estimated at £103,000, and the realisation is expected to be favourable. FATAL COLLISSION OFF BEACHY HEAD.—A Lloyd's des- patch says the Theodore H. Rand, from New York, arrived at Gravesend, reports that at four a.m. on Sunday she was in collision five miles off Beachy Head with the Statesman brigantine, which sank, and all hands excepting one were drowned. NARROW ESCAPE OF MR. FORSTER.—Mr. W. E. Forster, M.P., with his niece and Mr. Cropper, M.P., whilst staying at Foxhawe, Arubleside, had a narrow escape from a serious accident. The party had just driven over a bridge when the foundation was carried away by the swollen stream and the structure collapsed. Mr. Hugh Barclay died on Sunday at his residence in Perth, in his 84th year. He was senior judge of the United Kingdom, and for the long period of 50 years-1833 to 1883 —held the office of Sheriff Substitute of Perthshire. He received the degree of LLD. from the University of Aber- deen a quarter of a century ago. ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A POLICE CONSTABLE.—WiIIiam Henry Gregory, a Sheffield labourer, was charged on Mon— day, at Kendlington, with attempting to murder Police Con- • stable Vardy. The prisoner was apprehended by Vardy in the act of stealing potatoes from the Meersbrook Land Society, and while in custody suddenly plunged a knife into the officer's neck. He was committed for trial. TRAGIC AFFAIR.—George Reid, a farmer's son, while walking along an unfrequented road with his wife near Newton Stewart, on Saturday morning, cut her throat with a penknife, inflicting such injuries that she died almost in- stantly. The man cut his own throat, but is still alive. The pair had been visiting friends, but were heard quar- relling just before the crime was committed. There is said to be insanity in the man's family. ROBBERY OF A Sam—Last week a large safe, contain- ing more than £BOO. was stolen from the premises of the Express Dairy Company, in Bloomsbury, London. The ap- pearance of the pony and cart in the neighbourhood at an unusually early hour excited the suspicions of a police officer on the beat, who took the address painted on the cart. This address directed the police to the house of a marine store dealer at Stepney, where the stolen safe was found, unopened, and the dealer was arrested. A SCHOOLBOY'S Stumm—An inquest was held on Mon- day at West Bromwich, on the body of a boy twelve years old, named James Welsh, who hanged himself ha his parents' kitchen. The evidence showed that the deceased was much troubled in mind by fears of beisg unable to pass the school board, and had also been punished by an assistant teacher contrary to the regulations. A verdict was returned of "Suicide by hanging," several jurors requesting the coroner to communicate with the school board on the sub- 'tact.

BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.—At the Yorkshire Assizes on Saturday an action for breach of promise was heard in which the plaintiff was Miss E. J. Walker, of Newcastle, and the defendant Christopher Bnlman, a shipbroker and coal exporter, of Cardiff. A singular feature of the case was that the defendant twice fixed the weddiug-day, but was absent on each occasion in Barcelona, where he was bounding a branch business, and where he ultimately mar- ried another lady. A verdict of £5OO was agreed to when the evidence had been partly taken THE " CAT "AT LEEDS.—At the Leeds A.891Z09, James Marshall, 42 years of age, mason, was convicted, with two women, of robbing a stoker, named George Aker, of .£3l 10s. with violence, at Bradford. Marshall was ordered to be im- I prisoned for fifteen months and to be flogged twice, receiving twenty-five lashes each time. His lordship said that when- ever he had to deal with a case of robbery with violence he adopted a mode of punishment which he thought was the hest deterrent. The prisoner, before leaving the dock, said, "Please remit the lashes, my lord." MR. HENRY GEORGE IN THE PULPIT—Mr. Henry George occupied the pulpit of the Rev. David Macrae, Dundee, on Sunday night, as promised, and delivered a lecture on " Moses and Mosaic Institutions" to a con- gregation of over 2000, persons, many others being unable to gain admission. The lecturer traced the misery and un- rest of the present day to ignoring the spirit of the Mosaic institutions. Mr. Macrae, who followed, appealed to the congregation to give earnest thought to reform of the iniquitous land system now subsidised by law. OT. JOHN'S, MILES PLATTING.—The Bishop of Manches- ter, on Monday, instituted the Hey. Tom Taylor Evans, late curate of St. datthew's, Campfield, Manchester, to the rec- tory of St. John's, Miles Platting. After the late trial in reference to the bishop's refusal to institute the Rev. E. Crowgiß, the former curate to the Rev. S. F. Green, the bishop offered to the patron (Sir Percival Heywood) to forego his right to present and accept Sir Percival's presen- tation of a clergyman who was prepared to comply with the law, but the patron declined to make another presenta- tion.

DISGRACEFUL SOME NEAR BRIGHTON.—A disgraceful scene has been witnessed near Brighton. Several casks of wine washed ashore from the wreck of the Simla were broached, and a large number of people—men, women, and boys—held a carousal, which only ended when they were physically unable to assist themselves to more liquor. "Small gangs of boys," says a correspondent, "were sent home in a cart helplessly intoxicated." Three of the tip- plers—one a lad of 15—are in hospital, and a fourth, who had lain drunk in a cave throughout Friday night, has died. DISTITBANCE IN A SHEFFIELD CHURCH.—A remarkable scene occurred on Sunday night at St. Matthew's Church, Sheffield, which has been the scene of disputes between Mr. Wynn, people's warden and the Rev. G. C. Ommaney. Two men and a woman took possession, in the belief that the church was free and open of a pew which Mr. Wynn held was appropriated to another person. As they refused to leave it, Mr. Wynn called five men to his help, and they were removed by force, amid cries of " Shame " and great excitement. It is stated that the woman was struck and retaliated by breaking her umbrella over her assailant's head. Police proceedings are expected to follow. Mn. WADDINGTON IN LONDON.—The French Ambas- sador (M. Waddington) speaking at dinner in London on Saturday evening, contrasted the feeling now prevailing between the peoples of ,England and France with that which existed at the beginning of the century. He said the two countries had become so much united that it was al- most impossible to conceive a rupture between them. Such , an event would be such a calamity not only for France and England, but almost to the whole world, that it passed al- most beyond the limits of what we could conceive as a possible thing He had tome to consider any quarrels which might happen between the two countries almost as lovers' quarrels. A CLERGYMAN FINED FOR CRUELTY.—An extraordinary charge of cruelty to a horse, by causing its death through starvation, was preferred against the Rev. Thomas Yarde, of Chudleigh, on Tuesday, at Newton Abbey Petty Ses- sions. Inspector Aplin proved seeng the horse in an or- chard dead, lying in a pool of water, and its bones all but protruding through the skin. There was no grass or food of any kind in the orchard, and a post-mortem examination disclosed the fact that the stomach contained nothing but , gravel, stones, and roots of grass, and that death was due to ' starvation. The defence wasthat the horse did not belong I to defendant, but to his stepmother, who lived with him; that be was not in the habit of seeing the horse, which was 35 years old ; . and that he was not aware it was kept short of food. The defendant was fined £5 and £3 3s COMB. THE SUEZ CANAL AND ENGLISH SHIPOWNERS. Pub- licity is now given to Lord Granville's communication to M. de Lesseps respecting the agreement entered into be- tween the Suez Canal Company and British shipowners. On behalf of the Government, Lord Granville expresses ap- proval of the agreement as one likely to afford a satisfactory solution of the difficulties that have arisen, subject, how- ever, to the adoption of two recommendations which he makes—namely, that nautical men experienced, in naviga- tion shall, on the recommendation of the Government, be placed oaths Commission that is to advise as to the changes necessary for the improvement of transit; and that the official directors appointed by the Government shall be members of the London Consultative Committee. These recommendations have been adopted by the Suez Canal Board, and the agreement now only awaits confirmation by the shareholders. MR. GLADSTONR ON FRUIT Eaunnwn.—(To the editor of the Examiner.)—Sir, Referring to the Premier's speech at the acnual rent audit at Hawarden, Mr. Gladstone is incor- rect in stating that preserves are charged from 7d to 9d a lb, and that this is owing mainly to the energy of the French, Belgian, Dutch, German and American fruit growers. All 'the gooseberries, raspberries, strawberries, black currants, damsons, and blackberries used by me are entirely English—no foreign whatever being used—and to prove that the quantity is not particularly small, my usual season's make is :—Gooseberry, 300 tons. Raspberry, 300 tons. Strawberry, 200 tons. Black currant, 400 tons. Damson, 500 tons. Blackberry, 100 tons. And they can be bought retail from ready-money grocers in two and three- pound stoneware jars at the following prices :—Gooseberry, 5d t 6 5P per lb. Raspberry, 6d to 60. Strawberry, 63 to 60. Black currant. 50. Blackberry, sid. Raspberry and Gooseberry, 513. Plum, 4d. Greengage, 6d. Damson, 7d. Orange Marmalade, 4d. Jars extra, one penny each. Yours. &C., WM. P. HARTLEY.—BootIe, Liverpool. Ka s COMPOUND OF LINSEED, Aniseed, Benega, Squill, Tolu, Fre., with Obtorodyne. Old., Is. if d,, 2s. 9d., of Chemists. Advt.

GREAT POSTAL ROBBERY.—B4WeeII three and four o'clock on Wednesday motning, while a mailcart was being tdriven to the Berlin Railway Station. two letter bags were abstracted, containing a sum of 80,000 marks. It is be- lieved that the thief was well acquainted with the details of the postal service. THE " ARISTOCRATIC " GAMBLING HELLS. At Bow- street Police Court, London, on Thursday, judgment was given in the Park Club gaming case. The magistrate fined Mr. Jenks, proprietor of the club, £500; dismissed the case against Dalton, the secretary; and fined each member of the committee £5OO, and each defendant concerned in gaming £lOO, or three months' imprisonment in default. Notice of appeal was given. Muniona."—A verdict of "wilful murder" was on Friday found by a coroner's jury at Stockton-on- Tees against Thomas Smith, who stabbed his wife to the heart in a lodging-house, where she had been staying with his half-brother, a man named Shaw. Deceased's daughter ,'aid Shaw " enticed " her mother tram Darlington, where lived, but another statement was that Mrs. Smith left 1,11e:3 :husband on account of ,his neglect. ErcOß/BLE DISCOYERT AT BOOTLE—On Wednesday the dead bekdy of an unknown woman was found in the closet of an empty- house in Cyprus-road, Bootle. The body, which is that of a woman apparently from thirty-five to forty years of age, was in a most horrible condition. Deceased was wearing a black jacket, dark coloured dress, black bat, and boots very much the worse for wear. UPROARIOrS LOCAL OPTION MEETING.—AR uproarious meeting was held on Wednesday night at Croydon, in advo- cacy of the closing of public-houses oil Sundays. A large force of publicans and others were present, and created SO much disturbance that the speakers could scarcely be heard. Songs were sung, and a fight occurred when an attempt was made to eject the obstructionists. A resolution condemning the sale of drink on Sundays was carried amid great dis- cord.

THE LANCASHIRE &CRIER : MEETING OF OPERATIVES.- A meeting of operatives, at which from 15.000 to 20,000 persons were present, was held on Blackburn market ground on Tnursday morning, to consider the action of the dele- gates in agreeing to settle the wages dispute. The secretary of the Blackburn Society explained that the conditions ac- cepted were the best that could be obtained, but the meet- ing resolved, with only three or four dissentients, that a reduction of wages only be accepted on condition that the mills worked four days per week. ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT Crg DINTING VIADucT. —An alarming accident happened to the London and Man- chester express, on Wednesday night, at Din ting Junction, on the Sheffield and Lincolnshire line. The axle of one of the carriages broke just as the train was passing over Ditving Viaduct, which is over one hundred feet high. The carriage, which contained five people, was dragged along the viaduct, and finally struck the Dinting Station plat- form. Happily no one was hurt, but the line was blocked until five o'clock on Thursday morning. LIVERPOOL AND ITS FINANCES.—The Liverpool Corpora- tion on Wednesday authorised the issue of stock to the amount of two millions sterling. The money is required to pay debts falling due in the present year, and for the extension of public works—among the latter the purchase of 'in- sanitary property" and the provision of improved dwell- ings for artisans. According to the statement of Alderman Forwood, Liverpool is in a very satisfactory position finan- cially. The city owes nearly six millions, but the rate- payers are not inconvenienced, the revenues outside the rates leaving a surplus of £70,000 over the annual charge of the debt. GAMBLING IN LONDON.—At Bow-street, London, on Tuesday, Mr. Jenks, proprietor, Mr. Charles Dalton, secre- tary, and several mmnt-ers and committee men of the Park Club, St. James's, appeared to an adjourned summons, which charged them with contraventions of the Gaming Act. Mr. Russell addressed the court on behalf of the de- fendants contending that the secretary and committee had not been shown to have taken any part in the conduct of the business of gambling. It was not sufficient to show that a house was kept for gambling—the Act distinctly said unlawful gambling, and he contended that " baccarat " was no more unlawful than whist. Sir James Ingham reserved his decision. " GENTLEMANLY " AMUSEMENT IN THE POTTERIES.—At Hanley, on Tuesday, Joseph Stevenson, mining engineer, son of the late mayor of the town, and Harry Brown, another young man of respectable connections, were charged with doing wilful damage to a large amount of property in the town. It was proved that on Saturday night the prisoners removed 54 yards of coping-stone from the wall of the Shelton Parish Church, and unhung a gate from a gentleman's house and carried it away. They also broke several shutters of shop windows, tore up a large quantity of wood fencing belonging to the Corporation, and also removed a dentist's sign. The prisoners were sentenced to two months' hard labour each, without the option of a fine. The sentence was received by a crowded court with i considerable surprise, on account of the position of the ! accused.

OVER PRESSURE IN Sonoora.—The question of over - pressure in elementary schools was discussed at a large and influential meeting held in Bradford on lionday eve fling under the presidency of Lord Stanley of Alderley. A reso- lution declaring that the system of "payment by results" acts injuriously upon both health and education was moved by Mr. Pridgin Teale, and supported by Dr. Clifford Allbut, who said he did not think the Education Department durst publish what it had got in writing from its own inspectors. The resolution was carried, as well as one setting forth that home lessons were unnecessary, and that they ought not to be enforced on children under ten years of age, and only af- ter that age with the consent of the parents. THE REPRESENTATION OF BIRMINGHAM: LETTER FROM LORD RANDOLPH Citunartaa.—Lord R indolph Churchill, writing to a Birmingham correspondent, says —"I: thank you very warmly for the promises of support which you hold out. It is to me a subject of pride and gratification to have been chosen by many thousands of Conservatives in Birmingham as their candidate for parliamentary represen- tation of that town, and while fully sensible of the arduous nature of the contest, and of my own great imperfections and shortcomings, I promise faithfully to you and your friends, that no efforts on my part shill be wanting to represent courageously and honourably the principles which animate and unite us, and to study with care how I may best co- operate in pramoting the interests of you avning, intelli- gent, and industrious population. I hope it may soon be in my power to come amongst you, and I look 'forward with reasonable confidence to the issue of the struggle which before long we shall wage together." ENGLISH PATENTS. --- The following patents amongst others, published in the Patent Office Official Journal, were sealed during the week ending February 2ad, 1884:—John Briggs, Buxton, for improvements in the construction of kilns for burning limestone; Thomas Taylor and Johtl Taylor, both of Oldham, improvements in or applicable to electric gas lighters; Benjamin Alfred Dobson and William Isherwood Bromley, both of Bolton, improvements in machines for cording cotton and other fibrous materials; Alfred Godfrey, New Reddish, draughtsman, improvements in letter-press printing machines; Thomas Clarke, Sheffield, improvements in razors and razor sheaths; Thomas Brown, Walkden, and William Brown, Little Hulton, improvements in hoists for raising and lowering weights; Joshua Heap, Ashton-under-Lyne, tool maker, improvements in screw nuts and in arrangements for fastening or locking the same; John Thom, Barrow-in-Furness, improvements in and relating to slide valves for steam engines.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE., Fel. Inst., PA., Patent 4, St. Ann's-square, Manchester. THE DISPUTE IN THE COTTON TRADE.—We regret to have to report that the hope which was entertained on Wednesday night that the strike in the cotton trade of East Lancashire had practically been brought to a close has not been fulfilled. Meetings of operatives were held on Thurs- day at Blackburn and Darwen, at which a strong feeling against accepting the agreement was shown. The Black- burn meeting passed amid cheers a resolution that the terms should only be accepted on condition that it was coupled with four days a week. The chairman's remarks on the passing of the resolution seems to indicate an expec- tation that this decision will call forth the support of the trades of the country. The Darwenresolution was "to con- tinue the strike as before," and the action of the operatives' delegates in accepting the agreement was spoken of in terms of disapproval. There was some disturbance of the peace at Darwen on Thursday evening. A mob got up a demonstra- tion against a certain manufacturer, and the police are said to have "charged" them, with the result that several per- sons were slightly injured. A. few arrests were made. STRANGE EFFECT OF SEEING A PANTOMIMIC—AS Bottle Rock Ferry gentlemen (writes a correspondent) were pro- ceeding home from Liverpool between oae and two a.m. one morning last week, their attention was drawn to a house in the New Chester-road by seeing two women at an upper window frantically gesticulating and calling for help, say- ing burglars were in the house, as they heard the smashing of glass, and they could hear the lodger (a man) moaning at the back of the house, and that they dare not go to his help. On gaining admission into the house the gentlemen found the lodger (in his robe de nuit only) lying cut and bleeding in the back yord, he having while asleep fallen out of his bedroom window on to the flags below, a distance of more than 15 feet, and half dead from cold and loss of blood. Having bound him up as best they could under the ciroutnstances, it transpired that the young man bad lately come from the country to work in Birkenhead, and had been that evening to see the pantomime, which it would seem had such an effect on his brain as to cause him to annulate—in his sleep—the clown's performance of jumping through the window. He had never been subject to somnambulism be- fore and was perfectly sober at the time. THE GREAT STOCK EXCHANGE FAILURE.—OR Tuesday, at the London Bankruptcy Court, before Mr. Registrar Has- litt, an application was made in the affairs of Messrs. P. W. Thomas and Co., stockbrokers, 'whose failure has already been announced, for an extension of time for the filing of the accounts beyond the three days required by the Act. Mr. Baker, in making the application, said that the affairs of the firm were in a hopeless state of confusion, Mr. Blake way, the absconding partner, having been the sole manager of the business, and having had absolute control over the operations of the firm. Account books and securities had been made away with and loans had been contracted on fie' titious securities belonging to other parties, in respect of which latter claims were daily corning to band. The books relating to the stock and business were substantially in ,order, but very little information could be obtained froin Mr. Thomas, who stated that the absconding of his partner and the subsequent revelations had come upon him with overwhelming surprise, and though he was doing his bee, t to assist, he was wholly unable to prepare the aceounte. without assistance and further time. The Registrar exteqed the time for filing the accounts for one month, intimating that if they could be prepared earlier they shonld be filed forthwith.
