div.p: FOithiGN INTEIIIO-,c,::prE, GkANE DISASTER IN THE SOUDAN The Press Association on Tuesday learned that the Government had received a telegram reporting that Baker Pasha's:, army had been defeated, with a loss of 2,000 men. Baker is said to have himself escaped. The telegram was handed from the Government side to the front Opposition bench, where Sir Stafford Northcote showed it in turn to several of his colleagues. Later intelligence states that Baker Pasha, at the head of a force of 1,400 gendarmerie in two battaliees, 900 Soudanese, 700 troops of mixed race, 420 Turks, and 450 cavalry, departed from Trinkitat OR the 2nd instant, with tee purpose of relieving the garnisen of Tokar, 18 miles distant, which place was beleaguered by the tribes under the Mandr's lieutenant, Osman Digma. Baker Pasha's force was in addition strengthened by an artillery equipment of four Krupp guns, two gatlings, and two rocket tubes, and it was his intention, after relieving Tokar, to have advanced to the succour of Sinkat,which was also surrounded by the rebels. His movements were con- siderably retarded by the want of efficient equip- ments for his men, some of the Turkish soldiers being sent to the front without any arms at all, and others being only provided with old muskets. A portion of the force entrenched themselves in a strong Position on the shores of a shallow lagoon, four miles from Trinkitat, on the day of their march from the latter place, and the remainder of the force followed them on the 4th instant. No news had been received from Baker Pasha or lie force since Sunday, and rumours of the gloomiest nature have since been prevalent. These have been justi- fied by the intelligence received from Baker Pasha himself. According to the latest advices received from correspon- dents with the Egyptian army on Sunday, it was the inten- tion of Baker Pasha to press forward from his camp near Trinkitat towards the wells at Teb, five trifles distant, and about half way between Trinkitat and Tokar. It is in this locality, situated in the midst of dry arid arid hills, that the disaster is supposed to have occurred.—The Standard cor- respondent, who has survived the tight, sends a long and most interesting narrative of the battle dated Souakim, Tuesday.—The morning, he says, was'dull, and a rainstorm obscured their view as they advanced, and favoured the enemy. At nine o'clock they appeared in force near the water springs, and a few Arab horsemen galloped close to the advancing force as if to gauge its strength. While atten- tion was distracted by this incident a sudden commotion arose in Baker's cavalry on the left flank. The enemy had been lying concealed near them, and now, with wild cries, sprang to their feet and charged. The correspondent had been riding with the infantry column and noticed its dis- order. "I determined," he says, "if the enemy attacked I would not trust myself among them, and to that resolve I owe my life. As the cavalry rude wildly in, the order was given for the infantry to form square, but one side, seeing the enemy leaping and brandishing their spears, stood like a panic-striken flock of sheep. Into the gap thus left the enemy poured, and at once all became panic and confusion. The troops fired, indeed, but straight into the air. The miserable Egyptian soldiers refused even to defend them- selves, but, throwing away their rifles, flung themselves on the ground and grovelled there, screaming for mercy. No mercy was given, the Arab spearmen pouncing upon them and driving their spears through their necks or bodies. Noth- ing could surpass the wild confusion which the mien pre- sented; camels and guns mixed up together, soldiers firing in the air, with wild Arabs, their long hair streaming behind them, darting among them, hacking and thrusting with their spears. Generals Baker and Sartorius, adds the ac- count, having tried to rally the troops, were for a time un- able to extricate themselves. At last they succeeded in breakiag their way out and in cutting their way through the enemy. It now became a total rout, the shattered column Streaming across the plain towards Trinkitat, preceded by the flying cavalry, the enemy pressing hotly in the rear of the infantry and slaughtering at will all wounded. Men un- able to ride well were dismounted by the rush and killed. When last seen Dr. Leslie, Morice Bey, and Captain Walker, With drawn swords and pistols, were standing in a group, surrounded by the enemy, close to the buns." Official details received in London on Wednesday fully con- firm the accounts of the cowardice of the Egyptian and Arab troops under Baker Pasha's command, and of the indi- vidual courage and heroism of kuropean officers. A despatch received at the Foreign Office in the afternoon from Suakim gives a list of the officers who were killed— namely, Morice Bey, Dr. Leslie, Major Watkins, Captain Forester Walker, Lieutenants Smith, Carroll, Carrere, and Wells, Colonel Abdul Resselr, Colonel Yussuf, Major Recce, Lieutenants Berth), Morisse de Marchi, Cavalieri, Pallioko, Messeburg, Donabauer, Duporte, and Leonhardt. A meeting of the Cabinet was held on Wednesday to con- eider the latest phase of the Egyptian question, resulting from the utter failure of Baker Pasha to relieve Toka, and though no definite statement of the decision arrived at can • be made, enough has been stated to show that Ministers 'fully recognise the gravity of the situation. As stated by the Premier, in reply to Sir S. Northcote, a force of marines and blue jackets have been landed at Suakim, their being considerable fear of an attack on that place, and as a precau- tionary measure the transport ship Orontes, with about 1,000 blue jackets on board, and the troopship Euphrates, With a considerable force on board, are being detained at Suez pending the receipt of further information. The pos- sibility of troops having to be despatched from England is being kept in view, and should it be found necessary, 8,000 Men could start within a week.

News reached London, on Thursday, that General Gordon had been taken prisoner.— The town people of Suakim are (says the Daily News corres- pondent) becoming infected with religious mania, and it need not cause surprise if they turn on the Europeans. Large numbers of Bashi-Bazouks are loafing about the streets instead of being in camp. Their presence there causes uneasiness. Baker Pasha is now established in camp, and with the Admiral has surveyed the defences, which in some places consist of only a few sticks called a palisade, and guarded by a few feeble natives who seem to fear their own weapons. If this place is to be retained it must be • done by troops other than Egyptian. Sir Samuel Baker, before leaving London for Egypt, made some interesting statements with reference to the Soudan. He said that if that vast region were in British hands in a few years we should be entirely independent of the United States with regard to cotton and corn. To tap that immense • reservoir of wealth all that was needed was a railway from Suakim to the Nile "and a decent system of government." Sir Samuel said that he had received, and rejected, a few days ago a very pressing offer from a syndicate of English- men formed for the purpose of taking possession of the wreck of the Soudan. They offered to place a million ster- ling at his disposal if he would go out to the Soudan and establish a settled government in their name. He declines to believe that Gordon, if he gets to Khartoum, will give up that position to any enemy.

The directress of an institution for "the education of the daughters of the upper classes "at Warsaw, has been removed by the police on an accusation of "fostering Nihilist intrigues." M. Rouher, who was known as the "Vice Emperor" during the reign of Napoleon 111., died on Sunday. He was the most trusted adviser of the Empress Eugenie, and through his death Bonapartism has received another severe blow. IMPENDING BATTLE IN ZOLULAND.—Fresh disturbances have taken place in Zululand. It is stated that the whole of the Abaqulusiosi tribe are hemming in the chief Ottam, and that a battle may be expected hourly, in which Oham Will, it is believed, be defeated. The death is announced of Mr. Wendell Phillips, the Well-known anti-slavery advocate. He was born at Boston in 1811. Mr. Phillips was one of the most ardent advocates of emancipation, and since that great work was achieved by Mr. Lincoln he has been distinguished as a platform crator On various subjects. DytmoulTE MAGAZINES BLOWN UP Loss Or LIFE.—A terrible dynamite explosion occurred at lebeers, near Kim- berley, on the afternoon of the 10th inst. Eleven out of 14 magazines blew up, causing immense damage through- out the four camps. The loss is estimated at 33 tons of dynamite, seven tons of loose powder, 300,000 or 400,000 loose cartridges, and a large quantity of mineral oils. Three Persons were killed, and others are missing. Fragments of the bodies were found scattered about the Veldt. The French Government sustained two defeats in the Chambers on Saturday. The Senate struck out of the Trades Syndicate Bill a clause which proposed to legalise tl federation of all trades. The Chamber adopted, by a Ia ge majority, M. Clemenceau's proposals for the imme- diate appointment of a committee of inquiry. or tiltso the econ- omic condition of the working classes. Ferry opposed the motion. A Reuter's telegram states th a largeha d numbers of placards have been posted in Paris calling n the gendarmes to join the working classes in an attempt on better their position by force of arms. EGYPT, TURKEY, AND ENGLAND.—ID the course of an audience which Lord Dufferin recently had of the Sultan, his Majesty reiterated in friendly terms his wish that a very amicable understanding might be arrived at between Eng- land and Turkey in regard to Egypt. In the event of nego- tiations resulting from an exchange of views between the two countries. The interview took place at the request of • the Sultan. The British ambassador has not received any instructions from Earl Granville in regard to the affairs of Egypt. In the event enegotiations resulting from an ex- change of views, they will be held in London, and not in Constantinople. INTERESTING CEREMONY.—A brilliant and interesting ceremony took place on Tuesday, at Hyderabad. The Ninam having attained his majority, the Viceroy of India formally installed him in the administration of his terri- tories, which have been during his minority governed by a Regency, of which the late Sir Salar Jung was the head. Lord Ripon assured the Nizam that the settled policy of the British Government was to maintain the tributary states in prosperity and in their integrity. The Nizam has given great satisfaction by appointing as his chief adviser the son of the late Sir &Jar Jung. 'The Nizam is the most im- Portant of the native princes. Be rules over a country as large as Italy., and containing about ten millions of in- habitants. A FAMILY POISONED—In the part of the Hungarian capital lying just across the Danube from Pesth, a whole family was poisoned a day or two ago by an escape of gas Which had penetrated into the house from a disused pipe buried under the ruins of another house at some distance. When everybody in the house became ill on Wednesday evening, the doctor was sent for, and he said symptoms of gas poisoning wet e apparent, but as no gas was used in honse be was unable to account for it, and left after 1- ministering some medicine. The patients were relieved • ,K 1 Went to sleep : but next morning five of them were found 144 and four others in a hopeless condition. Only a nurse and a child, who happened 10 have their faces buried

lin the bedclethet, have recovered. One of the victims was I the gradinothtt of the children, who had come the night be- fore on hearing of the illness of the family. THE PROPOSED REDUCTION OF THE AMERICAN TARIFF. —Mr. Morrison, the chairman of the ways and Means Com- mittee, has introduced his Tariff Bill in the House of Repre- sentatives. [he bill proposes a reduction of 20 per cent. on numerous articles. In few cases is the reduction greater or less than this rate. No reduction is to be lower than the rata in the Morril Act of 1861. The Act is to take , effect from July Ist. The 20 per cent. reduction applies to cotton goods, hemp, jute, and flax goods, other than jute, butts, wool, and woollen goods; metals, other than ores, books, papers, &c.; sugar, tobacco, wood, wooden ware, except where otherwise provided ; to all articles an ad valo- rem duty—earthenware, glassware, provisions, except where otherwise provided; sundries, other than precious stones, salt, coal, bristles, lime, and chemical products, except where otherwise provided. No duty is to be levied in excess ' of 40 per cent. ad valorem on cotton or cotton goods; in ex- cess of 50 per cent, on metals; and in excess of 60 per cent. on wool, woollen goods, all unpolished cylinder, crown, and common window-glass, or cast polished plate-glass, unsil- vered, exceeding 24 by 60 inches square, and on salt in bags, sacks, barrels, or other packages, or in bulk. Variousl articles are placed on the free list, including iron and copper ores, black or culm coal, bituminous or shale coal, articles intended as substitutes for coffee jute, butts, hart for turn- sponges, British gum extracts, and indigo. The bill was referred to the Committee of Ways and Means. MUTINY ON TIE 1.11013 SEAS: A TERRIBLE STORY. The Times of India of the 11th ult. contains the following ' telegram from its Calcutta correspondent :—Captain Lewis, of the barque Kaffir, just arrived (January 10th, 10-20 p.m.) makes the following report: On the 24th of November, while on a voyage from Natal to Calcutta, he sighted the Swedish schooner Natal, Captain Enstrom, from Boston fer Brisbane, with a cargo of Yankee "notions." The Natal signalled that she required immediate assistance, that she was shorthanded, and that a mutiny had broken out among her crew. Captain Lewis ran down to the schooner, and saw men on deck with their heads bandaged He armed a boat's crew and went on board. He found the captain and mate suffering from severe wounds. The crew, consisting of three men, were kept at work by fear only. The vessel was then in lat. 37-16 S., long. 74-47 E. The story told by Captain Enstrorn was that the crew originally consisted of to officers and five men of various nationalities. The ring- leader of the crew, who hailed from Australia, understood, as he thought, how the cargo of sorts which the vessel car- ried could be turned to account among the islands of the Pacific. The man had given trouble during the voyage, but nothing overt had occurred till the night of the mutiny, 16th of November. Cap- tain Enstrom on that night was lying asleep in the cabin, when he was attacked by the crew. Two men, armed with axes, attacked the captain, while an- other man with a revolver attacked the mate, who was also asleep in his berth. The man who assailed the mate fired at him twice; but, whether from the powder being damp or the cartridges old, the shots were not mortal. One took effiect in the hollow between the eyes, and another in the chin. When Captain Lewis saw the mate the bullets were still in the wounds. As the man attacked the captain the axe caught in a low beam of the cabin, but he struck the sleeping man in the jaw, slicing off a portion of the bone and cutting the neck. A second stroke, which had lost its force from the same cause, crossed the first wound.ll The sailor who fired at the mate bolted. When the mate' rushed into the captain's cabin be found him struggling with two men, one of whom stabbed him in the neck with a sheath-knife On the entrance of the mate the two men left the cabin. The mate and captain followed the mutin- eers, but were assailed with handspikes and driven back. They then bound up their wounds and got their guns. The crew, seeing they were armed, ran forward. Four of them got down into the hold, but the fifth was made a prisoner and secured aft. The hatches were then pat on the hold to keep in the other four prisoners. On looking round after the struggle; the captain discovered blood on the port rail, showing that before making an attack on the cabin the mutineers had murdered the second mate and had thrown his body overboard. The crew were kept in the boll till Tuesday, the 20th November. They refused all terms and remained in a state of mutiny, and as the captain and mate were wounded it was impossible for them to navigate the ship. The captain had no altnernative, after fair warning, , but to proceed to extremities. Two of the mutineers were then shot, when the others submitted and agreed to work ;the vessel. Matters were In this state when the Kaffir spoke ' the schooner. Captain Lewis gave what assistance he could, and being in command of a small vessel himself he could not make prisoners of the mutineers. The leader, the Australian, had been shot. Captain Lewis called for volun- teers from his crew and gave Captain Enstrom two men. The Natal being thus strengthened resumed her voyage, the captain expressing his intention to call in at Adelaide.

GENERAL BOOTH AT WARRINGTON. General Both, the founder ef the Salvation Army, a sect of earnest and enthusiastic religious workers whose peculiar modus operandi is now familiar to every one, made his firkt lappearance among the Warrington corps on Saturday even- ing. In the public mind, as well as in the minds of those connected with the corps, the General's visit excited a con- siderable amount of interest. Long before the time he was I expected to make his appearance the Barracks in Academy- street were packed, although admission was only to be gained by ticket. At seven o'clock the General and his aid-de•camp (Captain Surtees) reached the scene of the evening's rendezvous incognito, this course being adopted in order to avoid an unnecessary crush. The reception which was accorded the leader of the greatest of modern religions • movements was almost indescribable. Waving their hand- kerchiefs around their head the assemblage rose en masse, and the stentorian blasts from several brass instruments, the tinkling of tambourines, and the thudding of the big drum, combined with the vociferations from hundreds of throats, constituted one of the most discordant and unearthly noises which it is possible to din into one's ears. When the con- fusion had subsided a number of songs were sung to inspirit- ing tunes, and the General delivered earnest words of exhor- tation during the intervals, the proceedings being concluded about half-hast nine. The campaign was continued on Sun- day, commencing at seven o'clock in the morning with knee drill. At ten o'clock the hand of the coil. and some 300 "officers and soldiers" formed an escort and proceeded through the streets to the General's quarters at Bank Quay, where they were joined by their Commander, whom they escorted to the Public Hall. The hall was filled in every part, the platform being occupied by members of the Army. The proceedings were of a most enthusiastic character and were led by Captain Surteee. Again in the afternoon the hall was crowded with a respectable and well- conducted audience. Short addresses were delivered by Captain Jones, Lieutenant Tilsley, and Lieutenant Carter, female officers stationed at Warrington, as well as by a number of other officers and privates. , General Booth followed. He referred to the neglect of the 'lower classes of the people by the churches, who admitted their inability or incapacity to reach them. There was nothing mysterious, or should not be, about reli- gion, and a "wayfaring man though a fool" could have salvation, but it was not to be found in creeds, sacraments, prayer-books or "the Salvation Army business." Their critics had got a false notion about the Army, and the criti- cisms that he had read contained so many palpable misap- prehensions that he would not have thought a child who had any notion at all of the work of the Salvation Army could have written them. The Salvation Army was founded 18 years ago by himself, because he was aware of the fact that 95 per cent of the working classes never went to any place of worship. For 12 years they fouzlit their way against discouragement; but from that time six years ago—when their present plans were adopted—they had met with great success, and the army rapidly developed to its present im- mense proportions. Last year they bad 430 corps, which had increased during the past 12 months to 650. Last year the number of officers were 1,027, and in the same period these had increased to 1,650. Of these 200 were abroad, their colours flying now in 12 dif- ferent nations. Some people said, "Why don't you have experienced and educated officers?" To those he said, "Why don't you clever men come and be officers ?" While those men were taking care of thei% skins and living at comparative ease, the earnest officers of the Salvation Army were being subjected to annoyance and difficulties both at bouts and abroad. He gave encouraging instances of the work which was being accomplished in New Zealand, Australia, and India. They had 16 "War Crys" in different parts of the worid, and the Army had made a profit .during the past year of £B,OOO. Where had that gone to, he asked. Into General Booth's pocket. (Laughter.) But net a farthing of it went into his pocket. Every penny of it went to keep the chariot rolling on. He remarked that when they got the great Salvation Army temple in Warrington which they intended to build they would be able to find accom- modation for about 3,500 persons, and if any other sect were ever hard up they would be willing to lend it to them. (Hear.)—ln the evening the Hall was again crowded, and the proceedings were similar to those in the afternoon. A largely-attended meeting was also held at the Barracks on Monolty morning, commencing about ten and closing about 12 o'clock. The General and staff were the guests of Mr. E. Bolton, of Whitecross. a gentleman who for some time past he identified himself with and taken great interest in the work of the corps.

JUSTICE BUTT ON LIVERPOOL RUFFIANISM.—Mr. Justice Butt, who addressed the Grand Jury at Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday, referred to the number of charges of "ferocious violence" and murder which appear in the calendar. He also commented upon the fact that a very large number of prisoners charged with those offences "bore Irieh names." During his membership of the liouse of Commons his Lordship frequently beard from the liome Rule party the statement that the Irish were the most peace- able and law-abiding people in the world, especially so when they removed from the scene of agrarian agitation., The calendar of prisoners before him was a singular conamentary on such a homily, the number of Irish prisoners accused of vlive crimes being entirely out of proportion to the number of Irish p.,ople residing in Liverpool and the district. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY, The fifth session of the tenth Parliament of qaeen Vic- toria commenced at Westminster on Tuesday afternoon, when the Queen's Speech was read by Royal COMMiSiOII. Mem- bers of the House of Commons began to assemble soon after twelve o'clock, and there was a full attendance. Shortly before two o'clock the Lord Chancellor and his co-Commis- sioners took their seats on the woolsack in front of the Throne in the House of Peers, and the Coromision having been read, Black Rod was despatched to invite the presence of the Lower House. Oa the arrival of the Speaker and his attendant Commoners at the bar, the Lord Chancellor read, as follows, THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN, I have called you together for the fifth session of this Parliament that you may again address yourselves to the discharge of your arduous and ever growing duties. I continue to hold friendly and harmonious relations with all foreign powers. My communications with the President of the French Republic, arising out of special incidents in Mada- gascar, have closed, as I had anticipated, io a manner such as tends to confirm ' the cordial understanding between the two countries. I have likewise, in conjunction with the President, ap- pointed a Commission which is now sitting in Paris to die- cuss a basis of arrangement which I had proposed for the future regulation of the Newfoundland fisheries and the avoidance of disputes. • 40 agreement has been arrived at With Portugal respect- ing the river Congo and the adjacent territories. This agreement will be presented to you forthwith. Arrangements are in progress for the resumption of diplomatic relations with Mexico, and special envoys have been despatched by each Government to promote that end. Negotiations for a treaty of commerce with Turkey have commenced. An agreement on commercial arrangements with Spain has been signed, which awaits the sanction of the Cortes. A revision of the commercial treaty with Japan, on a basis generally agreed to by the treaty powers, is nearly completed, and a treaty of commerce and friend- ship has likewise been signed with Corea. Having had every reason to be satisfied with the tran- quility of Egypt, and with the progress made in the estab- lishment of orderly institutions, I gave during the autumn instructions for the evacuation of Cairo, for the further re- duction of my military forces, and for their concentration mainly in Alexandria, but in the month of November the Egyptian army, appointed to maintain the rule of the Khedive in the Soudan, was defeated and broken up with heavy loss. Upon the occnrrence of this defeat I deemed it wise to recall the order I had given as a precaution agaMst the possible effects of the military reverse in Egypt itself, and to preclude all doubt as to certain maintenance of its , tranquility, while an unforeseen and calamitous necessity has thus required to suspend the measures I had adopted. The aim of my occupation, which has been explained to von at former times, continues without change. I have offered to the Egyptian Government such counsels as appeared to be required by a prudent regard to the amount of its resources and to the social condition of the country. I have also despatched Major General Gordon to report on the best means of giving effect to the resolution of the Khe- dive to withdraw from the interior of the Soudan, and have permitted him to act in the execution of the measure. Papers relating to this and to several of the foregoing subjects will be presented to you. I have directed communications to be held with the dele- gates whom the Government of the Transvail has sent to this country for the purpose of urging a reconsideration of the convention of Pretoria. In this interchange of views attention has been principally turned to the question, always one of difficulty in South Africa, bow best to make provision for the maintenance of order and the prevention of oppression on the frontier. Nothing has occurred to discourage the expectation that these communications may be brought to a favourable issue. Papers will he presented to you on the subject in due course, and likewise with r-spect to the condition of Zulu- land, which continues to be unsettled, as well as to the re- sumption of direct imperial authority in Basutoland, which is in Immediate contemplation. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE Or COMMONS, The estimates of charge for the public services during the year 1884-85 have been prepared, and wir speedily be laid before you. I anticipate that the revenue of the current wear will not fall short of the expectations upon which you founded your financial arrangements. MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN, The condition of Ireland continues to exhibit those fea- tures of substantial improvement which I described on the two occasions when I last addressed you. A measure will at once be presented to you which will have for its principle object the enlargement of the occupa- tion franchise in Parliamentary elections throughout the United Kingdom. 'the experience gained during half a century by the progressive admission of augmented numbers to a share in our representative system happily warrants the bei:ef that again as heretofore the result of a judicious ex- tension of the franchise will be a still closer attachment of the nation to the Throne, the law, and the institutions of the country. I anticipate a like effect from the extension and the re- form of local Government. This comprehensive subject embraces all that relates locally to the greater efficiency of administration, to the alleviation of burdens by improved arrangements, and to the enlargement of powers of ratepayers through the repre- sentative system, including among them the regulation of the traffic in intoxicating liquors. A plan *ill be laid before you for the extension of municipal government to the whole metropolis. Preparation under this head, however, which has been made by my directions, has not been limited to London, I but the actual presentation of further bills of the same class I moat depend upon the progress you may be enabled to Make ' I with the weighty business which has been already set

forth. Other public wants have not been neglected, and you will be invited to reconsider Bills relating to the security of life and property at sea, to the Railway Commission and its powers, and td the repression of corrupt practices at muni- cipal elections. Measures will likewise be laid before you for the better administration of Scottish business, for the promotion of education, and for the closing of public-houses on Sunday in Ireland; and also for the improvement of intermediate education in Wales. I humbly commend your efforts in the matter I have named to you, and in all other particulars, to the blessing of Almighty God. DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The Address of the House of Lords in reply to the Speech from the Throne was moved by the Marquis of TWEEDALE, and seconded by Lord Vnataorr.—The Marquis of SALISBORZ then rose. He said that though he did not purpose to naovii. an amendment on the Address, he could not subscribe *to the optimist view of public affairs which ran through both the speeches they had heard. The Speech from the Throne, too, was marked by the pecu- liarity that as public affairs became darker and more diffi- cult its tone became mere optimist and more complacent. The Government had been unfortunate in regard to Egypt. Matters had always gone wrong, and it had always been the fault of somebody else. He contended that the paragraph in the Queen's Speech relative to the Soudan indicated complete forgetfulness on the part of her Majesty's Go- vernment as to the conditfpne under which the Khedive held his power. The Soudan could not be separated by the simple advice of England, but such a proceeding would require the consent of the Sultan and the Powers who had guaranteed the whole of the territory belonging to the Ottoman Empire. The noble Maratturs also argued that the loan recently ob- tained by the Khedive through Messrs. Rothschild was in contravention of the firman under which he ruled, and that His Highness could not give any security for its rePayment; and he invited the noble Secretary for Foreign Affairs to give an explanation of the policy of the Government in Egypt. Lord Salisbury made a brief reference to the other subjects touched upon in the Queen's Speech, and complain- ing of the neglect of agricultural interests he announced that the Duke of Richmond intended to bring in a bill on the subject of the importation of foreign cattle.—Earl GRA:swum replied at length to the criticism of Lord Salisbury, who, he said, had not attempted to defend him- self against Mr. G-oschen's charge that he was the person most responsible for the difficulties which had occurred in Egypt. The noble Earl said in conclusion that the Go- vernment felt bound to maintain the security and tranquil- ity of Egypt until the purpose for which our army was sent thither had been accomplished.—The address was agreed to, and their Lordships adjourned at 6-30. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. Soon after the Commons met at two o'clock the members were summoned to "the other House" to hear the Queen's Speech read, and shortly afterwards the sitting was sus- pended. On the resumption of the sitting there was the usual ordering of new writs for vacancies, and the demon- strations on new members taking their seats. Mr. Houlds- worth, Sir F. Milner, and Mr. Eckersley were greeted with , exceptionally loud Opposition cheers. DIE FRANCHISE BILL. The Premier, to whom an enthusiastic reception was accorded, gave notice of his intention to ask for leave to bring in a bill to amend the law relating to the representation of the people in the United Kingdom. Notices of more than one hundred bills or resolutions were given by hon. members. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The Address in rAe.plyErattoroT member the Qben's Speech was moved by Mr. , for Roxburghshire, and seconded by Mr. S. SMITH, one of the members for Liverpool. "In obedience to the wish of the Leader of the Opposition," Mr. neer R. BOURKE moved an amendment in crndemnation of the policy of the Government in Egyptian affairs. Referring to Baker Pasha's expedition, the right hon. gentleman re- marked that no one was better fitted to lead a forlorn hope, but he had such bad materials to work with that it was to be feared there was some truth in the rumour that his army had been cut to piece% though it was to be hoped it was also true that Baker Pasha's life was spared. At the close of Mr. Bourke's speech the tarst sur- prise of the session occurred.—As no member on the Minis- terial rose to reply to the speech the SPEAXER was about to put the question, when Baron de WORMS interposed for a time and criticised the policy of the Government in Egypt at considerable length.— At the conclusion of this speech still no one rose on the Government side of the During the dinner hour the SPEAKER put the amendment, when there appeared for it 20, against it 77, a

result which was received with general laughter.—Mr. 111A.clvEn followed with his amendment on the depressed condition of commerce and agriculture.—lf was rejected without a divisio.a.—lt was suggested by the Government that the Egyptian question should again be raised on the report stage, and the debate on the Address was adjourned at half-past ten o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY,.. . .

DAKER—P-Asae's DEFEAT.—An informal debate upon Egyptian affairs was opened by Mr. ASHMEAD-BARTLETT' who asked for the latest information which the Government might possess regarding Baker Pasha's reverse near Trinka- tat.—The PRIME MINISTER said that if the debate on Tues- day evening had not been curtailed, it would have been Sir Charles Bilge's intention to read a telegram just then re- ceived from Admiral Hewitt, confirming the account of Baker's defeat and his retirement, to Suakim. In order to restore a little confidence, the Admiral had landed a num- ber of blue-jackets and marines from the Ranger. No far- ther intelligence had been received or was yet expected from General Gordon, and nothing which had occurred war- ranted the Government in extending his pawers, shich are already very considerable. FURTHER DEBATE ON TILE ADDRESS.—Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL wished to move an amendment CO the Address, requesting Her Majesty to dismiss her advisers and call to her aid "other persons possessing the confidence of Her Majesty's subjects ;" but he was ruled to be out of order. It was announced that the Government intended to introduce a bill enlarging their powers of dealing with cattle imported from countries where disease existed; blot Mr. GLADSTONE in reply to Mr. Chaplin, could not promise to give the bill precedence over all others. Lord R. CHURCHILL then moved the adjournment of the House, in order to condemn the conduct of Ministers in not continuing the debate on Mr. Bourke's amendment to the Address, their laxity and departure from the invariable practice of Parliament hav- ing turned the debate into a " periect farce." Mr. CHAPLIN seconded the motion. Mr. GLADSTONE denied that the Government had been parties to an organised suppression of the debate. It was not in accordance with Parliamentary usage, he said, that a Minister should rise in the dinner hour to defend the Government from a charge of Want of confidence, and the President of the Local Government Board (Sir C. Mike), who had arranged to reply for the Government, left before Mr. Bourke concluded, in the full anticipation that mem- bers would be found to continue the discussion. That no one rose behind the Ministers was, the right hon. gentleman thought, a proof of the discrimination of Liberal members, who preferred to wait for authentic information, and there was no eagerness on the part of the Opposition who only mustered twenty strong.—Sir Stafford Northcete having spoken doubtingly of the statement that the collapse of the debate was accidental, the motion for adjournment was negatived without a division. The debate on the Address was then resumed, Transvaal affairs coming in for the chief share of attention. The discussion was further adjourned. —Mr. Grnansrox.s; informed the House that measures had I been taken, in response to a late telegram from Admiral Hewitt, to supply him with increased forces for the defence of Suakim.—The House adjourned shortly after five o'clock.

_ HOUSE OF LORDS, TKURSDAT. PROPOSED VOTE OF Czxsung.—The Marquis 0 SALIS- BURY gave notice of his intention to move on Tuesday next the following resolution:—" That this House, having read and considered the correspondence relating to Egypt laid on the table by Her Majesty's command, is of opinion that the recent lamentable events in the Soudan are due in a great measure to the vacillating and inconsistent policy pursued by Her Majesty's Government." (Loud -Opposition cheers.) Intsr RATING, motion by the Earl of LIMERICK for a return giving certain statistics as to Irish rating was opposed, as to part of the particulars, by LorWCarlingfoid, who said he wan informed that it would be impossible to give the figures without interfering with the annual revi- sion of the valuation of Ireland.—On a division the motion was carried by 38 to 33.—Lord SALISBURY gave notice that on the 22nd inst. he should move for the appointment of a Royal Commission to inquire into the question of working- class dwellings. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIEURSDAY.

PROPOSED VOTE OF CENSURE.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE gave notice for Tuesday next of a vote of censure on the Govern- ment for their Egyptian policy. The (notion is identical in terms with that proposed to be moved by Lord Salisbury in the Upper Chamber. THE Sot:max.—The precise nature of the mission of General Gordon and the rumour that he had been taken prisoner were discussed by the House.—To the first inquiry Lord HARTINGTON replied that the General had been ap- pointed by the Khedive Governor General of the Soudan, but that the mission on which he had been despatched was on behalf of Iler Majesty's Government. On the other point the noble Marquis stated that no information had reached either the War Office or the Foreign Office on the subject of the reported capture, and Sir E. Baring, who had telegraphed at noon from Cairo, made no mention of such a rumour. FOOT-AND-MOUTH Disnasit.—A lively discussion on foot- and-mouth disease was raised by the representatives of agricultural constituencies, at the close of which Mr. CHAP- LIN announced that in consequence of the promise of the Government to bring in a bill to extend the powers of the Contagious Biseases (Animals) Act he did not intend to proceed with his amendment on the Address, but should propose another, and urged that the intended legislation should have precedence over other measures mentioned in Her Majesty's Speech.—The TIMMER replied that the Government intended to press forward the bill with every fair expedition, but they must decline to give it precedence ever the two most important Measures mentioned in the Royal Speech. THE DEDLTE ON THE ADDRESS. The debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. CEAPLIN, who pressed the Go- vernment to name toe time when they contemplated making progress with the bill promised on foot-and-mouth ,disease. —Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply, stated that notice of the bill would be given in the other House on a yery early day, and he hoped it would be on Monday, and the measure would be prosecuted with all reasonable expedition. —Sir M. HICKS-135ACR asked for a more definite pledge, and Colonel KiNGSCOTE accepted the assurance of the Govern- ment. —The debate was continued by Mr. Heneage, Mr. R. Paget, Mr. Newdeuate, and other hon. members.—Upon a division the amendment of Mr. Chaplin was defeated, there being 200 for it and 251 against.

WIDNlib i 1111) &MOUS. DISTRIBU LION OF PRIZES. 'rhe valuable prizes offered for competition amongst the children attending the Widnes Board Schools by MT. 'l'. S. Timinis, the Chairman of the School Board, and Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., were distributed on Tuesday evening by Mrs. Thnmis. As on the last occasion, the Volunteer Hall, where the ceremony took place, was crowded to the doors by the parents of the successful scholars and their friends, while on a large stage erected behia the platform upwards of 600 children were accommodated. Of the 2,000 chil- dren attending the Board Schools these scholars had been , selected for that honour because they had made 420 atten- dances out of a poasible 456, and their bright and intelli- gent faces, and their scrupulously clean and neat attire, formed, as one of the speakers remarked, a more beautiful nosegay than the most skilful hothouse gardener cau[d have formed. Daring the evening they rendered a number of of songs in capital style, and with such an intelligent ap- preciation of their performance, that the audience on awn occasion were loud in their demonstrations of satisfac- tion. The conductors, Mr. Hunter and Mr. Showan, are to be congratulated upon the successful results of their training. Mr. Gossage presided over the gather- ing, he was supported on the platform by the Rev. Canon Diggle, of Mossley Hill, Liverpool, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes, Mr. and Mrs. T. S. Tim- mis, Captain Brunner, Messrs. H. W. Deacon, J. Bradshaw, R. H. Davies, E. Carey, and G. H. Danby. The following headmasters and mistresses were also present: Messrs. Snoddy, Hunter, and Sbowan ; Mrs. Corns, Miss Strickland, Clayden, Strong, Broad, Hay, Pommy, Henderson, Clarke, Sawson, Sauber, and Sowerbutts. The CRAIRMAN commenced the proceedings by a short address, in which he expressed the pleasure it gave him to preside over such an assembly. He regretted that his wife was unable to be present to distribute the prizes, but her Place would be taken by a lady who had perhaps a great' deal more interest in Widnes—Mrs. Timmis. (Applause.) That night, 24 boys or girls would receive 23 shillings, which to an ordinary man, was on the average not at all a bad week's earnings. There were 66 children who would get 15s 44 each, and 112 who would get lie 64 and so on. He thought the recipients would sufficiently publish the fact that education in England was not being neglected, or if it was being neglected, it was through mismanagement of those who were over the people not giving them sufficient opportunity to make those advances in education which was being thrust upon England by other nations. He had never found a people more capable of receiving education or that had more self-reliance, power, and zeal concentrated in them than the people of this country. The opportunity up to the last few years had been wanting, and the meeting that night was sufficient proof that opportunities were not now wanting, and ought to encourage everybody who had power and will to work in the advancement of education. (Applause.) Mr. DARBY then read apologies from attendance from Mr. Sydney Maspratt, Mr. G. Pilkington, Major Cross' and T. Snape, and proceeded to read a report, which stated that this was the second year of the distribution of prizes. The prizes were divided into two classes. In the first class the fees were returned of all children who had not missed a single attendance during the past 12 months, and in the second CLASS half the fees of those who had not missed more than five attendances were returned. Last year the number that obtained first-class prizes in .Simms Cross School was 10, this year 94—(applause)—Warrington-road last year 7, this year .55—(applause)—West Band last year 7, this year ' 70—(applause)—making a total of 24 for the last year, and 219 fer. this year. (Loud applause.) The second-class prizes at SimisCroes last year numbered 42, this year 59 ;—(applause) —Warrington-road last year 11, this year 30 ;—(applause) Weet Bank last year 37, this year 48 ;—(applause)—making the total of first and second prizes for left year 114, this, year 356. (Loud applause.) In offering these prizes the donors had in view the encouragement of thrift, and they were glad to find that with one or two exceptions the money received by the children and put in the bank remained to the credit of the children still. (Applause.) In some instances the parents who received the half share of the fees also paid that to the credit of the child in the Post- office Savings Bank. (Applause.) The benefit that had accrued from this system was shown by the fact that -dur- ing the year many of the children had added to their bank- ing account, and the donors of the prizes felt that their ob- ject had been fully realised. (Applause) Mrs. Talons then distributed the prizes to about 24 children, representing the whole of the successfulacholars. These scholars had not been absent from school once during a period of two years. The value of the prizes given by Mr. Timmis amounts to £149, and of Mr. Gossage to £47. Canon DIGGLE then proposed that the best thanks of the meeting be given to Mrs. Timmis for the graceful manner in which she had performed her part in presenting the prizes, and in doing so he delivered a some- what lengthy address on the advantages of thrift and isunc- tality. He observed that Mr. Tim.nis and Mr. Gossage only undertook to give these prizes for two years, and now the scholars and Parents would be put upon their honour, and would have to shew what they could do without being paid for it. (Laughter.)

Captail BRUNNER seconded the proposition in a few appropriate words, and it was carried by load acclamation. Mr. Tunas, on rising to reply for his wife, was received with long continued applause. He said anything she could do to promote the happiness and welfare of the Widnes people she was always glad to do. (Applause.) Referring to the prizes, he remarked that he was speaking I Mr. Gossage's feelings as well as his own when he said that the enthusiasm shewn by their attendance that evening, and I the good results obtained by this prize system, freely repaid them for the cost it had entailed upon them. (Hear, hear, and applause.) It was most pleasing to him that so many children had come forward to claim prizes, and it was still more 'gratifying to find that the bank deposits which were made last year were now intact. He hoped that the habits of punctuality and thrift found in these children would gradually increase, and in the end attain very great , results. He believed the new scheme of the Council of Education, which the Rev. Mr. Diggle had aided materially to form, would be quite satisfactory, aud he hoped that the children would come forward in greater num- bers next year to claim prizes. (Applause.) lie concluded by moving a vote of thanks to the Rev. Canon Diggle for his address—Mr. H. W. DEACaN seconded the motion. He observed that a Council of Education had been formed in Widnes, and a nember of ladies and gentlemen had pro- mised to subscribe about £2OO per annum for three years, and a scheme had been drawn up for the distribution of that money. It was impossible with that amount to carry on the system already in force, and the committee had decided to pay a prize of 4s into the Post-office Savings Bank for every child that made every possible attendance whether in a Board or a voluntary school in Widoes. To a child that did not miss more than 10 of the possible 1 attendances a prize of 2s would be paid iuto the bank, and I those who missed not more than 23 or 30 of the possible attendances would receive a certificate very prettily printed , in colours, which would be an ornament on the walls of ' many of the houses in Widnes. (Applause.)—The motion was heartily carried, and Mr. DIGGLE suitably replied.—On the motion of Mr R. H. DAVIES, seconded by Mr. E. CAREY, a similar compliment was paid te the chairman, who re- ferred to the magistrates' position with reference to the administration of the Education Acts, remarking that he had the greatest sympathy with many of the people who came before the Bench, and neither he nor his brother magistrates had any desire to administer the law harshly. He pointed out the advantages now offered by Farnworth Grammar School and the school of cookery in connection with the Board schools.—The thanks of the meeting were accorded to Mr. Kershaw for his kindness in allowing the free use of the hall. The proceedings terminnted with the -children singing the National Anthem.

div.p: POLITICAL.

Mr. George Howard, M.P. for East Cumberland, an- nounces his intention, on purely private considerations, of resigning his seat at the next general election. It was announced at an agricultural dinner in Cara- bridge on Saturday that Sir H. Brand, the Speaker of the House of Commons, was about to resign his seat for that county. Colonel STorth, who has represented Oxfordshile for 32 years, has informed his constituents that it is not his inten- tion to offer himself for re-election after the termination of this Parliament. Two interesting election contests will be decided next week. The nomination for West Somerset takes place on Tuesday, and the polling on Thurday. The Paisley elec- tion will be held on Friday, the 15th. Mr. Gladctone, writing to Mr. Broadhurst, acknowledging the resolution passed by the Trades' Union delegates, says he can assure them he will not readily forget the remarkable gathering which assembled at the Foreign Office. Mr. Bulwer, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Hicks, M.P., spoke at a meeting of the Cambridgeshire Chamber of Agricultare upon the question of Fair Trade. It was resolved by 22 votes to 15 that the whole system of so-called Free Trade should be inquired into by an impartial committee of the House of Commons. BIRMINGHAM AND ITS CONSERVATISM.—Lord Randolph Churchill and Colonel Burnaby were on Monday evening unanimously chosen as the Conservative candidates for Bir- mingham at the next election. Lord Salisbury had sent a letter to the Conservative Association highly commending Lord Randolph's "courage and patriotism" in fighting a seat "generally looked upon as hopeless," and auguring success from the very boldness of the attack. THE SUFFRAKIE.—Mr. Woodall, M.P., has been asked by the parliamentary advocates of women's suffrage to move an amendment on the Franchise Bill with the object of I securing to women the franchise OE the same terms on which it is granted to men. This was unanimously agreed upon at a conference held at Westminster on 'Thursday night, and presided over by Mr. Courtney. M.P., and at- tended by about 25 members of Parliament. A little passage at arms has taken place between Mr. Herbert Gladstone and Mr. James Lowther. It was cur- rently reported whi'e the recent electoral contest was in , progress at York, that a disturbance arose at a Liberal meet- ing through a Tory intruder making some discordant I sounds, and the noisy gentleman was said to have been Mr. James Lowther. Mr. Herbert Gladstone gave currency to this story, which was told him by a gentleman who was at the election, but Mr. Lowther denies all connection with it, and, of course, Mr. Herbert Gladstone withdraws his re- marks.

SENTENCE OF DEATIL—AD Taunton Assizes, on Wednes- day, a young man named Charles Kite was sentenced to death for the murder of Albert Miles at Bath. The men had quarrelled, and the prisoner some time after the disturbance had ceased procured a knife and deliberately stabbed Miles in such a manner as to cause his death almost imme- diately. "Well," said a Yankee, proudly, to a travelling Scot, as they stood Dy the Falls of Niagara, "is not that wonderful? In your country you never saw anything like that!" "Like that," quoth the latter, "there's a far mair wonder- ful concern nae twa miles frae whar I was born." "Indeed!" says Jonathan; "and pray what kind of a concern may it be ?" "Why, men," replied the other," its a peacock wP a wooden leg !" TEMPERANCE LEGISLATION.—Immediately after the read- ing of the Queen's Speech, a conference of members of Par- liament interested in temperance legislation was held in one of the committee rooms of the House of Commons. Sir Wilfrid Lawson presided, and there was an attendance of about fifty members. The following were appointed a com- mittee to watch the progress of temperance legislation in the House :—Sir J Pease, Sir J J Jenkins Sir II Verney, Sir R Cunliffe, Messrs C Stevenson, Richards, Cropper, George Palmer, A Pease, Ross, J .Roberts, Ainsworth, Woodall, Parkes, Richard, Wilson, Cameron, S Smith, Car- bEtt, S Williamson, .1 Wilson, Caine, Fry, M.Lagan, C Ken- nard, Slagg, Walter, James, B Whitworth, and Sir W Law- son. An executive and convening committee was also elected.

div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
BURTONWO OD.

STEALING COALS To COWL A SUNDAY DINNER. John Burstow and Thomas Ankers, flatmen in the employ of Mr. Richard Abel, Runcorn, were charged at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with stealing from a flat at Buttonwood on the 27th ult. a quantity of coals valued 6d, the property of Messrs. Evans and Co. Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the prisoners.—lt seemed that on the day in question one of Messrs. Evans' flats, loaded with coals, was lying alongside the prisoners flat at Button- wood, and the prisoners were seen by a constable removing some of the coats into their own flat, which was ectipty.— Mr. Davies said the prisoners took the coals with which to coak their Sunday dinner, and intended paying for them the next day, hr return an equal quantity. There was no one in charge of Messrs. Evans' flat at the time, or they would havepaid for them then or returned a similar quantity of coal the next day.-Mr. Pritchard, who represented Messrs. Evans and Co., said that their men had no rieht to sell the coals or to lend them.—The defendants were each fined 5s and costs, the Bench remarking that the costs were heavy.

div.p: FRODSfIA.M.

THE ROE% BAND A FRODSHAM.—The celebrated and talented Till family made their second appearance at the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tuesday evening, and gave a choice programme of classical music to a highly apprecia- tive audience. The chief novelty and attraction was the unique instrument called the Rock Harmonicon, and al- though only formed of pieces of rock from Skiddaw, the I sounds emitted were as mellow and sweet as an instrument constructed on the most scientific principles of modern in- vention. Mr. Till and his two sons, with the aid of their magical hammers, gave a harmonious interpretation of diffi- cult music with a style and finish which can only have been acquired with years of constant practice together. The musical abilities of the family were further shown by Ocarina quartettea,..hc., a solo on the gigilera, a wooden in- strument, and songs by the Misses Till. An opportunity was afforded of inspection of the Roca Harmonicon, and Mr. Daniel Till, jun., gave an interesting account of its con- struction.

FRODSHAM GAS COMPANY LIMLTED. The annual meeting of the shareholders of this company was held in the Town Hall,Yrodshatn, on Monday evening, when Mr. Henry Linaker presided. The Auditors reported that they had audited the accounts of the company for the year ended 31st December last, and were able to state that they con- sidered the balance sheet a correct statement of the affairs 'of the company. The following report of the directors was read and adopted, viz :—" The directors have the pleasure of presenting to the shareholders a favourable report of the year's business. The income from all sources amounts to £1,092 13s 6d, being an increase of £77 lOs 10d over that of the previous year; this inceease is accounted for by an in- crease in the consumption of gas and better prices obtained for tar and ammoniacal liquor. The expenditure amounts to £717 93 91-. d, leaving a balance of profit ef £375 4s 3d; out of this sum £175 4s 3id has been placed to the reserve fund, the remaining £2OO has been carried to dividend account, which with the balance brought forward from the previous account amounting to £556 14s. 7id. is available for distribution. During the year it was found necessary to have a new scrubber erected at the works at the cost of £l3B Is. 614., which has been paid for out of the reserve fund. The directors recommend the payment of a dividend of 10 per cent. for the past year. The retiring directors are Messrs. William Hayes and Thomas Riley, and, being eligible, offer themselves for re- election." Messrs. William Hayes and Thomas Riley were re-elected directors, and Messrs. John Pollard and Charles E. Linaker were also re-elected as auditors. GOLBORNE. GOLBORNE CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL.—In this schoolroom on Wednesday evening the Rev. James Way- man, of Blackpool, delivered an interesting lecture entitled "Two visits to the land of the West, what I saw, and what I thought." The address was listened to with much pleasure by a large audience. THE Sr. JOHN AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION.—A meeting in connection with the Clolborne Branch of the St. John Ambulance Class was held in St. Thomas's schoolroom op I Wednesday evening, when there was a fair attendance. The Rev. C. T. Quirk, M.A. (Rector), was announced to pre- side, and addresses upon the principle and work of the asso- ciation—pointing out its advantages and benefits—were delivered by several gentlemen. THE WAGES DISPUTE IN THE Corron TRAlTE.—During the present week many contradictory rumours have been circulated with regard to the strike of weavers and spinners formerly employed at Messrs. John Brewis and Company's Parkside Mills. Considerable doubt and uncertainty as to the course events were taking prevailed among the hands themselves, and while some were expecting to start in a day or two others were firm in their belief that work would not be resumed for some time to coins. It is, however, a

fact that several interviews have recently taken place be- tween the firm and the workpeople's deputation, and as a result, we understand, the masters have acceded to the wishes of all except the card-room hands, that work should be resumed upon the old terms. With respect to the card- room hands we are informed that the firm jll presses for a reduction in their wages, but it is not thought that any portion of the workpeople will return to work unless all the hands are treated alike. This seems to be the general 'opinion, and very few, indeed if any, think work will be resumed upon other terms than these. HALTON.

- - HALTON PARISH CHURCH- MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—Gn Tuesday evening last an excellent essay was kindly read by Mr. J. D. Jones, the librarian of Runcorn, on" Shelley, the poet." The Vicar proposed that Mr. Jos. Stokes should take the chair. The Chairman remarked among other things what a pleasure it was for hina to be present, and how much he regretted his inability to attend more frequently. Such classes, he said, must be of great use in such a parish as Halton, and that evidently great care was taken that able gentlemen and useful subjects should be brought forvmd to create interest among, and give satisfaction to, their poorer brethren. As the present session is drawing to a close there was not a very large at- tendance. Mr. Jones's essay was delivered in a very pleasing and enjoyable manner, evincing admiration of Shelley as a pc-t, notwithstanding the many drawbacks to his character is a Christian gentleman. After the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. S. Peacock, J. W. Haddock, W. Chrimes, and W. Phillips had expressed their views upon the subject, a pleasant meeting was brought to a close by ihe usual votes of thanks. HAYDOCII. HAYDOCE WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—A very enjoy- able gathering was held in this school on Tuesday evening, when the annual meeting in connection with the "Round 0" class was held. There was a large attendance. Several songs, recitations, die., were capitally rendered, and the dis- tribution of prizes to the aceolars for regular and punctual attendance was an intareeting feature of the evening's pro-

ceedings. HUTTON. HxyToN TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—The weekly meet- I ing of thiabove was held on Tuesday evening. The Rev. l J. W. Walker, 8.A., presided. Songs were given by Messrs. W. D. Stoba and H. Capper. Miss Capperplayed the accom- paniments. Addresses were delivered by the chairman and , Mr. ri. V. Fricker (of Liverpool). CHIJRCJI OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY (HUTTON Baesrcw).—The fortnightly meeting of The above society took place on Monday evening, in the Infant School. The Rev. H. D. A. Hubbard presided. The proceedings con- sisted of service of song, entitled . " Poor Mike." The musical portion was given by the Eluyten Quarry Band of Hope choir. The,accompanirnents was played by Miss 1 Blizard. The connective reading ley Mr. E. B. Williams, who also gave an earnest temperance address. At the close new members were enrolled. The room was well filled. TAIGEI. DETERMINED SUICIDE.—OR Monday morning. a yon.ti:_f man, 21 years of age, of Wharf-street, Leign, suicide by cutting his throat. The young fellow c° badmn b e e n 4

in a low state for a ehort period in consequence of a ski. disease, and at a quarter to els, in the presence of kils mother and brother, went deliberately to the cupboard, took a rezor therefrom, and drew it across his throat. Assistance was rendered as speedily as possible, but without avail, death ensuing a few hours later. I LYNN.

1 ENTERTAINMENT. -The Prestwich amateur minstrels (gave a peformance in the Plough Hotel Assembly Room on iThursday evening, and there was a large attendance. . LIBERAL MEWIING.—E will be noticed from our adver- tising columns, that on Monday evening next a putdic meeting under the auspices of the Lymm Liberal Association will be held in the Plough Hotel Assembly Rooms, at which addresses will be delivered by Messrs. G. W. Latham, James Tomkinson, J. T. Brunner, U. Broadbent, and Edward Brewtnall, Esqs. William Long, lisq., LP, is announced to preside. We trust the meeting will be well attended.

RAINFORD. TEE ALLEGED THEFr FROX A RAINFORD BEER/1017SM —At St. Helens, on Friday, before Mr. William Blinkhorn, a middle-aged man, n imed James Cbisnall, was brought up under remand charged with stealing 8d from a till in the bar of the Eagle and Child public-house, Rainford, on the Saturday previous. Prisoner, who had nothing to say in answer to the charge, was committed to the assizes for trial. - -

THEFT OF PlPES—Three lads named Renbea Lomax^ William Kilshaw, and Robert Jones were charged at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, with haying stolen three wooden pipes, valued lir Si, the property of Harriet Pennington, Rainferd. The lads, it appeared, had taken the pipes out of a shop window by putting their hands through a broken pane. On account of the youth of the delinquents the Bench dismissed them, after adns!laish- lug the parents to look carefully after them.

„ RAINft ILL. PLATING "DUCILiTONE,"—On Tuesday, a: the Presect Police Court, two youths named James Lyon and Justin Park were charged with having obstructed the footpath at Rainhill, on the 19th ult., by playing at "duck-atone.”— They were each fined Is and costs, or seven days. ANNUAL MEETING OF THE LIGHTING INSPECTORS..--Tll6 annual public meeting of the Inspectors of the RainbE Lighting District was held on Thursday evening in last week. There was only a moderate attendance of the public. Amongst those present were Messrs J B Thomson and Johnson Brown (inspectors), Mr G W Rawlins (treasurer), and Mr G Eyre (secretary). The Chairman called upon the treasurer to read his annual statement, from which it appeared that by careful and economical management the Inspectors would only require the sum of £5O for the annual expenditure, the lowest amount ever required, heinc equiva- lent to a rate of 34 in the X. Messrs F Homer, J Johnson, and P Hawkswortla were appointed inspectors in the room of the retiring inspectors, Messrs II Baxter, W A Meadows. and the late P Whittaker. Mr E Johnson Brown was re- appointed inspector. Complaints having been made about the careless manner in which the lamps had been lighted, Mr G W Rawlins pfoinised to have the matter remedied. Arrangements were also made for an extra lamp to be placed on the railway bridge. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the business. SANKEY.

JUVENILE HOUSEBREAKEES.—On Wednesday, at Cyan. rington Petty Sessions, Robert Kirk, aged 12, Thomas Farr- ington, aged nine, and John Farrington, aged 11, of Sankey- bridges, were charged with breaking into the dwelling-house of Richard B. Wright, of Howard-street, Sankey, between the 14th and 18th ult., and stealing therefrom three pairs of trousers, two vests, and two coats, value £2 10s.—It appeared that en the 14th ult. Mrs. Wright put the clothes referred to in a drawer upstairs, and on the 18th discovered that they were missing. She remembered that between these two dates she had been away from home, and found on coming back that the scullery window had been broken, but did not notice that the articles were missing until the 16th. She did not inform the police of what had occurred, but went her- self to a number of pawn shops in Warrington in search of the goods., and found that they had been pawned by the pri- soner at Mr. Brigg's, Bank Quay. The parents of the pri- soners were communicated with, and they redeemed the the articles and returned them to their proper owner ; but the case was then takes up by the police. The two Farrington's were each ordered to receive six strokes of the birchrod, and Kirk was sentenced to one month's imprisonment.—Kirk was further charged, along with a lad named Edward Hughes, 14 years of age, with breaking into the dwelline-house of Joseph Stafford, of Sankey, and stealing therefrom a quantity of cakes, sweets, fish, oranges, marbles, clic., on the 21st ult.— Evidence having been given supporting the charge, Kirk stated, aster being cautioned in the usual way, that he and his fellow-prisoner got into the house through the window, having unfastened the latter with a knife. They tore a piece of paper off a newspaper which was lying on the table and got a light at the fire, then went into another room and took the articles mentioned.—The prisoners were committed to take their trial at the Liverpool Assizes. WLNSFORD.

StompsNcn.—The walls in front of Weaver schoo!s having shown a tendency to depart from the perpendicular in proximity to the causeway of Weaver-street, the s'•ur- veyor has had a protection put up preparatory to taking out a summons from the trustees to take the same down ar dangerous. SLLVATIONISTS.—The coming of " General " Booth, or _

"His Dignity," to this town on Monday was a red letter day to this body of people. Hosts with bands went to meet him, and in the Town Hall to hear him. Two enthusiastic meetings were held, and much anxiety was manifested in the streets respecting him. He spoke at great length at tuts evening meeting. LIBERAL CLI7B.—An excellent lecture was delivered oft Thursday last at the Libesal Club to the members and their friends by Alderman Briggs, of Crewe, subject, "Free Trade v. Reciprocity," in which, with a versatility of illus- tration and a clearness of grasp, the whole subject from its commencement WA9 laid bre. Mr. Slater (ox. Mayor) pre- sided, and was supported on the platform by Mr. Buckley, who proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer and chairman, which were carried with applause. THE MARKET HALL-113e great subsidence of Market- street and contiguous parts of Winsford occasioned the Market Hall.Comoany to pull down the old hall, which was erected in 1859—but which had gone down in 20 years about 25 feet—and build a new one orta different principke. The lower part is brick and the upper timber, the woolen portion embracing a gallery 10ft wide going round the hall , at a height of 12 feet from the floor at the sasement, which . .
floor .is in sections dowelled with iron dowels and supported

on adequate bearers without joints and unnailed, th'n's pre- paring for depression when it comes. The gallery will prove a great addition to the new hall whether for naarket purposes or public meetings—it is well lighted, and by day or night will be a great addition to Winsford. The length of the room is 80 feet, breadth 42 feet. It has cost about £6OO, and the builder, Mr. Pickstock, of Winsford, has carried out very efficiently the designs of the directors. It lis hoped that the room—open for the first time to the public and stall-holders on Saturday last—will prove a boon. The permanence of the strtet far some time past leads to the impression that no great changes will occur for the present at least. Indeed, since 1879 there has been no subsidence of the old market hall. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

CATTLE DISEASE IN CHESHIRE.—The chief constable of Cheshire states that foot-and-mouth disease has decreased by more than one-half during the past week. Only 41 cases remain tinder treatment in the entire county, against 83 last year. There has unfortunately been a fresh out- break at Frodsham Lsix farms and 43 animals remain affec- ted with sheep scab. AGRICULTURISTS AND THE CATTLIC TRADE —The Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture on Saturday passed a resotuiin advocating the prohibition of the importation of cattle from infected countries. Mr, IL J. Tollemache, M.P., and Mr. Stanley Leighton, M.P., were amongst those present.—lt was resolved by the Hampshire Chamber of Agriculture, at a meeting on Saturday, to petition the Central Chamber to urge the House of Commons to put into effect the resolu- tion of last July regarding the importation of foreign cattb —A. resolution was passed by the Sunderland Chamber of Agriculture expressing regret that no attempt had yet beec made to carry out the resolution of the House of Commons on July 10 last in regard to foreign cattle, and urging the Government to give it effect without further unnecessary delay.—Mr. Dockham, M.P., and Mr. George Palmer, MP., were present at a meeting at Reading, on SatardAy, at which a resolution was passed in similar terms to the foregoing.— The East Kent Chamber of Agriculture also passed a similar resolution.—The lion. E. Majoribanks, M.P., presided over a farmers' meeting at Berwick, on Saturday, at which a resolution in favour of increased restrictions upon the cattle trade, with a view to protection against the disease, was ited.

1 - EXTRAORDINARY DECEPTION BY A GIRL.—At Birming- ham. on Tuesday, a girl named llrarriett Holins, 19 years of age, was cLarged with obtaining several sums of money by means of false pretences. It was shown that the prisoner had gone to various people in the town and represented that she had met with a terrible accident through the negligence of an employer. She had one of her arms covered with \ bandages, and stated that a portion of her arm had been amputated. To make her story more plausible she pre- sented a subscription card, upon which the names of a clergyman and several persons known in the town were forged. The prisoner obtained large and small amounts of money from a large number Of persons. She pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. SHOCKING BABY FARM REVELATIONS.—A woman named Mackenkie, forty.seven years of age, has been committed. for trial from the Milton Court House, charged with the ' wilful murder of two little children, the one under two and the other four years, by starving them to death. She was ' : further committed on other charges for neglecting to pro- ' vide food and proper nourishment for three other children, 1 under her care, whereby their lives had beaome endangered, p The medical evidence showed tkat the two deceased children l had died from starvation, and that the other three who were ' taken to the infirmary were in a fearfully emaciated condi- tion through want of food, and were suffering from conges- tion of the luags from cold and exposure. WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSLEY,—House. surgeon's report for the week ending Thursday, Feb. 7. Patients admitted and discharged: Home patients, 17; out patients, 29-, accidents, 7; total, 53. Cured, 0 ; dead, 0 ; discharged, 0; total, 0. Present number of home patients, 36. In-patients: Admitted, 1; discharged, 0; remaining in hospital, 15. Hon. treasurer, J. R. Buckton, Esq. ; hon. secretary, Joseph Davies, Esq.; house-surgeon, Mr. C. E. Richmond. The House Surgeon will feel obliged for con- tributions of old linen, &c. Medical officer for ensuing week Mr. Gornall. ALEXANDRA THEATRE, LIVERPOOL—The pantomime of "Jack the Giant Killer" is having a successful run at the Alexandra Theatre, Liverpool. In the hands of Mrs. ' Sakes and her able assistants the familiar legend has been made to assume a most attractive garb, and everything is conducted on a scale of much magnificence. The specta- cular display is surpassingly fine, the dialogue is humour- one and witty, the music bright and ear-catching, and the songs abound with good "hits." The railway companies, are running special trains to Liverpool at reduced fares during the pantomime season, and we would strongly re- commend a visit to the "Alexandra." It will be seen from our advertising columns that the performances are now drawing to a close, and that unless the fullest advantage is taken of the pantomime next week, the opportunity to enjoy a treat will not present itself again this year.

IT is a long time since the opening of a session of Parliament took place when there was a more profound stirring of the political mind than has been the case with the session which has opened this week. Rightly or wrongly, it is believed in many quarters that the present session will witness a furious con- flict of parties; that the Tory party, feeling that they have in no way improved their posi- tion since 1880, will make a desperate and prolonged onslaught on the Government; that in fact we shall see, so far as they are concerned, what may not inappropriately be called the battle of despair, This belief has certainly some ground to rest upon. For a long time it has been recognised by all students of political history that if the Tory party fail to materially better their position in a session in which the Government set themselves to carry a great measure of reform, there will be little hope that they will be able to quit the cold shades of the Opposition benches for many years to come. Nobody sees this more clearly than the Con- servative leaders. What wonder, therefore, can be felt that they, together with the rank and file of their party, should, after having ignominiously failed during the last four sessions of Parliament to injure the Govern- ment, determine to make a grand attack op the position held by the GLADSTONE Admini- stration, That this assault is 1 ,be delivered with the concentrated strength of the whole Tory party is evident from the loud beating of the drums and the blaring of the trumpets which is now taking place. If discordant din and the hoarse repetition of calls to arms were in themselves potent influences in political warfare, the Tories would have wPn the battle already. But remembering the proverbial expression concerning the hollow-. ness of substances which give out a great deal of noise, we do not feel that there is reason for alarm in the present condition of things even to the most apprehensive Liberal. In order to put the matter at rest, let us at once inquire what there is for Liberals to , fear in the coming struggle ? Is the exten- sion of the suffrage to householders in counties likely to cause the downfall of the present Government? We think not, and we are confirmed in this opinion by the remarkable fact that no Conservative speaker of any eminence has ever been rash enough to say it would. It is undeniable that many Conservatives have been in hope that some- thing which they desired should be tacked on to the measure for the extension of the franchise would prove a stumbling block in the way of the Government, and lead to majorities hostile to the Government pro- posals being returned in the House of Com- mons; but the county franchise question in itself has never been considered one likely to lead to a change of Administration. And now that the Government have declared in the QUEEN'S Speech that the measure which they intend to submit to the judgment of the House "will have for its principal object the enlargement of the occupation franchise in Parliamentary elections throughout the United Kingdom," it would seem, that the hope of inducing Mr. GLADSTONE and his colleagues to incorporate into that measure a scheme of redistribution must be very faint indeed. For this much is certain, that the Government in leaving out of the Speech from the Throne all reference to the redistri- bution of seats, have not acted in that respect without premeditation. If it had ever entered into the mind of any member of the Cabinet that it was desirable a scheme of redistribu- tion should be considered along with the pro- posals for the extension of the suffrage in ' counties,, the empnatic and eager way in which so many Conservative orators have proclaimed the same opinion would have convinced him of his error. Conservative leaders have, in point of fact, shown their hand too clearly for any one to be deceived by them. However loudly they may call for the Govern- ment proposals with regard to the re- distribution of seats, they will fail to con- vince the bulk of the electors of the wisdom of the course they suggezt, for it must be ap: parent to everyone that the only object such Conservatives have in view in what they Pr°- pose is the entanglement and downfall of the Government. But, notwithstanding this fact! they will no doubt still endeavour to get et
