the intentions of the Government with regard to redistribution. At one time some of their number were, no doubt, in hope that the Irish party might be led to join them in a prolonged assault on the present Administra- tion, but now that the Government have indicated, through the Queen's Speech, their intention to bring Ireland within the scope of the operation of the new Reform Bill their expectations in that direction cannot be very sanguine. On what, then, can Conser- vatives rely in their campaign against the Government ? There is still a large Liberal majority in the House of Commons, and a majority which will vote with great solidity on all vital questions of policy. In estimat- ing the opposing forces in the House of Commons, the leading journal has this week expressed the opinion that in .critical divisions involving the fate of the Govern- ment, even where the bulk of the followers of Mr. PARNELL may be found joining the Opposition, the combined Opposition would number only 290 votes all told, while the strength of the Government would stand at about 350. It is, therefore, clear that the most probable effect of any determined on- slaught on the Government would be to con- solidate its power and demonstrate once more how thoroughly united Liberals can be when they meet a common foe. Is it not likely, therefore, that while the Conser- vative party, impelled by the reckless un- reasoning ardour of somr, youthful or in- experienced leader will make an occasional attack, if only to justify the bluster in which they have indulged during the Parliamentary 'recess, the chief aim of the more astute members of that party will be to bring about the gradual disintegration of a considerable portion of the Liberal force, in which contingenqt they might then steal one or two chance victories on minor questions ? Fortunately for the Liberal party, the Conservative members of the House of Commons are not all astute men. As a matter of fact some of them are the reverse. In some cases blind hatred of the Government prevents anythin7 like a free exercise of the judgment, while in not a few Others the desire of those who are princi- pally concert-I<A is simply to secure their own personal, aggrandisement, utterly regardless of the permanent interests of the party With which they are connected. An in- ordinate love of renown or notoriety, and an absorbing desire to win popular applause, Would appear to be the animating rnotives of the youthful chiefs of the Conservative party. These motives, however, never lead to abiding success. Any member of the party who is not troubled With much moral sensitiveness, and whose Mental cuticle is only thick enough to prevent the shafts of reason pene- trating it, may be the hero of a Political Balaclava charge which shall throw a momentary halo around him, but which Will, end in the rout of his followers. There are few men who can, in the face of a hostile majority, so dexterously Manage affairs as to keep their party intact, and at the same time inflict deadly injury on their opponents. Judging from the record of the past four Sessions, and the

Present undisciplined state of the' Opposition in the House of Commons, it would seem as if. the Conservative party does not possess even one such leader. We think, therefore, it may be taken for granted that it is in the highest degree impro- bable the Tory party will be able to derive any advantage from the struggle over the County Franchise Bill To what other ques- tions, then, will they look 'as likely to afford them the longed-for opportunity of doing grievous damage to the present Administra- tion? They are not likely to gain much during the discussion on the Bill relating to the security of life and property at sea, or the measure dealing with the Powers of the Railway Commission; neither is it to be ex- pected that they will send round the fiery cross when the measures intended to secure the improvement of intermediate education in Wales, and to prevent corrupt practices at municipal elections, come up for consideration. To what measure, then, can they look which is likely to place the Government in such a Position that the united forces of the Opposi- tion may attack it with any degree of success ? Will the desired opportunity be found when the London Government Bill is before the House, or when the measure for securing a reform of local government is under discus- -s'°n? .Certainly the two latter measures will !cit arouse political enthusiasm like the County Franchise Bill —for there is political enthusiasm at the present day though there are no long processions of unenfranchised householders and though the railings of Public parks are not in danger of being thrown down. There may not and Probably Will not be unanimity of feeling in the Liberal party on all the details of these two proposals. But if this be all on which the Conservative party in the House of Commons base their hopes of overthrowing the Govern- ?.,,lent their prospects are very poor indeed There is, to be sure, the question of Egypt to !an back upon. No one is disposed tq pre- dict, especially after the startling news from the Soudan this week, what will happen there, but considering the views which have been recently expressed by Mr. BOURKE with regard to the relation of this country to Egypt, and the fate his amendment met on Tuesday night, it is obvious the Opposition might have some difficulty, under present circumstances at least, in framing an indict- ment against the Government which would be supported in any very effective way by the 'whole of the Conservative members of the House of Cpmmons. It is therefore very ob- vious that the Conservative party are prac- tically in the position of Micawber ; they are 'waiting for something to turn up. They are not very particular as to that something, if it only provides a formidable weapon of offence against the Government. On the other hand Liberals, and with them, we think, may also be reckoned all fair-minded and moderate Politicians, are trusting that Mr. GLADSTONE and his colleagues may still continue to ex- hibit the wisdom they have manifttted in the 'last, and that, backed up by a majority of the people of this country, they will 'still tread the path of steady reform and set to all the world an example of enlightened and un- selfish legislation.

div.p: PERMISSION TO SHLL.—The Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, granted Edwin Field permission to sell at the Norton Arms Hotel, Halton, lately occupied by George Hargreaves. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Robert Plumpton, labourer, living at Wavertree, was brought up on a charge of assaulting P.C. Blackledge.—The constable stated that on the Ist inst. he apprehended the prisoner on a charge of being drunk and disorderly. Whilst on the way to the police station the prisoner struck him on the face with his fist and kicked him about the legs and body.—The prisoner, who had no recol- lection of the affair, was fined 103 and costs, or, in default, 14 days' bard labour. THE SLEEPING OUT NUISANCE AT WlDNES.—Before Messrs. G. Pilkington and F,H. Gossage, at Widnes Police Court, ou Monday, William Kinchley was charged with sleeping out. Early on Sunday morning P.C. Laing fauna the prisoner asleep on two boilers in, Messrs. Gaskell, , Deacon and Co.'s chemical works, and Inspector Wood in- formed the Bench that the prisoner bad only been released from gaol on Saturday morning, having just completed seven days' incarceration on a similar charge.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. BALLAD SINGERS IN TROUBLE AGAlN.—Elizabeth Mc- Cormick and Agnes McCormick were brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday morning, cparged with sell- ing ballads without a license. The prisoners were singing and offering for sale ballads in victoria-road on Saturday night. P.C. Evans demanded their license. They acknow- ledged that they did not possess one, and were not aware that one was necessary.--In default of paying a fine of Is and costs they were each sent to gaol for seven days.—They had 4s 4d In copper in their possession. RUNCORN UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.— The m mthly meeting of this committee was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. C. Reynolds, J.P., presided, and there were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lock- wood, Mr. A. Thomas, J.P,, Mr. Idighfield, Mr. H. Linaker (clerk). The salary of Mr. Riley, attendance officer for Frodsham district, was increased from £22 103. to £35; and that of Mr. De Prey, the officer for Stockton Heath dis- trict, was increased from £22 10s. to £3O per annum. The other business was not of public importance.

A MAN SUFFOCATED AT WONEs.—John Murray, a labourer, living in Water-street, Widnes, was suffocated on Thursday afternoon. He was employed at the works of Messrs. J. Pilkington and Sons, and at 11 o'clock he was missed from his usual place. It was supposed that he had gone to a neighbouring public-house, but at half-past three his lifeless body was found in a sewer which runs from the works to the river. In the bottom of the sewer was a quantity of mud a foot deep, and in this the face of the de- ceased was buried. It is not known how the deceased cams in that place, which is about 200 yards from the spot where he usually worked.

THE FRIENDS' FEUD AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Jas. Handley, Ellen Armstrong, a married woman, was charged under a warrant with assaulting Sarah Leeson, alsoa married woman.—lt was alleged that on the 24th January the com- plainant and her husband were walking down Waterloo. road, when the prisoner intercepted them, and demanded to know who had told Mrs. Leeson her house was mortgaged. Mrs. Leeson replied "herself." The prisoner then struck her three or lour times in the face with her fist, and made use of bad language to her. The parties had known each other for 19 years, and up to that time had been good friends.—The Bench could see no reason for the assault, and fined the prisoner, who pleaded guilty, 103 and costs, 14s 6d, or in default 14 days' hard labour.

WIDNES LIBERLL AssocwrloN.—At a recent meeting of the General Committee of this association the members re-appointed Mr. E. K. Muspratt to the position of presi- dent. Mr. E. Carey was elected vice-president and hon. secretary, and Mr. R. Shaw, hon. treasurer. The presi- dent and vice-president were deputed to represent the asso- ciation on the Executive of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Association, and Messrs. Henry Brunner, John Taylor, and H. B. Shores were elected the representatives on the General Council of the same body. The president and vice-president were also selected as members of the Executive Committee of the National Liberal Federation, and the two hon. officers, with Messrs. T. S. Timmis, T. Snapp, it. O'Keeffe, John Taylor, and H. B. Shores were elected representatives on the General Council of that organisa- tion.

--- WESTOM POINT STEAM TOWING COMPANY.—The annual meeting of the shareholders of this company was held at the offices, Weston Point, on Monday. Dr. MacDougall, the chairman, presided. Toe balance sheet, certified by the auditor, Mr. Thomas Handley, was presented and unanim- ously adopted. A resolution declaring a further dividend of 4s per share was passed, this making the total dividend of the year Ll 2s per share, or 11 per cent. Votes of thanks were passed to the chairman and the directors for their ser- vices during the past year, and Captain Clarke, the manag- ing secretary, was heartily thanked for the efficient way in which he had discharged his onerous duties. The retiring directors, Dr. MacDougall and Mr. J. G. Knight, were unanimously re-elected, and at a meeting of the directors subsequently Mr. T. Ward, of Northwich, was appointed chairman for the ensuing year. DAMAGES AQ&INST A RUNCORN MA.NIIFICTURER.—III June last William Williams was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on a charge of stealing a piece of paper pur- porting to be an agreement, the property of the Runcorn §oap and Alkali Company.—Mr. W. Wigg, the chief director and manager of the company, prosecuted, and the prisoner was defended by Mr. F.A.Lake, solicitor.—lt is unnecessary to relate the circumstances of the alleged theft. The pri- soner was committed for trial, but the grand jury threw out the bill. The prisoner laving received notice from his em- ployers to quit the vessel, commenced an action fer damages against Mr. Wigg, and Mr. Clement Higgin was instructed by Mr. Lake on the captain's behalf. The case was expected to be heard at the present Carnarvon Assizes, but Mr. Wigg has settled the matter by paying the sum of £6O for damages and the costs, which will amount to about .£lOO.

BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—The annual congrega- tional tea party took place in the Schoolroom, on Tuesdav evening. Upwards of 250 persons partook of the excellent tea provided ; and at the subsequent meeting there was a very large attendance. The Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor, occupied the chair, and delivered an address, in which be referred to the bright prospects of the chapel. The various! organisations were in good circumstances, and the week- night meetings had not been so well attended during his ministry as they had been during the Year just closed. The Rev. J. Yonge (Warrington) and the Rev. J. Chater (Southport) were present as a deputation from the Church Aid Society. In advocating its claims, each gentleman de- livered all able speech, The Rev. J. Cole (of Gatston) and the Rev. W. Vause (Methodist Free Church), and Mr. Hughes (Widnes) also spoke on general subjects. During the evening the choir rendered several anthems in an ac- complished manner, and Mr. J. R. Thomas sang the solos " Just as I am " and "Nearer my God to thee."

DEATH FROM Bram AT RUNCORN.—At the Devonsh ire Hotel, on Thursday afternoon, Mr. J. E. Worsley' the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Thos. Wm. Hunt, nearly three years of age, son of Alfred Hunt, a stonemasen, living in Lyon-street, Runcora.—From the evidence of Mary Ann Hunt, the mother of the deceased, it appeared that on the morning of Cristmas Day, about 7 o'clock, her son Charles, 8 years of age, went downstairs to put a fire in the grate. He took with him his brother Thomas. In a short time the parents, who were upstairs' in ignorance of what the children were doing, were startled to hear loud screams proceeding from the kitchen. On going there they found the deceased behind the door with his nightdress on fire. The father put out the flames by throwing an ulster over the boy, and Dr. Robinson was sent for. The doctor said the boy was very serionsly burnt, and there was no hope of his recovery. The womnds were dressed, and for several weeks the boy seemed to be improving, but on Sunday last he became much worse, and died on Tues- day morning.—Evidence was given by Charles Hunt, who stated that the deceased lighted a match at the candle, and then set fire to his nightdress.—Dr. Robinson was called, and said it was a wonder the child had lived so long. Death had resulted from exhaustion due to extensive burns. —The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

RUNCORN SOAP AND ALICLLI COMPANY, LIMITED.—The annual meeting of the shareholders of this company was held yesterday, at the Law Association-rooms, Liverpool, Mr. A. P. Fletcher, the chairman, presiding. The report of the directors for the past year showed gross proats of £27,656, and, after deducting all expenses, there was an available balance of £20,341. This it was proposed to dis- tribute as follows :—Dividend of 23s per share, £13,800; written off to nitrous towers, £1,000; and carried forward, £5,541. The report stated that the directors had been in- duced to erect plant at Runcorn for the manufacture of their own gas, and believed the outlay would soon be liquidated out of the saving effected. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, hoped the statement of affairs would prove satisfactory, for it should be remembered that the trade at the beginning of the year was very depressed. The improvement in bleach- ing powder mentioned in the last report had not continued, prices having receded both for bleach and for ash, until a loss was caused. Under these circumstances the largest of the alkali manufacturers, both here and elsewhere, agreed to reduce the production of bleach, and as they found they could not compete in the matter of soda ash with the makers of the article by the ammonia process, they agreed that the production of bleach shuold be restricted by 10 per cent. This had the desired effect. Soon after the arrangement came into operation the prices of bleaching powder increased; since then there had been a farther reduc- tion of 5 per cent, in the make and it was not anticipated that any further reduction would be found necessary. It was not the wish, and in saying this he believed he was speaking the views of the largest manufacturers, to force up the prices to an excessive degree. It would be against their interest to do so, for it would only•lead to competition and further production. With the improvement in bleach- ing powder had also occurred a general improvement in the other branches of the trade, so that the directors had good reason to say the prospects for the present year were very satisfactory. They expected to effect a saving from the new gas works; but those at Weston were in a very dilapi- dated state, and must be renewed during the present year. The contracts for pyrites which expired this year had been I renewed for the following three years at a considerable re- duction for sulphur, although the .terms for copper were not , so favourable.—Mr. Ifigson seconded the motion, which was carried.—Messrs. C. Langton and E. W. Rayner were re-elected directors, and the sum of .£9OO was voted to the board as remuneration. Messrs. Harmood, Banner and Son t were re-appointed auditors, and votes of thanks to Mr. Charles Wigg, managing director, and to the chairman were passed unanimously.
OUR LONDON LETTER.

OPENING OF THE SESSION—THE PLAIN STORY OF THE COLLAPSED DEBATE—EXCITING CHASE AFTER THE PREMIER AFFAIRS IN THE SOUDAN—CHINESE GORDON'S JOURNEY—POTT- ING A PROPHET—A NIZ AM SHOPPING—BANK- RUPT M.P.'s A PENDING ARREST—FRED BURNABY IN THE SOUDAN—SIR FREDERICK LEIGHTON'S FORTHCOMING WORK IRVING AND ELLEN TERRY THE QUEEN'S NEW BOOK.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

The Parliamentary Session, as far as it goes, does not pro- mise well from the point of view of public business. It be- gan with a fiasco, and has continued through a wrangle. The collapse of the debate on Mr. Bourke's amendment was a very simple accident, which it is difficult for Sir Henry Wolff with grave countenance to affect to misunderstand or misconstrue. What happened simply was that Mr. Bourke, a good man but a dull speaker, talked the House into a dinner hour, finishing up with an audience of something like a dozen. Mr. Gladstone, who had listened almost up to the end of the speech, went away and left instructions with Sir Charles Dilke that he was to speak at half-past nine. Sir Charles, thus re- lieved from responsibility, left the House, when Baron de Worms rose, and only Lord E. Fitzmaurice represented the Government on the Treasury Bench. Baron de Worms, who is usually good for three quarters of an hour, spoke for only a quarter. There was no one on the Liberal side to follow. Sir Stafford Northcote, who had put up Baron de Worms peremptorily, stopped Mr. Onslow, who would have followed, and the debate died out.y This is a plain matter- of-fact statement of the matter, from which each one may judge for himself who was to blame, and above all whether it was reasonable or justifiable to occupy the greater part of Wednesday afternoon in solemnly discussing the matter.

Mr. Gladstone has baffle back to his work as full of life and energy as if he were still ten years off seventy-four. A colleague to whom fell the duty of reporting the Pre- mier's replies to the four deputations that called upon him last week gives an amusing account of the Premier's ac- tivity. Having finished in Downing-street the reporter packed up his notes and pencil, seized his hat and hurried over to the India Office, to find Mr. Gladstone there before him. A second speech; increased swiftness of movement; the reporter was back at Downing-street, where, in another room, was the Premier facing a new deputation with not a hair turned. By this time the spirit of emula- tion had risen strong in the reporter's breast. The next trysting place was the Foreign Office, and he Made up his mind at whatever cost ho would beat the Premier. As soon as the speech was over he bolted, reached the Foreign Office, and near the top of the flight of stairs, mounting two steps at a time, was the Prime Minister. With three speeches on his note book, and the prospect of a fourth, the reporter felt he could not not mount two steps at a time, and so Mr. Gladstone won in every heat.

The defeat of Baker Pacha's forces in the Soudan con- clusively proves the wisdom of Ministers in peremptorily declining to conquer the Soudan and ;hand it over to Egypt. It is not in the course of nature for the stronger to be held in thrall by the weaker. The manhood of the Arabs who inhabit the Soudan is proved to be of far higher quality than that of the Egyptians, who coulhl no more hold them in leash than a kitten could a bull.dog. Nothing in the history of war is 'so pitiable as the conduct of the Egyptian so called troops, when attacked by the Arabs. That they should run away was a conclusion not unexpected. But that they should lie flat down on their faces and scream and whine till the Arabs made an end of them with spear thrusts is beyond measure contemptible. The policy of the Government in this matter is very clear. It was set forth by Lord Derby last night at the House dinner of the Na-, tional Liberal Club. While protecting the Red Sea Do rts said Lord Derby, the Government will not engage the hon- our and resources of this country in the impossible task of recovering the Soudan for Egypt. It is a comfort to have this assurance set forth in plain language, and to know that the Government are not likely to be moved from the straight path by the jeers and taunts of members of a party who brought about the war in Afghanistan and the sorrow and disgrace of the South African eampaign.

The journey of Chinese Gordon across the pathless desert is watched with absorbing interest. Since General Roberts disappeared on his famous march there has been nothing like this hidden and lonely tramp of the chivalrous Gordon. The papers laid before the House yesterday trace the history of the mission, and shew how the intentions of the Govern- ment, formed early in December, were frustrated by the disinclination of the Khedive to have Gordon anywhere about him. This dislike is mutual. I have seen a letter written by Gordon to an English Officer who was about to proceed on a mission to Egypt. In this Gordon warns him above all things not to trust Tewfik, with respect to whom he uses exceedingly plain language. The interview of the two men when Gordon passed through Cairo must have been curious to witness, for the Englishman is not so good at temporising in manner or accommodating in language. The opinion of men who know the country and the people is painfully unanimous in the opinion that Gordon will not escape with his life. He is, however, a tough customer to tackle, and has for a man of pronounced piety slain more men with his own hands than anyone except the prophet Elisha, whom in other respects he much resembles. There are many stories of the deeds of his tertible right hand. That of his potting the inspired Arab during his last visit to the Sou- dan shows his'grira humour. Moving down a river to re- join his forces the operations were watched by a sort of a wizard, who, with uplifted hands, stood on a high place and prophesied unutterable things against Gordon. After this had gone on for aboat an hour Gordon took up his rifle. "A most unhealthy place to prophecy in," he said, and the prophet toppled over with a bullet through his brain.

• • - The Times is the only paper which finds room for tele- graphic accounts of the ceremonies attendant on the instal- lation of the Nieam of Hyderabad. Yet the affair is watched with intensest interest throughout India. Hyderabad is one of the richest of the native States that are permitted to keep up a sort of independence. They have their own prince, who keeps up his court, his little army, and his rate of taxation, particularly the latter. As far as the people are concerned, they pay dearly for this shadowy indepen- dence since the taxation is higher, and trade less active in the semi-independent states than in those which come directly under English Government. Hyderabad is deeply in debt, though no one would think 5o t 0 meet the young Ni- zarn out shopping. I had this good fortune in Benares the other day. The Nizam was on his way to Calcutta to see the Exhibition, where I believe he bought as much as loaded a railway van. He entered wtih his suite a shop in Benares, where I chanced to be looking over the famous in- laid brass work. The NiZRM stayed about half an hour, and in that time bought nearly a third of the stock, for which it was evident he cared no more than if the works of art were se many bricks. It was the custom for the Nizato to fling about money with a princely hand, and the present holder of the title was equal to his duty. He is a young man just turned eighteen, of boyish appearance, with a
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 9, 1884.
pleasant face. He speaks English admirably, as do all his highest officers. With a Nizam of eighteen, who has a Prime Minister of twenty-one, Hyderabai is likely to have a cheerful time.

The nation at the present time loses the services of more than one man of the House of Commons whose private affairs have led him into bankruptcy, whilst against another well-known member a county court judge has just issued an order for his committal to prison. What will come of this is a matter not without interest. According to the law members of Parliament are free from arrest during the sitting of Parliament, and for such period preceding the opening of a session as would give them opportunity to reach Westminster. The plaintiff in the action against Captain Aylmer seems de- termined to go to extremities, and possibly before this letter is published you may hear of the arrest, unless, indeed, the member for Maidstone or some of his friends produce the small sum at issne. With respect to She other members who have been adjudged bankrupt, the law declares them incapable of sitting and voting in the House for one year from the data of the order of adjudication, unless within that time the order b 3 annulled or the cre- ditors satisfied. They need not be paid 20s in the 2. If at the end of this year of grace the order I be not annulled, and the creditors not satisfied, the Court would certify the feat to the Speaker, who would forth- with declare the seat vacant. What usually happens, and what is not unlikely to follow in at least one of the cases alluded to, is that the member would apply far the Chiltern Hundreds, and a fresh election would take place. It is within my knowledge that early last year Captain Aylmer intimated to the Conservative leaders a desire to retire from the representation of Maidstone. But he was asked to hold on till a more convenient season for fighting the boroagh. Colonel Burnaby is safe at Suakim, and the anxiety of his many friends is set at rest. Burnaby went out in his private capacity, ostensibly with the intention of writing a book, but really to see 90/110 fighting, for which his soul yearns. I never knew a man more anxious to get killed, or who has had narrower escapes. He was all through the last Carlist war, and performed some deeds of personal prowess which make his name familiar in bye-places of Spain to this day. But he has gone out to the Soudan strictly en amateur, and the accounts of the massacre on the road to Tokar are silent as to the part be took in the eagagement. He was like the Quaker in " Uncle Tom's Cabin," who happened to be on the rock where the fugitive slave had entrusted himself. When the slave-owner's head and shoulders appeared above the entrenchment, the Q iaker quietly observing. "Friend, thee is not wanted here," shoving him ever. He was not there for belligerent purposes, but all the same, he broke the slaver's neck. Burnaby was a mere onlooker at Tebs, but if any Arabs came within reach of his sword arm (an uncommonly long reach) the subsequent proceedings would interest them no more.

Sir F. Leighton has not quite finished his picture of " Cyrnon and Iphigenia," which is great in 5.1Z3 as well as in subject; but it will be ready for the Royal Academy Exhibition. The other three or four works which he tells me he will exhibit are lesser stars round a great planet, but will nevertheless shine with a lustre of their own. They include a charming girl of the auburn type of beauty, clad in a jacket of warm brown, a dark hat trimmed with fur, and a handkerchief around her neck harmonising with her fair hair. Another is the portrait of a lady, likewise dressed in a costume of warm brown relieved by a pale amber feather in her hat. A third is a little child, who must be younger sister of the model for " Kittens" of last year. She makes a very pretty picture, reclining asleep on a cushion of green in a simple dress of dark grey and white frill. Sir Frederick also showed me the handsome silver bowl and album lately presented to him on his retirement from the active colonelship of the Artists Volunteer Corps he has so long commanded. The album, which is mounted with silver and beautifully de- signed, contains an illuminated address and the signatures of about seven hundred old and present members of the Corps.

The stories about Irving playing to thin houses in the ' United States are sheer nonsense. He has had an unquali- fied success, and will bring home a mint of money. At the , same time it is true that in the States, as here, the pecu- liarities of his acting are matters of direrse comment. His Hamlet in particular tickles the midriff of the Americans, who are also exercised by the circumstances that the ghcst of Hamlet's father visits the mundane sphere arrayed in a sage green grown. Why, if he comes at all, he should not wear a sage green gown it is hard to say. For Ellen Terry there is unbounded and un- qualified admiration. When she was at Baltimore she *gave a dinner to a party exclusively formed of ladies. This is a curious American custom which reaches its most painful exaggeration when the social meal is a lunch. It is not at all uncommon fora lady to give a luncheon to her friends, the meal beginning at one or two o'clock, and lasting up to seven. This is an arrangement which makes men thank Heaven they are excluded from the scene.

The Queen's Book is to be issued on Monday, and the price fixed by her special direction being comparatively low, the:first edition will consist of 10,000 copies. The book is awaited with much interest in the political and social world, for it is well known that whilst abstaining from political comment, Her Majesty has a good deal to say both about Lord Beaconsfield and Mr. Gladstone.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the offices, Bridge- water-street, on Wednesday morning. There were present the Revs. Canon Barclay, Father Fennelley, Messrs. Nor- man. J. Pritchard, P. Brisc ,e, R. Lea, and F. Rigby (clerk).

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COM- MITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. W. Handley presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Simpson, P. Briscoe, F. A. Lake, T. Riley, W. 'Brookes (secretary), and J. D. Jones (librarian).—The Librarian reported that during the month of January there had been 1,301 borrowed from the lending library, a decrease of 261 compared with the corresponding month last year. From the reference department there had been issued 205 volumes, making a total of 1,506, classified as follows :—Theology 24, phil- osophy 14, history travels biography 200, science and art 68, poetry 18, prose fiction 1,109, and miscellaneous 731. The Secretary tendered his resignation, observing that his reason for taking this step was that his duties in connection with the Commissioners demanded all his attention.—The resignation was accepted on the motion of Mr. Lake, who expressed his regret at Mr. Brooke's retirement,.—lt was understood that the appointment of Mr. Jones would be moved at the nest meeting.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present , the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. W. Handley, T. Norman, R. Ashton, J. Mclntyre, J. Highfield, J. Stokes, J. Challoner, J. G. Hamilton' J. Weir, W. Whittaker, C. Rigby, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.)—A letter was read from the Local Govern- ment Board with reference to the bill of costs incurred by Mr. Dolby, the district auditor, in recovering certain sums of money certified to be due from William Tipping, late overseer for the townships of Halton, Walton Inferior, and Walton Superior. The costs, the letter stated, were to be charged to the respective parishes to which the accounts related.—Mr. RIGBY : That will do for me. They are well qualified to pay.—Mr. WEIR thought it was hardly right for the three townships to pay the costs. They ought to come out of the common fund.—Mr. HANDLEY inquired what the other townships had done to incur the expenditure, but he received no reply, and the subject dropped.—There was no , other business of public interest.

div.head: COURAGEOUS WESTON LANDLADY.
div.p: A COURAGEOUS WESTON LAND- LADY.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Seneor, a boatman, 60 years of age, was brought up in custody charged with stealing 25., the property of Thomas Roughsedge, I landlord of the Dock Hotel, Weston.— Superintendent Williamson said on Thursday the 24th ult. between one and two o'clock Mrs. Roughsedge was getting her din- ner, when she beard the gingle of coin in the bar. On go- ing there she found the prisoner leaning over the counter with his hand in the till. She asked him if that was not the second time she had caught him with his hand in the drawer. He replied "I haven't touched anything," and then made his escape as Mra. Roughsedge called upon her husband to fetch the police. Mrs. Roughsedge ran round and caught hold of the prisoner's coat collar Just as he was disappearing through the vault door. He gave her a violent blow in the 'chest with his list, and she was compelled to release him. Her husband followed • hint to Runcorn, but ' he made his escape, and was only captured at Nurthwich on Saturday. About two shillings had been stolen from the till. This statement was corroborated by Mrs. Roughsedge and P.C. Finney.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty, and stated that he oily went into the house for a glass of beer.— Superintendent Williamson said there WAS nothing against the prisoner's character on the books of the police.—ln con- sideration of the prisoner's age and previous good character, a Sae of 10s and costs was imposed.—The Bench advised Mrs. Roughsedge to have a snap lock placed upon the till.

div.head: "ELF.CTION OF CIIAIRMAN AND VICE.CHAIRILAN.
div.p: "ELF.CTION OF CIIAIRMAN AND VICE.CHAIRILAN.

Mr. PRITCHARD said there would he no difference of opinion on the proposition he was about to submit, that the Rev. Canon B,arclay be appointed chairman for the ensuing three years. During the last six yeara the II ,ard had had his services at their disposal in that position. and the busi- ness had been conducted to the satisfaction of the Board and the public at large. His well known business capacity and his intimate knowledge with educational matters had been of the greatest assistance in carrying forward the business they had before them in the past. But further than that, where practicable it was bath desirable and proper that a gentleman of the scholarly attainments of Canon Barclay should be induced to take the presidency of an educational , Board of this character. He believed his appointment would meet with the approval of the members of the Board, and he thought would be according to the wishes and de- sires of the community which they represented.—Mr. BRISCOE had great pleasure in seconding the motion, and he quite agreed with the remarks male by Mr. Pritchard.— The motion was carried unanimously, and the Rev. Canon BARCLAY took the chair. He said he was very much obliged to the proposer for the complimentary terms he had spoken of his past services. It was gratifying to see such confidence evinced by gentlemen, three of whom he had sat with for nine years as member of the Board, and six years as chairman. He only hoped that his f stun conduct would justify the appointment they had so kindly made; and he did say it was kind, because his health was not what it was, and he did not feel so much up to the work as he used to do. But he thought with God's blessing his health would be restored, and he hoped that his future proceedings would justify the confidence placed in him.—The Rev. Father FENNELLEY then moved that Mr. James Pritchard be ap- pointed vice-chairman for the next three years* They all knew that he was elected a member of the first Board nine years ago, and had been re-elected at every succeeding Board since. They all know the attention he had paid to the busi- ness of the Board, the knowledge of the Education Acts which he had displayed, and the great interest and zeal he had taken in the promotion of the educa- tion of the children.—Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion, observing that Mr. Pritchard would be the right man in the right place—The proposition was unanimously carried.— Mr. Pnuctratin returned thanks for the honour which the Board had conferred upon him. He trusted that the chair- man for the coming three years would be able to attend the meetings so constantly and regularly as he had done in the past, so that his duties as vice-chairman would be exceed- ingly small, and more of honour than of work.

div.head: AEDIT.
div.p: THE AEDIT.

The CLERK reported that the annual audit of the accounts was made on the 11th January, and the auditor had certi- fied the correctness of the accounts. The total amount of the expenditure was £525 4g. 5d., and the expenditure for the purposes of the Act £392 is. 4d.

div.head: VISITOR'S REPORT.
div.p: VISITOR'S REPORT.

Mr. BOWYER, the visitor, presente I his monthly report. It stated that the adventure school kept by Mrs. Ainsworth, in Suffolk-street, Duke's-field, is being crowded to excess. , There is now on the register at this school 38 children, principally girls, varying from 7to 13 years of age. On the 23rd January be visited this school, and found 28 chil- dren all crowded together in one small room 11 feet square. There were no desks in the room, and very few seats. He had several times spoken to the teacher about overcrowd- ing, but she still persisted in admitting more scholars. The register of attendance was not reliable, as he had several times called and found children attending whose names had not been on the register. He further stated,that she had a family of five children, all residing in the same house. He also reported a list of cases which had been dealt with by the committee, and as no improvement had taken place in the attendance it would be necessary to bring the cases before the magistrates.— The visitor was instructed to caution Mrs. Ainsworth and to prosecute several persons for contravening the Education Act.—The CHAIRMAN, referring to the work of the past year, said the magistrates had assisted the Board et onder- fully.—The CLERK observed that there had been fewer obstacles placed in the way of educational work In Runcorn than in any other place.—The VISITOR, in reply to the clerk, said there had been 80 persons summoned before the magistrates during the year, and only three cases had been dismissed.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, under the presidency of the Rev. John Lock- wood, and there were present—Messrs. C. Reynolds, J.P., A. Thomas, J.P., A. Thomas, J.P., Stokes, Challoner, R. Ashton, Mclntyre, Hamilton, C. Rigby, J. Weir, J. High- field, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. IL Linaker (deputy clerk), J. Adams (deputy medical officer'', and J. Farrington (nuisance inspector). MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT. . .

The MEDICAL OFFICER (air. J. G. Bride) presentel his annual report. It WAS a very elaborate compilation extend- ing to 24 folios, and stated that the area of the Authority's district WAS 45,941 statute acres. included 36 townships, and had a population in 18E1 of 18,887. During 1883 the deaths of 337 persons, 205 males and 132 females, for all ages Find from all causes, were recorded in the district, as against 327 in 1882, showing an increase of 10. The death-rate was 175 per 1,000 of the population. Of the deaths 83 or 43 per 1.000 were of children under one year, and 103, or 54 per 1,003 of persons aged GO years and upwards. The births recorded during the year were 600; 322 males and 278 females, as against 626 in 1882; equal to an annual rate of 31.2 per 1,000, showing a decrease of 26. There had been 14 outbreaks of infectious disease, but two only of these assumed the character of an epidemic. His sugges- tion that forms of notification of infectious disease should , be printed and forwarded to the medical practitioners and registrars was adopted by the Authority this year with satisfactory results. No less than 28 forms of notification giving the fullest information having reached him since his last distribution of them. The general condition of the district at the end of the year was very satisfactory. There had been a mgked falling off in the number of cases of scarlatina during the last quarter. During the year he ' visited every portion of the district, sometimes in company with the inspector of nuisances. The medical officer gave an elaborate account of these visits, and, referring to Kings- ley, said the frequent occurrence of typhoid fever and other zymotic diseases had, led to the belief that some serious evil lurked in the brook, and some measures should be taken to prevent people from drinking water taken from it. The filthy practice of throwing excreta into the water of this brook was much to be condemned. The water taken from the wells had been found pure.—Mr. FARRINGTON, the nuisance inspector, also presentei his annual report. Mr. MCINTYRE moved, and Mr. Asn'Torr seconded, that the report be printed and circulated amongst the Guar- dians.

div.head: TYPHOID rEvtxt OUTBREAK AT FRODSHAM.
div.p: THE TYPHOID rEvtxt OUTBREAK AT FRODSHAM.

Mr. ADAMS (the deputy medical officer or health) pre. sented a report on the prevalence of typhoid fever within the district of the Authority. At a cottige in Bradley. Frodsham Lordship, occupied by John Woods, Sarah Woods, his wife, aged 40 years, had been attacked by typhoid fever. The source of infection in this case was in his opinion to be traced to her personal attendance on the family of Thomas Once, alias Carter, also of Bradley. who hid already been reported to the Authority as suffering from typhoid fever. The drinking water used at these houses was impure, being turbid, and containing decaying vegetable matter and living organisms. Four persons had been attacked with the disease at Frodshatn Bridge. The source of the disease was, in his opinion, to be found in the impure drinking water at present used by so many of the inhabitants of the district. He had also to report the oc- currence of typhoid fever at Manley at a house situated near the school and occupied by John Blythe. The patient was Martha Blythe, h s wife, aged 53 years. This else was in his opinion an imported one, and had not arisen in con- sequence of local sanitary defects. The sanitary arrange- ments and water supply appear to be efficient. In all these cases he had issued urgent recommendations to ensure the efficient isolation of those suffering from the disease, also to disinfect the premises and to disinfect and afterward bury all the excreta coming from the patients. By these measures as also by the use of a superior water supply, he trusted soon to be able to report that the disease had been stamped out. The CLERK observed that in accordance with the resolution passed at the last meeting of the Authority he had written to the Local Governtweit Board calling attention to the outbreaks of typhoid fever at Frodsham Bridge, and asking the Board to report the result of the inquiry held by Major Tulloch it Frodshain on the 6th December last, but that he had received no reply to his letter.—lt was resolved unanimously on the motion of Mr. Mclerrynit, seconded by Mr. R. ASHTON, That this Authority regrets the apparent indifference of the. Local Government Board to the facts reported to them, and that the clerk again write to them urging the necessity of their giving attendance to the sub- ject matter of the Local Government Board inquiry held by Major Tulloch above referred to."

div.head: TTEVir HOUSE AT HELSEY.
div.p: TTEVir HOUSE AT HELSEY.

The Inspector of Nuisances reported that proceedings had been taken in the above case in accordance with direc- tions given on Decemler 11th, 1883, and the owner was ordered to pay the costs amounting to 58 sd, and he was directed to produce the requisite certificate of occupation to the Justices at the neat sitting of the Court. Full par- ticulars had been sent to the owner since the case was heard as to the mode of obtaining such certificate. The owner had replied to the effect that he considered it an act of in- terference on the part of the Inspector. After some con- sideration it was decided that if he (the owner) did not comply with the requisition of the Justices, further pro- ceedings be instituted. WATER SUPPLY TO PROUST:IAM BRIDGE. Samples pf water from three sources of water supply 'about Frodsham Bridge had been submitted for analysis, and returned as being second-class waters, but it , was thought that the samples could scarcely be considered to be fair samples, .and the Inspector was directed to submit other samples. PUBLIC PUMP AT ANTROBUS. ' A plan and estimate were submitted for the erection of a Ipublic pump in Bvber's Lane, Antrobus, and after the in- spection of the same, it was adopted, the cost being £23 10s.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF _COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF _COMMIS- SIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Wednesday, Mr. John Meadowcroft, the chairman, presiding. There were also present Dr. Steele, Messrs. Briscoe, Fisher, White, Lake, Whittaker. Timmins. Williams Dobson, R. Shaw, T. Norman, P. Speakman, J. W. Lightburn, W. H. Linear (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretar)), Dr. Mouritz (medical officer), and M. Barker (surveyor.)

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

Dr. Motfarrs (the medical —officer) presented his monthly report, which stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 26. Four deaths were due to brain disease, four to pulmonary com- plaints, four to liver disease, three to phthisia, two to croup, two to dropsy, two to scarlatina, and two to cancer. Atro- phy, peritonitis, and senile decay account for one each. Mel:teeth rate was 20 per 1,000. Of the above deaths five occurred amongst children five years and under. HIGHWAY AND gANITARY COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committ;e—ce-aa.ined-T resolution that the part of Blantyre-street running parallel with the railway arch be named Brindley-street.—Letters have been forwarded to M. Nistor Clolus, complaining of a nuisance from the glycerine works.—Mr. J. N. Lello wrote with reference to completing the flagging in Halton-road, and the secretary was instructed to reply that the subject would have attention when the estimate of the next rate was under consideration.—The Surveyor reported that the carrying out of the bakehouse regulations was now trans- ferred to the Sanitary Authority and that the duties would now devolve on the Sanitary Committee. He suggested that bills setting forth the several regulations be printed and circulated throughout the district, and a copy left with the occupiers of all bakehouses. The committee issued instruc- tions according to the suggestion.—The Surveyor also pointed out a recent decision of the Local Government Board that Cooper-street aught to have been made at the expense of the ratepayers at large. He thought that some other streets which had not been yet adopted but which had been made in a certain way for 30 years would prove to be highways reparable by the ratepayers. He referred to Cross-street, Princess-street, Nelson-street, and perhaps some other. If this was so and the Board was responsible for the repair and safety of these, some portion of them should be done every year until they were complete. In consequence of the estimates being cut down for the last two or three years the roads generally were not in so good a condition as it was desirable they should be. Much of the flagging in different parts of the town was becoming more or less dilapidated, a great quantity of it having been down more than 30 years. It was resolved that the surveyor sub- mit an estimate of the cost of putting the following streets in a proper state of repair, viz.: Mason-street, Old Pen- nington's-row, Princess-street, Nelson-street, and Cross- street. It was recommended that Messrs. Meadowcroft, IFairhurst, Norman, Fisher, and Briscoe, be appointed a committee to consider the question of providing a public clock; that Mary Jackson be appointed caretaker of the Town Hall, to keep the Board's offices clean, and attend to the heating apparatus, and that she be paid 10s per week, dating from January Ist, 1884, also to be provided with coal, gas, and water, and to be free of rent. The minutes were passed orl the motion of Mr. T. Sou- MAN, seconded by Mr. P. SPEAKMAN.

div.head: SHIP CANAL SCHEME.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME.

The minutes of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee contained a resolution that seven copies of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill (session 1884) be obtained, and that the property owners, manufacturers, traders, and others be in- vited to meet the committee to consider the bill, and in what way the scheme will affect the interests of Runcorn. On the .17th January the conference was held.

Mr. R. SILAW 'remarked that at this conference a represen- tative committee was appointed. At a meeting of this committee several gentlemen were appointed to meet the promoters of the Ship Canal, and they did so. He believed the promoters had shown their willingness to meet the Commissioners in what they consider would benefit the town, and had agreed that if the Manchester Ship Canal Company purchased the Bridgewater Navigation Company they would have a great monopoly, and that it would only be fair to the trade of Runcorn that there should be a deep water dock, so that they would be in a much better position than if the docks remained in their present condition. It was obvious that if one com- pany owned both the waterways to Manchester their object would be to divert as far as possible the traffic along the deep canal. It was quite apparent that if Runcorn could get a dock which would admit vessels of 2,000 tons burden the position of the traders would be much improved. The Ship Canal Company said they were quite willing to do tkis and they had asked the committee to meet them on Tuesday next with a draft clause embodying what the traders and others considered would meet their ,wishes. These pre- liminary stages would not be costly, but if they had to op- pose the bill they would }save to ask the ratepayers for powers. . .

At a subsequent stage of the proceedings the Law Clerk was instructed to draft a clause. The Property and Legal Committee recommended that the balance £75 4s 11d, due to Mr. W. H. Linaker in re- spect of his charges in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal Bill in 1883, be paid. It was also recommended that legal proceedings be taken against Mr. IL Beckett for the recovery of the account for repairing lamp in Greenway- road, if the amount was not paid within 14 days._
Mr. Snew moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded the confir- mation of the minutes.

Dr. STEELE moved an amendment that Mr. Beckett be prosecuted under the bye-laws, An d took advantage of the opportunity to express his regret that the ratepayers should be put to the gat expense of a deputation going to London respecting the Ship Canal,Bill, when they had a law clerk who was quite competent to conduct the business. He I thought Mr. Linaker's bill a very reasonaLle one. Mr. LIGHTBERN pointed out that the deputation was ap- pointed by the Board. Mr. Snew agreed that only the law clerk should have gone, but it was not the time now to blame the depu- tation for doing what the Board asked them to do. The Lew CLERK said the poor bill had been pretty well thumbled, and the chairman of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee (Mr. Shaw) had taken the liberty of placing the word "doubtful" against the first item, thus expressing doubt whether he (the Law Clerk) had received instructions on the subject. Mr. Sitaw: lam very glad that ihe Law Clerk sees that ' we are looking after these matters. _ _
The Law CLERIC did not think it was fair to place such remarks on the bill when he had received instructions. Mr. NORMAN contended the deputation was not too large.

The minutes were then passed. THE FINANCES. The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for December, including £5Ol Is. 101 for sale of the offices in Bridge-st. and £638 13s 6d for a general district rate, was £1,209 16s 6d Accounts amounting to £930 16s 3d were recommended for payment. A letter from the Local Govern- ment Board with reference to the loan account was read It was recommended that an application be made for a provisional order to amend the local Act as to the repay- ment of loans.

Mr. FISH-ER moved the confirmation of the minntes, and referring to the leans, said they had not been worked exactly in accordance with the views of the Local Govern- ment Board. From the accounts, it appeared that from 1853 to 1874 there was something like £16,995 had been borrowed on loan, and since then there had been £11,895 paid off, leaving a balance of £5,100. According to the books there was standing in the bank to loan account £263, and at the end of next March the Board would have to deposit £226 more, which it had been customary to put on one side as,a sinking fund. These sums amounted to £489, which deducted from £5,100, would leave £4.611 to be dealt with. The Finance committee wished to apply to the Local Governmentßoard for powers to consolidate these loans and extend the repayment over 30 years. Now they were paying about £4lO a year including interest, but if they got the desired permission they would have to pay only £266 per annum, which would be a lessening of the expenses by £144. This was a matter which ought to be settled at once. Five years ago a loan of £6,000 was taken up, and about £6OO had been paid off. If they got the provisional order to deal with this also they would be putting themselves in a very easy position. Mr. Noumea; seconded the motion. Mr. LIGHTBIIHN took it that there was something like £lO,OOO due from Runcorn, and he thought it was very creditable to be in that position. The minutes were carried. THE FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

In accordance with the notice he had given Mr. Smaw moved "That the resolution, dated January 3rd, 1882 as to the appointment of the Library Committee be rescinded and the following substituted, viz.: That the Library Committee should consist of the chairman of the Board and six gentle- men appointed by the Commissioners annually. These resolutions to take effect after the election in September Inext." He remarked that seven gentlemen would be quite sufficient to manage the business of the committee, and pointed out the inconveniences of the present system of electing the committee. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion, which was passed without dissent. IMPROVEMENTS AT THE RAILWAY STATION. Mr. Nortmes said the chairman, himself, and Mr. Barker had that morning met Mr. Shaw, of the London and North- Western Railway Company at Runcorn station. Mr. Shaw informed them that it was intended to make a good footpath to the railway station from the gates, on the left hand side, and he wished the Board to make a crossing across the road leading to the path. The CHAIRMAN observed that he had pointed out that the left side was not used at all, but Mr. Shaw replied that they hoped to put the footpath in that condition that it would be used. _
_ Mr. NORMLN moved, and Mr. SPEIIIMAN seconded, that the crossing be made at a cost not exceeding £l5.

THE LIVERPOOL WATERWORKS SC—HEILE. Mr. FISLIER said he and Mr. H. Linaker, of Frodsham, had made an inspection with the view of ascertaining the best place for the Board of Commissioners to put a junction in the pipes being laid for the Liverpool water scheme. Mt. Linaker had since written him stating that the best places to put in a junction and obtain a supply of water would be on the road from Frodsham to Warrington, a little on the east of Sutton Weaver station, or on the road a little to Norton Tower. The distance pipes would have to be laid to Runcorn waterworks was in the former case 4,147 yards, and in the latter about 2,000 yards. If the pipes were laid

1 the longer distance they would be along the public high- ' way, and way-leaves would be saved, which was very int. [ portant. Mr. Parry, the engineer to the Corporation of Liverpool, said either point would suit. Mr. Fisher con- cluded by moving that the junction be made near Norton Tower. Dr. STEELE seconded. .. ' _

Mr. TIMMINS moved an ameadment that the junction be made on NorthwiCh-road, where they would be more likely to get a supply of water for Halton as the pressure would be greater. A junction in Northwich-road would be worth thousands of ponds more than at Norton as the land was more likely to be built upon. Mr. NORMAN seconded the amendment. The LAW CLERK stated the Board could not sell water anywhere outside the Runcorn district. Mr. TIMMINS : We can sell water to anyone we wish. The LAW CLERK: Only within the Commissioners' dis- trict.
Mr. FISFIER'S rnotion was then passed by seven votes to six, and the meeting concluded.

• RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY- , ALLEGATIONS AGAINST THE LATE SECRETARY. The 43rd half yearly meet* of the members of the Run- corn Co-operative Industrial and Provident Society was held on Tuesday evening,, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Riley. There was a good attendance. From the statement of accounts which was read, it appeared that the total sales for the half-year amounted to £34,063 78 lid, being an increase of £554 over the corresponding period of 1882. The profits, after paying interest and trade expenses, amounted to £4,652 lh 4d, which, less checks purchased and drapery club bonus, left the gam of £4,501 Ifis posable as dividend at the rate of 2s 8d in the £.—Mr. Ward (secretary of the wholesale society, Manchester) addressed the meeting, and observed that while the balance sheet was certainly reliable, he could not say that it was accurate in every respect, and advised (he members to have the books audited on a proper basis in fhture. He recommended them to leave the appointment of a secretary in the hands of the committee, who should also superintend and control the accounts. He understood that they were indifferent about creating a reserve fund, but he would remind them that the greater the reserve fund the greater their security. The balance sheet was adopted. Mr. R. Royle moved that a vote of sympathy with the family of their late secretary, Mr. Gleave, be passed.—Mr. Withington seconded the motion, which was carried.—A member asked Mr. Wood if he had found anything discre- ditable to the late secretary when examining the books.— Mr. Wood said no. There were a few items which had not been entered correctly. The arrangement of the books was not on the most approved system. He hoped a new system would be introduced, and that there would be no necessity for them to call in hi m or anyone else again to assist in making their balance sheet.—The Secretary pro tern (W. Upton) said there was a slight discrepancy in the accounts. He went to Mr. Gleave before his death, and be had suffi- cient money to reeet any discrepancy. He believed they were purely errors on Mr. 411tleave's part and that be had no evil intention. The speaker stated the secretary had almost to work day and night to keep body and soul together. (Ap- plause.) They ought to pay their officers better, and not give the workmen the same money they gave their Secretary or treasurer. (Applause.)—Mr. Appleby (of Manchester) said the lata secretary had an obsolete system of bookkeep- ing, by which it was scarcely possible to keep the accounts in a satisfactory manner. He Advised them to exhibit no temper, but act as men of sense aed leave the appointment of officers in the hands of the committee, and let them be sufficiently paid.—Mr. Wood said when a man oa his death bed could say "If there is any deficiency take it from my investment in the society," ought they in a true Christian spirit to demand more? (Applause.) It was only a matter of three or four pounds. Let it rest, and let the secretary sleep in peace and not cast any reflection upon the family he had left behind him. (Applause.)—Mr.R. Hoyle thought it was a great shame to cast any reflection on Mr. Gleave. (Hear, hear.)—The speaker was unable to proceed in conse- quence of the uproar in the room, and he was met by cries of "Sit down." Personal recriminations were indulged in in various parts of the audience, but at length the noise subsided, and it was decided that a sub-cemmlttee be ap- pointed to audit the accounts, which should in future be kept according to the system brought out by the wholesale society. The meeting then concluded.
A COWARDLY RUFFIAN AT RUNCORN. THE MOTHER-IN-LAW AGAIN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. A Thomas, William Hancock, a young fellow living in Surrey-street, was summoned on a charge of assaulting Jane Hancock, his wife.—The complainant said she could not live with her husband because his ill- usage and language were most awful. She never knew when she was doing right, and he came home from hie work at all hours in order to find her with other men. She gave him no cause whatever. She had been a widow fire years' and bad only been married to the defendant eleven weeks. On Wednesday evening, at six o'clock, he came home from his work and pushed her about and struck her because he said she had called him a foul name to another woman who lived in the next street. He then 'rent out and got drunk, and when he returned he threw her out, and she WAS out all night. She had a Lamp on her shoulder as big as an egg. He had so mercy in him. He had no patience; he would not wait a minute for his meals, nor give her a civil answer. He struck her on the head and side on VI ednesday, and she gave him no cause to do so. She had done everything she could to please him, but she could not.—Elizabeth Ann Dean, of 55. Surrey-street, said she heard the complainant scream "Murder," and saw the defendant throw complainant and her mother on their back into the street.—Mary Ann Ashcroft gave corroborative evidence.—The defendant said when be came home he pulled off his coat and waistcoat with the intention of going to bed. His mother-in-law told him to go to bed, and seed bad language. He replied, "Well, Pm going to bed," knowing that she was a woman with a bad temper. He put his foot upon the "iron stool" to unlace his shoes, when she gave him a push, and his head went against the chimney-piece. He thereupon told her that she was going out, and asked her if she saw the door. She replied that she came there before he did, and should continue to come. He then put her out, but she came in again and he pushed her.—Mr. Banks said the Bench considered it a gross assault upon his wife. He was a cowardly ruffian to abuse her in the way he had, not only striking her but throwing her into the street. She might have been seriously injured had her bead come in contact with a stone. He would be bound over to keep the peace for si2c months, himself in £lO and two sureties in £5 each ; or in default a month's imprisonment.

- - - DISESTABLISEIMENT. Sir,—Once more the air is filled with the sounds of strife on this question. Along with that other and compar,ssa question, the franchise, it now occupies largely the matslic attention, and is a fit subject for the exercise ct public opinion. I believe that this is a question upon vihic-nwe as Englishmen shall shortly be called upo.n to array our- selves, either with the attacking of the der the noisa of the conflict thickens as it n.ears us. From the green slopes of Erin te the bare mountain sides of the Prin- cipality, where even now the battle rages with characteristic fury, the invader is steadily but surely advancing to the attack in our own land. This being the case, it behoves us as Englishmen, and therefore lovers of fair play and justice, to decide which side we shall take in the battle. With the contest now going on in Wales, I contend that we, as non- residents, have no moral right to interfere. It is a question for residents, or persons having titheable property in the Principality, to decide. The principle involved with them is the same as it will be with us when our time comes. And it is this: The law allowing us to dissent, build chapels, and to support our own ministers and , forms of religion according to the dictates of our owl con- ' sciencies, shall it continue to contribute to the support of the teacher and teaching of another denomination? Now, it is evident that this is a Welsh question for Welshmen to settle; and I would ask what right have the English, or the Irish, or the Scotch, or, indeed, any other nation or people but the Welsh to interfere to prevent them attaining the ob- ject of their just desires? None whatever. And yet it is one of the anomalies of this establishment that we have the right legally, if not morally, thin to handicap our Welsh neighbours in their race for religious freedom. The Church of England being established by Act of Parliament puts it in the power of every man in the United Kingdom who pos- sess a vote, although he may be entirely unconnected by residence or property with the country, to meddle inju- riously in this matter. lam astonished that there should be any man found to uphold a system so evidently unjust. But when this man is a clergyman, who ought to be first to uphold the right and to denounce a wrong, makes the matter much worse. This remnant of the " ignorance of our ancestors," who tried to make men good and their religions opinions uniform by Act of Parliament, places the Church clergy in a most anomalous position. Dissent being lawful, the compulsory payment of tithes makes the Establishment a huge system of outdoor relief,and its clergy arrant and often arrogant paupers. Had not custom, which is apt to render the beneficiary oblivious of abuse, blinded the Church clergy to this evil, they would see how it comes to pass that the tithed regards the tithers as clerical requisitionists, taking that to which they have no moral right, although they may have the power to do so. From this galling position there is one means of escape. Let the payment of tithes be made optional, and this reproach will no longer be applicable to an honorable, and an honor- living body of men. If the Church dare so far trust her , own communicants as to do this act of justice, she would convert her enemies, if not into friends, at least, into differ- ent spectators, and free herself from the galling position of being the recipient of compulsory doles alike from the geathen, the Gentile, or the Jew.—! am, &c. JOHN PEERS. Green Bank, Penketh, February Bth, 1884.

A BROTHER'S LOVE —Robert Clarke, of Church-street, was bound over to keep the peace for 6 months for fighting with his , brother on the 26th ult. OBSTRUCTIONISTS.—John Hammond, of Horsemarket-street, was ordered to pay the costs, 31 6d, for obstructing the f tot- path In Temple.court, by a lowing a number of boxes and crates to stead thereon on the 'fitti ult.—John Lewis. of: Crown-street, was similarly dealt with for obstructing Crown- street by allowing a cart aro a number of boxes to stand thereon on the 28th and 29th ult. AN EXEMPLARY FUNISHMENT.—John Bentiy and Alfred Nooks, of Mersey-street, were sent to prison for four months with hard labour for having on the previous day aided and abetted John Felan. a soldier, to desert.—lt appeared that the soldier was on his way to Sheffield to see a relative, and the prisoners had by some means persuaded hlm to change his regimentals for a suit of plain clothes. Having obtained the poor fellow's clothes, the prisoners allowed h m to go on his way, and then repaired to Buttermarket-street, where they were found by Inspector Spinks offering the soldier's clothes for sale. It was pointed out by Sergeant Cambridge, of Orford Barracks, that a soldier, when he put on the clothing of a civi- lian, became a deserter. It seemed that the defendant went into Dallarn Forge, and the constable seeing that he was drunk insisted upon his leaving the preinoses. The defendant lovame violent, and struck the constable several times. The case, however, was not pressed, and the defendant having an excellent character he was diseharged on paying the costs. 35. With Mr. Monks, he believed- when they had a man who dealt with large sums of money they ought to give him a good salary; and although £156 a year might seem a good deal to the ratepayers, he thought if they bad to do with gentle- men in similar positions they would consider £156 a year was not an excessive salary. The MAYOR, speaking of the memorial, said it had been presented to them, and of course it was their duty to deal with it. Al hough they could not very well deal with it in the nature of a public discussion, they could cer- tainly take it into account. They rested entirely on a false Issue when the question was pat in the way Alderman Kean put it. He objected because trade in Warrington was bad. If the Town Council were asked to contribute to the Infirmary or to the Ship Canal, it would be a fair question for the Town Council to discuss— were they in a position to afford to contribute? But when they came to deal with a man's salary, the question did not at all arise. He said that, with all possible submission to those gentlemen who differed from him, the question was this, Is this servant of ours receiving adequate compensation for services rendered? That was the only question to deal with, and all the rest was "leather arid prunella." It was their duty to deal in the first instance with Mr. Fair- hurst's salary. In reference to the comparison instituted by Councillor W. Pierpoint, he might say the Town Clerk of Warrington received £5OO a year, but there were many legal duties for which he got nothing. It might be that the Town Clerk of Bury, while he was witty receiving £3OO, might have it considerably improved by other charges which he was entitled to make for professional services ren- dered. But the arrangement with Mr. Brook precluded him from doing anything of that sort; and therefore they could riot draw a reliable comparison between the Town Clerk of Bury and the Town Clerk of Warrington, without taking into consideration all the circumstances in connection with their engagements. If they were to refuse to increase any salary, do not let it be done on a false issue, but on the I ground thathe was adequately paid for what he did. Alderman HOLMES said with reference to the remarks of Alderman Burgess as to the arrangement for discussing the increase of salaries, the gossip and excitement showed the great advantage of considering them all at one time. If the salaries were increased one by one, one this month and another two months hence, the aggregate increase did not come before their minds so thoroughly as was the case when they were taken altogether. Therefore he thought it was exceeding' y wise and convenient to have adopted that scheme. There was another reason why this was done. The Borough Treasurer had to provide estimates as to haw much he would require for the various departments of the Corporation, and amongst other things the salaries had to be estimated. If the increases of salaries were taken at dif- ferent periods of the year, the calculations of the Borough Treasurer were thrown out of order. Therefore it was a good thing to have adopted that resolution. The Tom; CLERK said he had a statement which gave the salary of the Bury 'Learn Clerk at £400; he had in ad- dition £250, so that it was £650 instead of £3OO. Councillor W. PIERPOINT said his remarks were not speci- ally pointed at the Town Clerk, because he thought he was worth what he got and much more. The TOWN CLERK said he did not regard the remarks as being directed against him. Against : Alderman Kean, Councillors Ashton, Francomb, Wright, Marsh, and W. Pierpoint. THE LIGHTING OF THE TOWN. COURCBIOT PLATT, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Lighting Sub-Committee, said they recommended a number of additional lamps in various parts of the borough as the committee had to keep pace with the growth ot the town with regard to the lighting. The Council ' might congratulate themselves that there were no applications before them for the increase of salaries in this department. (A laugh,) Councillor WRIGHT seconded the adoption of the minutes, which were thereupon agreed to. STREET PAVING: A COMPLAINT. In discussing the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee, Councillor FRANCOMB referred to the rules of the Corporation which directed that the smallest pocket street must be made exactly in the same manner as they made Church-street. That might be a good thing for the Cor- poration, bat it came very hard on the ratepayers and owners of property, and he did not think it was a very sen- sible arrangement. If those streets could be paved at a much less rate, it would be an excellent thing for the town, and they would soon get every street in the town properly paved. Councillor Bonanss called the attention of the commit- tee to the state of Museum-street. It was one of the prin- cipal approaches to Bank Quay Station, and it was utterly impassable for the foot passengers. He hoped the surveyor would see his way to putting a few loads of cinders on the street. Alderman BURGESS thought that when a gentleman got up to defend or argue against the correct making of pocket streets because they were pocket streets, that gentleman did not understand the duties he owed to his constituents. Pocket streets could not under any conditions be as good as thoroughfares, and the people who lived in them were under a disadvantage. The people who built in pocket streets were of that class known as " jerry builders," who, he thought, ought not to be tolerated. Councillor FRANCOMB did not object to the paving of pocket streets, but he objected to the paving of pocket streets as they paved such as Church-street. Councillor SUTTON agreed with what Councillor Fran- comb had said, and, referring to a remark made by Alderman Burgess, said that it was useless to say that they ahould not have pocket streets, because such streets were unavoidable. It was only reasonable that persons should sell their pro- perty for building purposes, and it was equally reasonable that someone should buy it. •Councillor PLATT did not think there was any reason at all in putting down the extraordinary good streets that they were doiag in Warrington, when from all appearances those streets would never be required. ALDERMAN KEAN, the Chairman of the Committee, in replying, said that Councillor Francomb was anxious to make pocket streets at something like half the cost. He (the speaker) contended that a person living in a pocket street bad as much right to a good access to his house as a person who lived in any other kind of street. (Hear, hear.) He thou,tht that the comfort and convenience of the tenants ought to be considered. With respect to the suggestion of Cr. Burgess, that they should cart a few loads of cinders on to Museum-street, that gentleman did not know that if they did so they would make themselves liable. The Council could not do as they liked with streets that were not their own. If he, as Chair- man of that Committee, could see his way to making pocket streets at a less cost than they were doing at present he would gladly do so. The minutes were confirmed.
