HIGHWAYS AND SANITARY MATTERS. At a meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sani- tary Committee it was ordered that the arrangements with the Warrington Corporation for hospital accommodation of infectious cases from this district be continued. It was ordered that the footpath on the.south side of Earle-street, between the Viaduct Works lodge gates and Earle Cottage, be repaired, the flags re-laid, and the boulder pavement substituted with blue chequered brick pavement. It was ordered that Southworth-road be curbed and the boulder pavement broken down into macadam in such lengths and time as the surveyor reight consider best. The minutes were confirmed without comment. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this Committee, the gas works carboniz- ing account for the past month was submitted, and showed the amount of fuel used was 296 tone, 15 cwt, gas made, 2,971,100 cubic feet, averaging 10,002 feet per ton of fuel used.—The minutes were passed. FINANCES. At a meeting of the Finance Committee, a resolution was passed that Mr. Thomas Thompson, of St Helens-road, be appointed auditor in the place of Mr. Davidson, who re- fused to act. Accounts amounting to £1,092 4s were ex- amined, and cheques signed for payment.—The minutes were confirmed.

'The MAYOR : It would be competent for us to reduce the salary to the amount of fees received. The magistrates' clerk would not expect to be paid more. Alderman Horarns : But we should have to make up his salary for the first year. Counctllor W. P/RRPOINT said he should be glad if the Mayor could mention any sum which they would be likely to be called upon to pay for Mr. Wolfe Barry's ser- vices, he preparing his report, seeing that his last report cost them £546 14s 61. He questioned whether it was worth the oad £46, and he should like to know what this report was likely t cost.
Toe MAYOR said the Town Clerk waa of opinion that it would be a very inexpensive affair—something under £lOO.
The Tows CLERIC, correcting Mr. Pierpoint's figures, said Mr. Barry's charges on the last occasion amounted to .£450.

Councillor J. PIERPOINT proposed an amendment, tkat the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the clauses respecting Mr. Wolfe Barry and the increase of the magis- trates' clerk's salary. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Wairmn ssconded the amendment. The Towle CLERK said he thought it right to state that, in consequence of the urgency of the matter. Mr. Wolfe Barry had already given his advice. (Laughter.) He thought it was only fair that they should have that ex- planation. When they were dealing with Parliamentary matters, if they wished to avoid expensive opposition, they could only do so by approaching people with the object of getting suitable clauses inserted in the Bill. The advice had been got, and Mr. Barry's charges for one day were £l2.

Councillor J. PIERPOINT said he must withdraw that por- tion of his amendment. They would allow him to state that he had found fault with that sort of thing before. Con- tracts were entered inett, bills passed, and even paid before the sanction of the Council was obtained.

Alderman WEBSTER said it wasluiteiMpossible foram to deal with the matter of the magistrates clerk's salary. If they did not grant him £25 out of the £BO excess of fees, he would very probably demand the whole of the fees. The law gave it him, and they had made a bargain with him by which they were benefited.

Councillor Enebrcosts asked if they had a right to appoint a gentleman at a fixed salary independent of fees. The MAYOR said they might if they chose to make an arrangement with him. He might tell them in explanation tkat Mr. James Nicholson had some difficulty with the then existing magistrates. There was an appeal made to the Secretary oeState, and that gentleman said the Corporation had no right to make a profit out of the clerk's fees. It was competent for them to make an arrangement whereby the clerk should get an equitable proportion of those fees, and an arrangement of the kind was made, and they had received altogether some £3OO out of the fees to which Mr. White was strictly entitled. . . . . .

Councillor ScrTrox said if the clerk was entitled to the fees, then they would nat be the friends of the ratepayers if they objected to give an increase of £23. The Tows CLERK said he thought they should know that the ratepayers could not make a profit out of those fees. If the fees were in excess of the salary they must be read- justed. Councillor Buotett sail he was just about to ask a question on that very point. He thought the sooner they arrived at a more equitable arrangement the better. Councillor J. Plaupowr stated that the profit from the fees was carried to the credit of the borough rate fund, al- though Mr. Sutton said it was not taking a surplus out of the ratepayers' po:kets. The MAYOR: Exactly.

The votes were then taken, aril Mr. Councillor Pierpoint's amendment was carried. The result is that only the salaries of Messrs. Fairhurst and Riley are increased. There was no other business of interest before the Council.

Gillespie, Del-, John Hillock, a glass maker, residing in Gas-street, CroW° lane, was charged with stealing an earthenware dish and s quantity of tapioca pudding, the property of Joseph Shone, of the Old Crow Inn. Between two o'clock and half-Peet two the prisoner had some drink in the house, and When leaving picked up a dish containing the pudding, put it under his coat, and walked away. The landlord gave information to the police, and P.S. Commins afterwards apprehended the prisoner at his residence where he also found the dish, but a portion of the pudding had die - appeared. div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNEAL REPORT. __ ___
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNEAL REPORT. __ ___

Dr. J. W. WATKINS (medical officer of health) attended to read his report for the year 1883, which contained the fol- lowing items :--There were registered in the year: Males, 237 births, 82 deaths, natural incr.ase 155; females 204 births, 75 deaths, natural increase 129 ; totals, 441 births, 157 deaths, 284 natural increase. The birth rate was 39.41 and the death rate 14.03 per thousand of the population estimated to the middle of the year. Compared with 1882, there is a diminution of nearly two per -thousand. The deaths were classified as follows :--70 under five years, 87 five years and upwards. The deaths (20) from zymotic diseases were 12 73 of the whole number; the infantile mortality being 44.52 much too high for a country population. By his quarterly reports the Board had been kept informed of the health of the district, but he might summarise some of the facts rela- ting to the deaths. The only fatal case of scarlatina was imported from Wigan, and the disease did not spread. After alluding to the cases of enteric fever, the repott went on to speak of diarrhcea and continued: "As may be judged from the above tables the general health of the township during the year was good. In the absence of a compulsory registration of infectious disease it is impossible to record how many cases of such a nature there were. I regret to say that although there were in all twenty deaths from zymotio diseases, only one of these eases was notified to your Board during the life of the patient. Indeed, only four notifications of infectious diseases in all were made by private practitioners. Water supply con- tinues abundaht and good. The extension of the supply to Vista-road and the bottom of Newton Common is a boon very greatly appreciated by the residents in those locali- ties. Sewerage and Scavenging : Much requires to be done at Wargrave, but I trust the larger plan is se far developed that its accomplishment is not far distant. The connection of the greater number of the houses in Cross-lane with the new main sewer has not yet been effected ; this should be made without further delay. The sewerage.from the upper part of Newton (Rob-lane to Crow-lane) traversing the border of the Mesnes to its overflow in Newton brook near the mill renders the area of land between Park-road and the brook little better than a huge sewage tank, and the tip- pling of the materials removed from ashpits on to this same land (of which I have only just heard) is also improper, and may in future be injurious to the residents in the vicinity, and will certainly etlectually ruin the land for building dwelling-houses on. The removal of nightsoil is mainly regular and efficient. The removal of nuisances ordered by your Inspector has been carried out, as far as I know, for he has not bad to apply to me during the year in a single in stance of refusal to comply with his notice. Gas: The illuminating power and purity have both been improved since my last reference to it. Situated as Newton is close to one of the richest, if not the richest, beds of cannel coal in Great Britain, I venture to suggest to the Board that the township might be supplied with pure cannel gas ad- vantageously, provided always, waste being avoided. The cost of such gas should be economical compared with that of gas of lower illuminating power, and the benefit to the health and eye•sight of the users would be beyond all ques- tion. The electric light does not, and I believe never will, wholly supercede coal gas light. It might, therefore, be a wise economy to avail ourselves at our day of the richest treasures nature has placed at our very feet.—The CHAIR- RAN was glad to k.now the health of the district was in such every satisfactory condition.—Dr. WATKINS remarked it was below the average.—Mr. EMMETT thought they had already met Dr. Watkins' argument with reference to the latter portion of his report—that referring to the use of can- nel in snaking gas. Since the last report the gas had won- derfully improved in illuminating power and purity.—Col. McCotigronemc thouirht it would be still further improved, according to Dr. Watkins' report, if they. made full use of the " richest treasures at their feet!'—Mr. PAIMY said the Committee would consider the matter; and it was decided to refer the report to the Highway and Sanitary Com- mittee.
THE NEW CEMETERY. Following the reading of the minutes, Mr. I#OUSLEY, in reply to Mr. Emmett, observed that the amended agreement with reference te the purchase of the land for the cemetery.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTEND&NCE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTEND&NCE.

At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee, the School Attendance Officer read his report, and the Chair- having examined the attendance book, Mr. Ball was direc- ted to keep the same regularly entered up as to cause of ab- sences. Mr. Brierley submitted a series of questions from the Education department on the working of the Education Acts, together with answers which were given and ordered to be returned to the Education department.—The minutes Iwere signed as correct by Mr. STONE.

LHE NEW LOAN. Mr. WORSLEY reported the receipt of a communication from the Local Government Board sanctioning a lean of £5,000 for the cemetery.—Mr. MCCORQUODALE thought they applied for a loan of £6,ooo.—The CHAIRMAN ex- plained that in their application form were two columns, one headed "immediate requirements" and the other "prospective"—and the Local Government Board had only sent what was sufficient for immediate requirements. This was the only business of interest.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday, Mr W Tyrer presiding. There were also present Messrs J Leatherbarrow, J Fidler, T Dobell, J R Puckley, J Jackson, J T Hall, W 0 Ashton, J Lowe' W Birchall, E Syder, T Eatock, R Tuson, T F Hill, WSwift, J Fisher P Longton, W B Longton ; the Revs. T Chambers, T Finegan, and J Barnacle; and Mr S H Hartley (clerk).

div.head: MASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: MASTER'S REPORT.

_ The WORKHOUSE MASTER reported that there were 457 inmates in the Workhouse this week, as compared with 474 last week and 570 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 282 inmates in the hospital. Fifty-three vagrants had been relieved daring the past week, as com- pared with 71 in the corresponding period of last year.

THE ST. HELENS VAGRANT WARD. The CLERK reported as to the result of the meeting of the deputation from the St. Helens Corporation and the Guar- dians respecting the proposed vagrant ward at St. Helens. It was agreed that the clerk should be instructed to inform the Corporation that the relieving officers were empowered to hire conveyance for the removal from St. Helens to the Workhouse of any destitute wayfarer who was unable to reach the Workhouse without that assistance.—This was agreed to.

div.head: PLACED-OUT CHILDREN.
div.p: PLACED-OUT CHILDREN.

Mr. Cam/nits thought the members of the Placing-out Committee ought personally to visit the children placed out, in order to see that they were properly cared for. The Guardians, he said, were really the foster parents of these poor children. They were in locum parentis, and ought, therefore, to make personal visits.--It was, however, ex- plained that such Guardian, in whose parish children were placed out, and they were furnished with a list of the names of those children and were supposed to visit them.—The matter then dropped, Mr. Chambers promising to bring it forward again.

div.head: PROTEST FROM PRESOOT.
div.p: A PROTEST FROM PRESOOT.

The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board with respect to the sanction required from them to the borrowing of .£BOO in order to sink a well for water at the Workhouse. In the letter was included a resolution passed by the Prescot Ratepayers' Association, protesting against the expenditure owing to the fact that within a short distance of the Workhouse there were the water works of the St Helens Corporation, and also the water works of Mr. W. Longton. The Local Government Board wished to have the observations of the Guardians on this protest.— Mr. HALL asked if the Guardians could not manage their own business without outside people interfering. He sug- gested that they tell the Local Government Board that they have nothing to say about the protest, and that they could manage their own business very well. This work, he said, would save the Guardians £l3O a year.—The CHAIRMAN said unfortunately some of the Board had not seen the figures which showed that this £l3O a year would be saved. The figures had not been before the Board, and when the subject was up before the Board it was dealt with rather hastily.—Mr. HALL said he did not stand up there to make statements that were incorrect.—The CHAIRMAN had not said that, but at the same tims he considered more particu- lars ought to be given.—On tbe motion of Mr. LOWE, , seconded by Mr. JACKSON, the letter was referred to the General Purposes Committee.

div.head: LARGE DEMAND: THE COST OF THE POLICE.
div.p: A LARGE DEMAND: THE COST OF THE POLICE.

The CLERK said be had received a precept for £5102 Ils 6d, which was due on the 28th February, so that they did not need to sign the cheque at that meeting. This amount was rather less than for the corresponding period of last year; but one item of expense, that for the constabulary of the Prescot division, was very heavy. It was £2,563 2s id out of the £5,102 Ils 6d. The cost of police in that division, he said, was higher than in any other Union in the county.—Mr. CHAMBERS desired that the Press might take note of this, as he thought it ought to be known to the rate- payers.

div.head: TILE ALLEGED NEGLECT BY A BELIEVING OFFICER.
div.p: TILE ALLEGED NEGLECT BY A BELIEVING OFFICER.

The CLERK stated that Mr. Harrison, the relieving officer, charged with neglect at last meeting, had tendered his resignation to the committee appointed to inquire into the charges.—The resignation was accepted, and an order given that another relieving officer should be advertised for.
APPOINTMENT OF ORGANIST.
There were four applic tuts for the post of organist at the Workhouse Chapel. Miss A. Barton, of St. Helena, was appointed.
CATHOLIC. CHILDREN AND PANTASAPH.

The following letter was submitted :—" Gentlemen,—By a communication at the hands of your Clerk some months ago, I was informed that your Board had passed a resolu- tion to the effect not to send any more children to Panta- saph. May I humbly beg of your charity to re-consider the said resolution, and to adopt the following paragraphs as a permanent rule for dealing with the poor Catholic girls that are thrown on your hands by the hard necessity of poverty—let: All Catholic girls (now at Kirkdale Indus- trial Schools) belonging to this Union are to be transferred at once to Pantasaph. 2ad : Every Catholic girl from 3 to 14 years of age coming into the Workhouse shall ' be handed over to the care of the sisters at Pantasaph. 3rd: The Guardians allow the sisters on every child 4s per week for maintenance and 3d for education. 4th : The Clerk has orders to execute these resolutions. Allow me, gentlemen, to add the reasons which lead me to put these motions before you:—let: Every child has a strict right to be educated according to the tenets of its Creed. 2nd : The removal to Pantasaph takes from the poor child the taint of pauperism. 3rd: The education given at Pantasaph has been acknowledged repeatedly by the Guardians as excel- lent; it raises the child in its social position, enabling it to get a home in a respectable family. 4th: Pantasaph, put against Kirkdale, means a ponsiderable saving to the rate- payers.—l am, gentlernen,, respectfully yours, JAMES HENRY, S.J.—To the Board of Guardians of Presaot Union."—The meeting soon after ended.

HORRIBLE DEATH THROUGH THE BITE OE A Do,—A death from hydrophobia occurred on Tuesday afternoon at Clayton-le-Moors, near Accrington, the victim being Laur- ence Tattersall, aged 14, living in Arthur-street. The lad was bitten on the cheek by a rough-haired terrier about three months ago. The wound was slight, and nothing was thought about it till Saturday, when the lad became strangely affected. Dr. Tattersall was called in, and on Sunday two other medical men also, but were unable to render any effectual service, and the lad died in great agony. RIDING UNDER AN EXPRESS TRAIN: MIRACULOUS ESCAPE —On the arrival of the 12-45 Scotch express at Crewe Station on Thursday morning, a young man named George Adams, of Wolverhampton, was found suspended by a rope under one of the carriages. The rope had been thrown over the axle.bar, and the man had placed his head in a noose at one end and his feet M a loop at the ether. In this position be had travelled from Liverpool. He was observed by a carriage examiner, and fetched out in an exhausted condition. The dirt on his face was half an inch thick. Having sufficiently recovered, he was brought before Dr. Atkinson in the afternoon, on the charge of travelling from Liverpool without paying his fare. He said he wanted to get to Wolverhampton, bat not hav- ing sufficient money to pay for a ticket he got under the train, having previously secured a piece of rope to balance himself. He admitted that as the train flew along he be- came terribly frightened, and would have got off, but was afraid of being cut to pieces. The train travelled at such a rate that the current of air would have dislodged him from his position had he not held on to the chair. The magistrate said it was a most miraculous escape. As the prisoner ap- peared to have suffered for his foolhardiness he was let off on paying the court fees. He sensed to have been terribly shaken by his perilous adventure. THE LANCASHIRE CONGREGATIONAL

UNION. MEETING AT WARRINGTON. A meeting in connection with the Lancashire Congrega- tional Union was held at Wycliffe Church, Warrington, on Monday evening last, and was largely attended by ministers and others. Mr. William Crosfield, J P., of Liverpool, pre- sided. The Casement first referred to the circuit business meet- ing held that afternoon, and then proceeded to speak at some length of the Congregational system or organisation. That organisation had ter its motive power a brotherhood and friendliness towards one another. They met from time to time with the strongest bodies of their denomination so that they might assist those who were weaker than tbnieselves. They had that day been considering the claims of various ,churches in the West Derby ifintedred, and they bad made each grants as their best judgment showed was required. Leeemehire was sometime regarded as a purely manufactur- ing coun:ey, but he must remind them of the diversity of spheres in i'hich their Union worked. They had in one dis-, trict a group of farmers Who were helped by a grant from the Union, in another, an outlying district in the neighbour- hood of Orbeskkie, there were a party of colliers, and from a personal visit be could testify to the great-work which was being done there; People sometimes thought that colliers %dere a highly paid class of men, and that it was not expecting trio much that they should look after their own religiotes requirements, but when they remembered the class of men and what these he referred to were dOing it was their duty it? afford them help. Then there were the "chemiets "of Widnes. (Laughter.) He thought the less said about Widnes the better, because any man condemned to live itt Widnes Wanted all the help that an organisation, whether composed a religions men or or- dinary citizens, could give to him.' (Renewed laughter.), They hid also an opportunity of helplieg on the dock la- bourers of Liverpool. Having spoken Of the suburban work of the Union, and likewise of its national work by which the more wealthy contributed to the less capable counties, he concluded by earnestly commending the labours of the Union to his hearers. The Rev. S. J. BABE% of Edgehill, followed with an in- teresting and practical ad,dress on "Preaching the gospel to the outcast poor." Haying first referred to the revelations made by the pamphlet, "The bitter cry of outcast London," the articles in the Liverpool Post, by George S. Sims in the Pietortal World, on "How the poor live," and by the letters which had more receatly appeared in the Times on the subject, be said the facts which had been revealed told them that there had been growing up within the shadow of their own churches, under the very glory and pomp of their great wealth, a state of thing hardly to be compared to the days of heathen Rome. They should be members of one "another, not merely in a local sense in being members of the same church, but in the brotherhood, seeing that God had fashioned all their hearts alike. They must realise in their hearts not that they were separate atoms, but parts of the great masses about them, and those responsibilities in the eyes of Goi could never be adequately discharged until they were more fully realised by them. There must be a more distinct and aggressive effort made by the associated churches of that Union not only to extend the cause in their suburban dis- tricts, but plant with all their energy quite into the heart 1 of the neglected districts (Hear, hear.) When their poli- ticians and social reformers had done their work there was still work for the churches to do. Whilstmen brought out social or radical changes, they could not possibly effect that which the Church could do, ME., to change per- sonality and alter character. (Hear, hear.) They should consider that without that filth would be filth still. They might take a family from the slums of Liverpool and put them in a suburban villa and keep them there a week, but it would be found that they would very speedily make the villa analogous to the place where they were taken from. It was by the infusion of right and true principles in their midst by making men Christian, and by their changing their hearts, or, to use an old fashioned word, by their conversion through the instrumentality of Christian charity that the work of transformation in their lives would be finally and thoroughly effective. (Applause.) The Gospel would have to be preached—that Gospel of tender,. zees and pathos—which might change the present circuni- stances and bring about a glorious transformation in the mind and heart of man. Congregationalists had been waking up to the fact that their mission was not only to the well-to-do and cultured classes, but they had a mission distinctly to the poor and outcast ot their land. If they seriously entertained the idea that Congregationalism Was only fitted for those of the middle clasees it would be both a policy selfish and mistaken. It was true The poor you have always with you," but he feared they had been with them so long that they had almost, forgotten their presence, but the revelations which had been made ought to make their work a rieere direct one, not merely for themselves and the middle classes but a true soul-saving work, a personal evangelising work among the masses. A new departure must be made in the establish- ment of mission homes for the uplifting and elevation of the people, clubs, coffee rooms, smoke rooms and such like, and open their arms wide to receive them. (Applause.) The Rev. E. R. BABearrT, 8.A., of Norwood Chapel, Liverpool, next proceeded to speak on "church consolidation versus church extension," and in his opening remarks ob- served that although he believed in church consolidation be believed quite as much in church extension. It was said that in London alone in order to provide religious accom- modation amongst the whole of the population it was neces- sary that the church should build at once 1,500 new churches, each capable of seating 1,000 people, and there- fore the problem came how to cope with the present emergency, and provide religious ac- commodation for the growing community. lie did not think that they, as Congregationalists, were doing what they ought in this matter. To meet the 1,500 churches re- quired they, if they did their share, should provide 150, a tenth part.- They were not doing that, and worse, that whereas it was their duty to provide six new churches every year to keep pace with the growing population of London they were only providing two. It was only some kinds of church extension that he was opposed to. In certain dis- tricts where the population was small and gradually de- creasing there was a condition of things quite as lamentable and certainly humiliating as that to which he had referred. He merit to say that in many rural districts there were villages that were over-supplied with places of worship— (hear, bear)—and where too frequently there was engen- dered an unholy spirit of rivalry and antagonism, whereas by the consolidation and merging together of these separate places of worship there would be one strong, healthy church. (Applause.) He ventured to think that money had been wasted, and the fends of the central societies un- necessarily drawn upon whilst their ministers were spend- ing their energies in directions where they might be con- served and retained for a power of good. With regard to that question he did not think they—Congregationalists—had so much to complain of as other bodiet. They bad not erected in places of worship in districts where there was no room for them simply for the purpose of perpetuating or propo- gating their denomination. There was no hindrance to a wise extension so bad as the multiplication of churches in districts where there was no roam for .them. The speaker then referred in detail to districts in Derbyshire where such an overerowding of places of worship existed, and said that to sum up Derbyshire as a whole there were no less than 50,000 wasted sittings, which was equal to 200 places of worship. With a view to mitigating the evil he suggested the formation of a committee as a managing committee of representatives of various societies and churches to assist in a scheme of amalgamation. In con- elusion he said that in the face of socialism, atheism, Romanism, and other foes the great question to be asked of those seeking admission to their churches would be not "Are you a Congregationalist? " or "Are you a Presby- terian ? " or "Are you a Baptist?" but " Are you a brother " (Applause.) The Rev. P. W. DiENTON, 8.A., ef Wigan, was the next speaker, his subject being, "Pulpit and pew." In the course of his address he observed that the question was being seriously asked at the present day whether people who regu- larly wont to church and sat in their pew listening to sermons Sunday after Sunday were really the better for it, and he was inclined to think that there were many who gave that question a negative answer. There was a danger in their church going when they obtained the spiritual nutriment they required with too much ease. What was Wanted 90 much was a response in their own heart and mind to the heart and mind of the preacher. If they were not responsive they were not obtaining good, but injury, to their moral and spiritual nature. Notwith- standing, however, of all that was said that preaching was useless, and that the pulpit had lost its power, be thought I there was room for preaching yet. People loved to hear the human voice, to see the eye of the preacher kindle in its earnestness, and he did not think that ever the printed page would take the place of the voice of the preacher. When(Rear theyhea) beard Buotf fhtheeoroendwifaisonsoofmestohwoiinhogfiych x ealfseefbriesetqpeurdei:o theredo.t day, when they read of the infidelity h world church e hour lre h wantedggoo igoing, going, a it somethingd requiredan iiu t rt ao tmoreiosh ne e ft. the ehta what goodw e as of preached s o old-fashionedmucin the pulpits. lie was sure that a great change was coming over the minds of the English people on the subject, and before long they would see such changes as they hardly dreamt of seeing. and one great change would be that men would make less of going to church as a mere matter of form, but they would take the truths of the Gospel to the outcast and poor. They must make up their minds to under- stand that church going was not to be their religion. It might be a very useful thing, and so it was if they knew how to use it, but like everything else, if it was not used rightly it became a curse instead of a blessing. (Ap- plause) On the proposition of the Rev. JOHN YONGE, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman for presiding, and to the rev, gentlemen for their addresses, which haying been replied to the proceedings closed with the singing of the Doxology.

VIOLNNT ANSAci7Li IN WIDNIIB POLICE CELLS. At Widnes Police Confti on Monday, Thomas Brown, a labourer, living in idosdale, was brought up in cuitody charged with assaulting Charles Rotherham, an elderly man of respectable appearance, who lives at Ci ow Wood. On Saturday night the prisoners were taken in ct 'stody to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly, 3, nd they were put in the same cell at the police station. About midnight P.C. McM'astera inspected the cells and i'oood that all was right. At half-past one be heard crick of "Murder" and "Help" proceeding from the cell where O. se' prisoner was, and he went there. Rotherham was lying ot his back on the cell floor, and the prisoner was standing over him in a threatening attitatie. The former was re- leased from his uncomfortable position by the constable, . who discovered that he was bleeding profusely from wounds on the face, and had a black eye. Inspector Wood Ordered him to be sent te his own home at Crow Wood. —Rotherham, whose face .bore marks of ill-usage, was placed in the witness box, and stated that he gave the pri- soner no provocation whatever. The prisoner suddenly set upon himtin a ferocious manner, knocked him to the floor, and then jumped upon him several times.—The pri- soner, was fined £1 and costs, in addition to a fine of es and costs for being drunk.

II t's FX NIINER, 'SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 9,1884. LIAM LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board room on Thursday evening. There were present Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Dewhurst, Rogers, Callender, Woolley, Foster, Gibbon, Appleton, Thomason, Ridgway (clerk), and Mallard (assistant-clerk). MR. MARSH'S COMPENSATION. The CLERK said that Mr. Marsh had now expressed his willingness to accept £l3 in settlement of his claim for com- pensation—Mr. THOMASON thought that considering Mr. Marsh first asked for £2O and the Board offered him £lO, the difference had been equitably abridged.—lt was decided to accept Mr. Marsh's offer. LIMM GRAMMAR SCHOOL. The CLERK said that as the governors of the Lymm Grammar School were appointed in 187 g for a period of I five years, their term of office had now termiaated, and it was for the Board to fill the vacancies. The governors now going out of office were Mr. Dewhurst, Mr. Richard Dutton, and himself.—Mr. DEWHIMST said that perhaps the mem- bers of the Board would like to hear a report of what the governors had done daring their term of office, and how the scheme now stood. (Hear, hear.) When the present governors were appointed five years ago they had cash in hand £134 13s 4d, and they had several plots of land, the gross rental of which was about £lB5 per annum, but the land required a great deal doing at in the way of draining, Icc. If they had kept the land some yeare would have had ,to elapse before they could have made it anything like profitable. The scheine was that they should provide a house for the master and a school for 60 or 70 boys, and that they should invest about £5O a year towards the stipend of the master, and £lO per year towards the repair of the school. For the reason mentioned they offered the land for sale ha, auction, but there were no offers. All the land, how- ever, was eventually sold with the exception ofaa plot at Statham. On the 51h lust. they had in hand, in the way of investmen's, about £5,848, and a bank balance of £468, making £6,316. The governors amongst themselves, and a number of gentlemen in the parish, got up a subscription to the building fund amounting to £525, making their total funds about £6,841. In addition to this, there was a charge of £5 on the Thelwall glebe, and a plot of land at Statham which produced a gross rental of £l5. Of this about £3,000 had been authorised by the Charity Commis- sioners for laying out in master's house, schools, grounds, &c., leaving an income of bout £l4O or £l5O per annum for the expenses of the school. Ile thought that the school would be a great advantage to the parish. One of the questions had been the matter of a site for the school. Mr. J. C. Dewhurst had given the site near the eld :cricket 'ground—about l acres— and would make a new road and approaches to it from Higher-lane. The gist of it was that they would be able to. have a master's house and a school, and an income of about £l4O or £l5O per annum for the stipend of the master and the repairs of the school. If the schoolmaster had a family they would be able to accommodate about 10 or 12 boarders; if he had no family there would of course be accommoda- tion for more boarders. As far as he could learn from the Charity Commissioners the scheme of the Lymm Grammar School was now in as good a position as many of the schools.—Mr. ROGERs said that the report they had just heard was very satisfactory. If they were to compare the position ol the scheme at the beginning and its position now they would come to the conclusion that great things had been done. (Hear; hear.) He proposed that the best thanks of the Board be given to the three gentlemen for their services in connection with the school.—Mr. THOmA- soN seconded the proposition and said he thought the school would be one of the makings of Lymm.—The vote of thanks was heartily accorded, and the three retiring governors were re-elected for the ensuing five years. THE ENSUING ELECTION. The Chairman was appointed returning officer for the ensuing election. COMPLETION OF THE SEWERAGE SCHEME. Messrs. Wits:ma and MULLINER reported :—" We ex- pected to have been able to report to you that the whole of the work at Lymm would have been completed to-day. There, however, remains Some little matters yet to be finished, and by this day week we trust the whole will be finished. We have, however, forwarded you a certificate for the balance of the works, as set forth in our statement of December 3rd, a copy of which has been forwarded to the Local Government Board. This balance will be due as soon as the work is complete, and rib doubt you will retain it in hand until we are able to advise you of the comple- tion. Wears in receipt of a letter from White, Mclver and Co., of Warrington' dated February 2nd, in reference to the fences on Marsh's land, field 245. By an agreement with Captain Fox you are required to rid certain fences, and Messrs. White, Mclver Co. request that the ditches be- longing to these fences be laid with pipes; also make a pipe drain in field 242 at the foot of the sewer bank, to carry off the water which accumulates there. This will require your consideration and sanction. On January 24th there was a considerable flood in the meadows ; at the Pools the water was Mt. above its Ordinary level. At the outfall the whole of the land was covered, being about 18 inches deep at the upper end, and about 3 feet 6 inches at the lower end. The flood water was forced into waves by the action of the gale, which, continually beating on the top edges of the lower fender, has somewhat broken the same on the inner side. There are.also three small gaps in the distributing channels. Considering the force of the gale we are surprised that so little damage hes been done, and half a dozen men will repair the damage in one day. Had the fenders not been weakened by cattle the mischief would have been very slight indeed. We think that when the fenders have had a full spring and summer growth, and the grass roots well knitted, that there will be very little damage done in future floods. We are also pleased to find that the flood water very soen drains away through the soil, showing that the soil is capable of perfect downward filtration. On February 2nd the land was again flooded, being enly about six inches lower than the flood of Janualy 24th. No further damage was done by this flood. We have examined the whole length of the new sewers by means of a lamp suspended in the lampholes, which in every case 'we have been able to see from the next manholes. This, of course, does not apply to a few small lengths where the bends have been unavoidable, as for instance along the brook between the canal and flour mill. The work generally, we are pleased to say, appears satisfac- tory, and Mr. Brazendale has evidently done his best to ensure a good job. The contractor will be liable for the maintenance of the work for a term of six months, dating from the present certificate, and will have to make good all damages or faults in the work he has done under this con- tract. He will repair the fenders and the channels at the outfall next week. We may here remark that the fences belonging to adjoining owners are not yet repaired. The automatic flushing chamber on Rush Green is acting very, well, but as it has had but little effect at present on the Rush Green sewer, we are of opinion that there most be some solid obstruction at the old flushing chamber. This yet requires to be opened up and made good. We have examined Pepper-street, op- posite Mr. Lawrence's house, and taken some levels there with a view to deviating the sewer and avoiding cutting through Mr. Lawrence's garden. Our levels show that we can extend the sewer along Pepper-street te the watercourse, and then into Mr. Rewhurst's land by raising Pepper-street for a short length, about 18 inches, and at the same time keeping the sewer rather lower. There is, there- fore, no difficulty in making the required deviation. On February 4th we examined the field belong- ing to Mr. Fairclough, through which ths line of sewer has been cut t The spring is now within live inches of its former level, and we see no particular damage done to the land. A manhole and lamp- hole we have ordered to be lowered down to the ground level, they standing rather high at present, but the manhole in the corner adjoining Mr. Jackson's land we should require to stand abova the surface as at present, lobe above flood level. This is generally a waste corner. The contractor has got to the subsoil drain, disturbed by the sewer. This will be done at once. We also inspected the field occupied by Mr. Hutchinson. There is a little soil to remove, and this will be required. At the tenant's request we lowered the mound over the sewer trench soon after the sewer was laid, the result being that the filling of the trench having naturally settled, the trench is now rather hollow, and requires filling again. We have also ' arranged to have the metal lamphole cover sunk to the sur- face of the flag. Since the above report was written we have received a letter from Mr. Brazendal saying the con- tract work will be completed by to-night, and that he would repair the damige to the outfall works to-day." MB. FAIRCLOUGH'S CLAIM. • The CLERK stated that Mr. John Fairclough had given notice that he intends to submit his claim to arbitration, and that he bad appointed Mr. William Owen, of Warrington, as his arbitrator. It was necessary for the Board, in the interest of their own business, to appoint another arbitrator. If they did not appoint one, Mr. Owen would act as sole arbitrator.—The Board resolved to appoint Mr. John White, of Warrington, as their arbitrator, and the Clerk was em- powered to take such steps as were necessary in the Board's interest. THE BOARD AND THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME. The Chairman and the Clerk had had an interview with the solicitors to the promoters of tne Ship Canal scheme, and the results of some exceptions were satisfactory. Several 'clauses were submitted to the Board by the Clerk, and subject to certain altarations by him were ap- proved.

div.head: WEsLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.
div.p: WEsLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.

RUNCORN BRANCH. The annual meeting of the Runcorn. Branch of the Wesleyan Home Missions was held last evening in St. Paul's Chapel, Runcorn. There was a good audience, Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst presided, and there were also present the Revs. E. J. Robinson, Simpson, Johnson, Geo. ',Hack, Hughes, and Evans; Messrs. T. Norman, T. Simieter, H. Randle, and Dobson (of Liverpool.)—The Rev. Gao. Hack read the report for the past year, describing the objects of the Mission and the work it accomplished. The income for the year, ending withlbe conference of 1883, was £34,921 Os. 7d., and the expenditure during the same time; was £35.203 4.1. 10d. Mete was therefore a deficiency on the • year of £282 41. 3d. Towards the income the Run- corn c rouit contribt tsd £63 9s. Cid. last year. (Applause.)— The Chairman expressed his pleasure at being present that evening, and went on to say that there was scarcely any- thing that affected thi national welfare in any appreciable degree that was not connected with Home Missions. What a glorious effect upon Home Missions the Queen's speech of last Tuesday would have! The paragraph relating to county government and the regulation of traffic in intoxi- cating liquor—(hear, hear)—and the paragraph relating to the promotion of education, which concerned the national welfare, also concerned their Home Missions. Christ's kingdom was naturally advancing in the form of piety. It I was advancing in education, in sanitary science, in art and sciences, and in the general brotherhood of humanity. A better social feeling existed now than existed 100 years ago. In all these things Christ's kingdom was surrounding the kingdom of the enemy. What influences for good they had in Britain. He did not know that there was any more p)tent influence for good than that strong feeling of liberty ttat every Englishman had. (Hear, hear.) We had the greatest liberty of any nation of the world. Then what good men we had in England! (Hear, hear.) What a good man stood at the head of the Oovernment—(applause)—and what better guarantee could they have that the principles , of Christianity would be the basis of our Government. (Hear, hear.) Then the Royal Family was a great in- fluence for good in Britain. He believed that the Queen had exercised an influence on the Court more virtuous and pure than Was ever exercised by any king or queen that had ever sat upon the throne. With a good man at the bead of affairs, and a royal house that would maintain the purity of the Court, and with the deep feeling of religion that pervaded almost down to the lowest class of society—because with all the evil that existed, he believed that a substratum of good was working its way to the surface than had ever been in times past—and with these measures coming before the House of Commons this session, he thought he might fairly say that the Home Missions were in a most prosperous and vigorous state, and they might well take courage for Christianity in England. (Applause.) Mr. Dobson then delivered an address, in which he des- cribed his experience as a missionary in Liverpool, in graphic language. Other speeches followed. CATHOLIC SOIREE AT WARRINGTON. In aid of the new organ fund, the fifth annual soiree in connection with St. Mary's Catholic Church, Butter- market-street, was held in the Public Hall, on Wednesday evening. The attendance was very large, and the gathering proved a great success Evidently no pains had been spared to add to the comfort and pleasure of the visitors, and the hall looked attractive after the careful decoration it underwent. The gallery front was draped with scarlet cloth, at intervals being flags and shields in the form of trophies; while festooned cur- tains adorned the pillars supporting the gallery, and in the orchestra were a number of rare plants. Dancing commenced about nine o'clock, Mr. Maskell's quadrille band having been engaged for the occasion. One of the principal features of the programme were two leap-year dances— lancers and quadrilles—in which the ladies had the choice of partners, and in which a lady also officiated as M.C. The stewards were Messrs T Mather, T Lythgoe, George Tomlinson, Joseph Williams, William Allen, and Edward Caldwell, while Mr Joseph Dolan efficiently performed the duties of M.C., except in the two leap-year dances pre- viously mentioned. The refreshments were supplied by Mr. Booth, of Buttermarket-street, and Mr Clarke was left in charge of that dapartment. At Liverpool Assizes on Thursday, Margaret Smith (39), of no occupation, was indicted for having, at Windle, on the 17th ult., stolen AEI overcoat, the property ot Caleb Greenhalgh. The prisoner, who was an old offiender, was sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment with hard la- bour.

NEGLECT OF FAMILY, &c.—Michael Glynn, a labourer of Widnes, was, on Tuesday, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, sent to gaol for one month for deserting his wife.—Nathan Banner, who also belonged to Widnes, was ordered, at the same court, to pay is. 61. towards the maintenance of his mother, at Present in the hospital of the Prescot Union Workhonse.—Edward Lewis, of St. Helens, but at present working at Widnes, was committed to gaol for six weeks for neglecting te comply with the order of the Bench to contribute towards the support of his aged mother.

THE NEW INN AND ITS LICNNSE.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, Mr. J. G. Swift applied on behalf of the owners for a temporary transfer of the license of the New Inn, Liverpool-street, from Arthur Gregory Asling to Joseph James—Superintendent Johnston said the man James was a perfectly respectable man, but the grounds on which he objected to that transfer were that Asling, the present holder of the license, who was not about just now, had been convicted at that court a few weeks ago for per- mitting gambling in his house. He was fined in three , penalties of £lO and costs each, and his license was en- dorsed twice. There was an appeal pending in the case, and he objected to the transfer of that license until after the appeal in April next.—Mr. Swift said that Aiding had dis- appeared, and so far as he could see the appeal wsuld not be prosecuted. The owners were liable for the payment of the fines, and as the whole of the expenses they would incur in the Case would probably be from £l2O to £l5O, he thought the Bench would consider they had been punished heavily enough for unwittingly placing an unreliable man in the house.—After a little discussion the application was granted by the Bench.

PRESCOT Monw.ky BOARD—The monthly meeting of this amid was held in the Board-room, Prescot, on Tuesday morning last. There were present Messrs. W. Lowe (in the chair), J. Newton, J. Leatherbarrow, T. Pilkington, and R. Tyrer.—.The Surveyor (Mr. Goldsworth) submitted a statement of his expenditure for the five weeks ending January 31st, 1884, whidh was as follows :—Bold £39 5s 61, Knowsley £29 Os 6id, B.iinhili £lB 35 10d, Whiston £l9 4s 6,1, team labour £66 14s 11f1, new materials £34 55 9d, incidentals £22 43 Be, total £228 19s 914—The Chairman said the first business for the Board to consider was the notice of motion that a treasurer to the Board be appointed at that meeting.—The Clerk (Mr. Cross) said the only ap- plication for the treasurership was by Mr. G. Cochrane, the newly-appointed manager at the Prescot branch of Parr's Bank.—Mr. Leatherbarrow complained of the war Parr's Banking Company had treated the Board in not letting them know of the resignation of their late manager, who was treasurer of the Board till so long after it bad taken place. fie therefore moved that Mr. Cochrane should be appointed only till the end of the Board's financial year, the 25th March, when the treasurership should be further considered. lie Mr. Leatberbarrow) also mentioned that a Stanch of the Manchester and Salford Bank would shortly ' be established in Prescot.—This proposal was, however, not seconded.—Mr. Tyrer then moved, and Mr. Newton seconded, that Mr. Cochrane be appointed treasurer without any restriction as to the period of his •treasurership. This pro- posal was carried, Mr. Leatherbarrow only voting against it.—The remainder of the business was routine.

div.p: A WARNING TO TRESPASSERS:

It was decided that a person be appointed to watch the ontfall field on Sundays, and that the first person who is found trespassing thereon be prosecuted, in order that it may act as a deterrent to others. There was no other business of public interest.

HAVING IT OUT.—TWO men named Patrick Donnolly and Philip McKay were on Friday charged, at the St. Helers Police Court, with haying committed a breach of the peace. —lt was stated by two officers that they had been called into a lodging house on Greenbank, and on going into the back yard they saw the two defendants stripped and fight- ing. Donnollv's shirt waS almost torn to pieces.—They were each bound over to keep the peace for three months. -

ABUSING HOSPITALITY.—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, a girl, named Margaret Halph• son, was charged with stealing a pair of boots, the property of Thomas Moore, Denton's Green-lane' on the let instant. The prisoner had goner on that day to Mr. Moore's house and had tea there. After she had gone out the boots were missed, and it was afterwards ascertained that she had pawned them for is. GI. at Mr. Houghton's, pawnbroker.__ z•he had, it appeared, been before convicted of a similar offence, and was now sent to gaol for 14 days.

STOCK AND SHARE MARKET. Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 1:', Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Feb. 7th):--

We have once more to record lower prices prevailing as a rule in the leading markets, the further depreciation being attributeable to several and various causes, but all having the effect of helping the downward movement. The revelations in the case of the recent large failure have produced much uu- easiness-in the market. Railway traffics are unhealthy, and the advance in the Bank Rate all combine to restrict busi- ness and depress values, and the natural result thus followed. Foreign Funds too are dull, but the declines here are not severe except in Egyptians. a fall which is not to be , wondered at 'in the present state of affairs in that country. Unifiei are l to 2, pref. to j, and Daira Banieh lf lower. Italians. Spanish, and Turks stamped to are little down, whilst Mexican 3 per cent. and Russians are each the turn better. Mexican railways have not had much attention, and with another large decrease in trafficquote down on the week. The total of business in miscellaneous investments is moderate, and indeed fairly good compared with the record for some weeks lately past, and prices on the whole show better figures marked In the majority of the alter- ations, but some of the classes are distinctly changed both for and against.

Peter Graney (19), labourer, James Kearns (17), tabourer, and Thomas Davies (18), labourer, were, at the Liverpool Assizes this week, indicted for having, at Windie, on the 25th ult., stolen 481bs of bones, the property of John Cart- wright. Graney and Kearns were found guilty and sen- tenced, the former to four months and the latter to two months' imprisonment. Davies was discharged. KILLED AT Sr. HELENs.—On Tuesday morning an in- quest was, opened by Coroner Brighouse, at the Crescent Hotel, St. Helels, regarding the death of Wm. Maddocks, aged 35, who lived in Playthian-street, and was a shunter employed at Messrs. Bibby and Sons, Copper Works, Raven- head. On Saturday afternoon he was engaged in shunting operations when be fell, and was run over and killed by some waggons. The inquest was adjourned for the atten- dance of the Gpvernvnent Inspector of Factories till Thurs- day next. The Rev. F. R. Lee presided, and the following members gave songs and recitations to enliven the proceedings of the evening. The Misses Ada Bixter, Lucy Mercer, Fair- hurst, Mereditiv, and Masters W. Case, W. Dever, S. Waine, A. Hoyt, James Naylor, C. Bixter, and C. Johnson. The meeting was closed with hymn and prayer, after which several new members joined the society. LATEST NE WS.

' THE SOUDAN. LATEST PARTICULARS.—A despatch from Paris yesterday morning, says the cdrresposdent of the Figaro states that General Gordon was made prisoner by the Asbmarich tribe at two hours' march from Koroso. At the War Office yes- terday, no confirmation had been received of the report of the capture of General Gordon. A state of siege has been proclaimed at Suakim.

An Egyptian steamer has arrived from Massowah. She brings news to Baker that the rebellion is extending from Kassala, on the Abyssinian frontier, to the Red Sea. Abyssinia itself is perfectly quiet, hut the frontier terri- tory is declaring for the rebels, with whom the so-called friendly tribes are now co-operating. The conduct of the friendly tribms is apparently determined by the policy of the abandonment. The religious revival will now become more widespread and formidable than ever. The Central News says vague rumours were again in cir- culation in London yesterday of some mishap to General Gordon; but not the slightest credence was attached to them by the Government, whose advices from Cairo—which are ample and continuous—give no hope of good or bad news of Gordon for some time to come. It is considered almost certain that the first news of General Gordon will come from Berber,:for which town he is now making, and it is confi- dently believed that it will take the form of a tale- -1 gram from the gallant officer himself announ- cing his arrival. The fact that telegraphic communication :with Berber is again open, and is accepted according to ad vices from Cairo, as a hopeful augury of the friendly disposition of the tribes on Gordon's line of march ; and the arrival at Berber yesterday of a vessel from Khartoum, whilst disposing of many alarmist reports which have been current for weeks past, afford satisfactory grounds for the hope frequently expressed, in quarters best qualified to judge, that once General Gordon has passed safely through the desert to Berber his further progress to Khartoum will not be accompanied by very serious risk. Meanwhile excitement rune high in political circles, and rumours are current of formidable secessions from the Liberal ranks and of coalitions against the Government. Telegrams fro.n the Mediterranean state that the Monarch and the Rods have already sailed for Suakin with reinforce- ments; and other instructions from Whitehall are being followed at Malta with energy and promptitude. In the home dockyards and garrisons official orders are being also rapidly executed. The Chatham contingent of marines paraded this afternoon, fully eqaippeci for service in Egypt, although the order was received less than 24 hours previously. This fine body of men, numbering about 200, will start for Portsmouth this morning for embarkation on the hired transport Poonah. It is confidently believed at Chatham that at least a couple of companies of engineers will be required for Egypt, and preparations are being made accordingly at Aldershot. Orders have been received to bring various regiments to service strength, and this neces- sary work is being proceeded with all despatch. At Sheer- ness Her Majesty's ship myrmidon, commander Alfred Carpenter, recently commissioned for service in the Red Sea will be taken out of deck to•day upon the completion of her refit. Her officers and crew of 112 men have already taken possession, and the vessel will leave for Suez to-day, proceeding thence to Suakim if required. Within the last few days numerous applications have been received at the Horse Guards from officers volunteering for service in Egypt, but the 2entral News is authorised to state that up to the present moment no demand has been made by Sir Evelyn Wood for more English officers, nor is any such request anticipated.

SENTENCE ON A SOCIALIST.—John Neve has been sen- tenced, at Berlin, to six months' imprisonment for dis- tributing large numbers of copies of the Freiheit in various places in Germany. Neve, it will be remembered, was manager of that journal during its existence in London. DEATH OF MR. SCCDAMORE.—Mr. Frank Ives Scuda- more, well known in connection with the purchase of the telegraphs in England by the Government, in the arrange- ments for which he took a prominent part' is dead. Mr. Scudamore had in recent years been engaged in the work of reorganising the Turkish Post Office. I LATEST FROM MADAGASCAR—TWO companies of colonial troops arrived at Tamatave from Reunion, on the 6th inst., and on the 14th the French made reconnaissance, but met with firm opposition from the Malagasy forces. The United States war vessel Pensacola arrived here from Batavia, on the 18th instant, and left again for the south coast of Mada- gascar. The British Consul left here, on the 22nd instant, on board Her Majesty's corvette Tourmaline for Mahanaro and the southern coast. SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHESHIRE GENTLEMAN—Dr. Churton held an inquest at Malpas yesterday morning on the body of Mr. Rasbottom, a well-known country gentle- man living near Malpas. Mr. Rasbottom had attired him- self in hunting costume for the purpose of attending a meeting of the Cheshire hounds at Alderley, and while sitting at the breakfast table fell forward and died almost immediately. A verdict of death from natural causes was returned.

MR. BRADLAUGH.—The Central News understands that the paragraph in the London newspapers yesterday morning respecting Mr. Bradlaugh's intention is unauthorised, and purely conjectural. Mr. Bradlaugh says his course of action will depend entirely upon circumstances. The Cen- tral News learns that until the Bradlaugh incident termi- nates the public will be excluded on Monday from Palace- yard, and persons with petitions to present in favour of Mr. Bradlaugh will not be permitted to admittance beyond Westminster Hall.

A SOCIETY BREACH OF PROMISE CASE. The Globe hears from an authoritative source that the courts of law are likely soon to be engaged in hearing a breach of promise case in which Miss Finney, herterlmewn as Miss Fortescue, of the Savoy Theatre, is the plaintiff, and Lord Garmoyle, the eldest son of Earl Cairns, is the defendant. All attempts at a compromise it is said have failed, the lady being de- sirous to bring her case before the public, and so large a sum as £lO,OOO in settlement has recectly been refused by her. Miss Fortescue is likely soon to rei urn to the stage. Mr. H. Winch, of the Middle Temple. is retained by the plaintiff, and the forensic ability of Mr. Russell will also, the Globe believes, aid her cause.

MISCELLAIEOI7B.—The ATTORNEY-GE/ORAL, replying to Mr. Norwood, said the Lord Chancellor had ander considera- tion a plan for reducing the number of judges going circuit, and thns facilitating the business in the High Court of Justice.—Lerd Frrzmaratton, replying to Mr. Magniac, said it was not intended to make a survey of the presedt dimen- sions of Suez.—Mr. MAGNIAC gave notice to call attention to the subject.—Mr. BANNERMANN, replying to Sir J. Hay, said that besides the thousand men who were on the road, and who were not time expired men, five hundred more had been ordered from Malta to reinforce Admiral Hewitt's force at Suakim.—Mr. TREVELYAN, replying to Mr. sexton, said that since the suspension of Lord Rossrnore no magistrate in Ireland had imitated his example. If anyone did so the Government knew how to act._

A PROPOSED LOAN TO THE KHEDIVE,—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir H. Dyke, read letters from Earl Granville to Sir N. Rothschild, saying that he learnt that Mr. Vincent had applied to him (Rothschild) for a loan of one million, that Sir E. Baring approved of it, and that the Government would be glad if Rothschild was able to come to some agree- ment with the Khedive, and to settle conditions with him. THE VOTE OP CENSDRE.—Mr. GLADSTONE trusted the adjourned debate would be so arranged as to enable the vote of censure to be poposed by Sir S. Northcote, to come on on Tuesday. It was a motion that ought to be taken speedily. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. PARNELL, who moved his amendment censuring the policy of the Executive Government in Ireland. He insisted that the result of the visit of Sir S. Northeote to Ireland had been civil distur- bance, and the perpetration of outrage by the Orange party. He contended that the visit had been a political misfortune for the party of which the right hon. baronet was a leader, i for he had by his conduct n Ulster dragged that party at the heels of a defeated and discredited faction in Ireland. He passed a general condemnation on the oratory of the Orange platform during the late attempt to introduce the National League into Ulster. He severely censured the suppression of public meetings and free speech of the Nationalists, whilst the Orangemen were allowed full pos- session of their rights. The Orange movement in the North of Ireland, he insisted, was unconstitutional ; that it was violent, seditious, and intimidatory ; and that every person, from the chief leaders down to the poorest bandsmen, who took part in it were open to persecution. Having passed a general condemnation of the conduct of Lord Rossmore, he concladed;by moving his amendment which deplored the wanton prohibition of legal public meetings and free speech to Ireland, and bondemned the executive for having permitted bodies of magistrates to make with impunity public dcelarations applauding the conduct of Lord Ross- more, an ex-magistrate, superseded for disturbing order and provoking and strife between different classes of her Majesty's subjects, which public declarations had directly incited her Majesty's subjects in Ireland to Illegal acts, disorder, and violence.—Viscount Cum:crow defended the conduct of Lord Rossrnore, and insisted that the dismissal from the magistracy was most unjust, and insisted that a Royal Commission, as in the case of the Earl of Roden, should be appointed to inquire into the whole subject.— Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN insisted that the conduct of the Orangemen in Ireland had caused most of the disturbances that had occurred there of late, and he called upon Lord Claud Hamilton to justify in that Legislature, and before the people of England, the incendiary harrangues he had delivered in the North of Ireland. Sir IL BRUCE defended the conduct of Lord Rossmore, and insisted that the loyalty of the people of the North to the crown of England was undoubted.—Mr. O'BRIEN condemned the action of the Irish executive as an attempt .to sup- press the liberties of one portion of her Majesty's subjects in Ireland.

FIRE AT ECCLESTON Hata..—On Wednesday night a firs broke out at Eccleston Hall, the residence of Mr. J. C. Harvey. The floor of an upper drawing room and a portion of a wooden casing of the room took fire, but on the arrival of the fire-engine from St. Helens the flames were quickly extinguished, not much damage having been done. S. HELENS CAFE AND RECREATION COMPANY: ANNTILL MEETING.—The annual ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of this company was held in the Market Tavern, St. Helens, on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by Alderman Cook, and there were also present Dr. Mc- Nicholl, Messrs. H. Martin, C. Sharpies, W. Middleharst, B. W. Leach, E. Burgess, Pennington, and several others. The annual report of the directors stated that the amount of business done had been a little in excess of that of pre- vious years. The nett profits of the company for the year amounted to £217 5s 3d, which, together with the balance brought from last year, made a total of 023 2s 10d. The directors recommended that a dividend of £lO per cent. on the called-up capital be paid, and in addition a bonus of 15 per share (both free of income tax), which, with interest on the portion of the capital which had been subscribed to anticipation of calls, would absorb the sum of £202 fle, leaving a balance of £l2O 13s 10d to be carried forward to next year. The report was adopted. Ibe retiring directors, Mr D. McKechnie, Mr. W. Middlehurst, Mr. J. B. Leach, and Mr. H. Martin, were re-elected, as was also the auditor, Mr. J. W. Pickton. The usual votes of thanks were passed. TRH DROWNING CASE AT Sr. HELENS. Last Fridal morning an inquest was held at the Whiston workhouse Dy Coroner Brighouse, respecting the death of Mary 51,/§/evio, the circumstances of which we gave last week. It appeared from additional particulars given at the inquest that the de- ceased was the wife of William M‘iNeyin, who lodges at the aeorge Hotel. St. Helens. They had not, however, lived together for the last eight years. About 12 o'clock on Mon. day night last week she was seen by P.C. Stalker in Camp- bell-street, St. Helens, apparently under the influence of drink. About an hour after that a man named W. M. Bew-. ley, of 27, Random-street, was alarmed by cries of "Murder" from the direction of the brook, and on going to the Vet ' these noises came from he found deceased in the water where which was mot more than three feet deep at the place. He was assisting her out when P.C. Stalker also came up, and ; together they carried her to the police station. She was very drunk and cursed and swore all the way. In falling down the banks of the brook her head and face were badly cut, and after receiving medic 41 aid she was taken to the workhouse.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned, and the jury added a recommendation that the brook in ques- tion be properly fenced.
